He has had four bloody stools in the past 12 hours, severe abdominal cramping, and minimal vomiting. Temperature is 37.8 °C, heart rate 110/min; he appears mildly dehydrated.
Previously well child with no chronic medical problems, no recent antibiotics, and no international travel. Immunisations up to date. No sick contacts at school.

Initial labs: white cell count 9.6 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 124 g/L, platelets 280 × 10^9/L, creatinine 38 µmol/L. Stool microscopy shows numerous fecal leukocytes. Stool culture yielded gram‑negative bacilli that grew on MacConkey agar; an enzyme immunoassay detected a protein toxin that inhibits protein synthesis in cultured Vero cells.
Abdominal ultrasound performed to exclude intussusception shows segmental thickening of the descending colon wall with preserved peristalsis and no free fluid.
Parents report the child ate a hamburger at a local fair 48 hours before symptom onset; other family members who ate the same food remained well.

explanation: The diagnosis is Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli. The acute onset of severe abdominal cramping and bloody stools after eating a hamburger, the presence of fecal leukocytes, and detection of a protein toxin that inhibits protein synthesis in Vero cells are characteristic of Shiga toxin producing E. coli and distinguish it from non-toxigenic bacterial causes. Shiga toxin can damage renal endothelium and predispose young children to hemolytic uremic syndrome, which is a key complication to watch for after STEC infection.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with a 2-week history of watery, foul-smelling diarrhoea and post-prandial bloating. She notes four to six loose, greasy stools per day, crampy periumbilical pain but no visible blood or high fever, and an unintentional 4 kg weight loss. On exam she is afebrile, mildly cachectic, with soft, non-tender abdomen and hyperactive bowel sounds.

She returned 3 weeks ago from a 3-week backpacking trip in the Himalayas. She reports multiple days of drinking water from mountain streams and using rustic hostels with shared toilets. No recent antibiotics, no chronic medical conditions, no immunosuppressive medications.

Complete blood count: haemoglobin 125 g/L, WBC 6.2 × 10^9/L. CRP 3 mg/L. Stool culture negative for enteric bacteria; stool microscopy shows no faecal leukocytes and a qualitative faecal fat test is markedly positive.
Abdominal ultrasound and non-contrast CT performed to exclude inflammatory or obstructive causes are both unremarkable, without bowel-wall thickening, lymphadenopathy, or biliary pathology.

Two other hikers who drank from the same unfiltered streams developed similar prolonged, greasy, foul-smelling diarrhoea without fever; symptoms in this patient improved substantially after a single course of nitroimidazole therapy prescribed empirically by a travel clinic physician.

explanation: This is giardiasis caused by Giardia lamblia producing chronic malabsorptive, greasy diarrhoea after freshwater exposure. The prolonged foul-smelling, fatty stools with postprandial bloating and weight loss after drinking unfiltered mountain stream water, absence of fever and fecal leukocytes, a positive fecal fat test, and rapid response to nitroimidazole are all typical of Giardia and not of invasive bacterial enteritis. Giardia is a flagellated protozoan that adheres to the small intestinal mucosa causing fat malabsorption and is best diagnosed by stool antigen testing or repeated microscopy because cyst shedding can be intermittent.

hints.text: A 3-year-old boy is brought by his mother with 10 days of bulky, pale, foul-smelling loose stools occurring several times per day and poor appetite. Parents note he has not gained weight as expected and is more irritable; there is no high fever or bloody diarrhoea. On exam he is afebrile, mildly pale, with a soft, mildly distended abdomen and otherwise normal cardiorespiratory exam.

He recently started at a new daycare 2 weeks ago; two other children at the centre have similar prolonged loose stools. He has no chronic medical problems, has not received recent antibiotics, and has normal developmental milestones for his age.

CBC: haemoglobin 115 g/L, WBC 7.8 × 10^9/L. CRP <5 mg/L. Stool bacterial culture negative; stool exam shows increased fat and no faecal leukocytes. A point-of-care stool antigen test performed at the clinic returns positive for a single intestinal protozoan antigen.
Plain abdominal radiograph obtained to evaluate persistent symptoms shows no obstruction or bowel dilatation; abdominal ultrasound is normal without intussusception or masses.

Child was treated with a 5-day course of oral nitroimidazole; diarrhoea frequency decreased markedly within 48 hours and appetite improved. Repeat stool antigen testing four weeks after treatment is negative and weight trajectory has normalized.

explanation: This presentation is giardiasis causing malabsorptive, fatty diarrhea and failure to thrive in a toddler. Bulky, pale, foul smelling stools with increased fecal fat, absence of fever or fecal leukocytes, daycare exposures with other affected children, a positive stool antigen, and rapid improvement after a nitroimidazole all point to Giardia lamblia rather than bacterial or inflammatory causes. Giardia is a flagellated protozoan that adheres to the small intestinal mucosa causing fat malabsorption, and its cysts are hardy in cold water which facilitates person to person and waterborne transmission in settings like daycares.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man with COPD presents with 3 days of fever, pleuritic right‑sided chest pain, and increasing productive cough with green sputum. He had an influenza‑like illness 10 days earlier that briefly improved then worsened. He is an active smoker and uses an inhaled corticosteroid.

No known immunodeficiency. Lives with adult family; his toddler granddaughter had purulent conjunctivitis and an ear infection two weeks ago. He received seasonal influenza vaccine last season; no recent travel or hospitalisation.

On arrival: temperature 38.6°C, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 91% on room air. Blood tests: WBC 15.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 12.6 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L. Sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils and small pleomorphic Gram‑negative coccobacilli; blood cultures pending.
Chest radiograph demonstrates a dense lobar consolidation of the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and no pleural effusion.

Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone plus oral azithromycin was given; he defervesced and oxygen requirement fell within 48 hours. Sputum culture later grew a fastidious small coccobacillus on chocolate agar but not on plain blood agar unless plated adjacent to Staphylococcus aureus, supporting identification of a mucosal respiratory Gram‑negative coccobacillus.

explanation: This is acute lobar pneumonia due to Haemophilus influenzae, most consistent with a nonencapsulated respiratory strain complicating COPD after a viral prodrome. The sputum shows many neutrophils and small pleomorphic gram negative coccobacilli, the organism grew only on chocolate agar and displayed satellitism next to Staphylococcus aureus indicating a requirement for X and V factors, and the clinical setting of COPD and recent influenza like illness favors H. influenzae over other Gram negative pathogens. Non typeable H. influenzae lacks a polysaccharide capsule and commonly causes mucosal infections such as COPD exacerbations and otitis media, while encapsulated type b strains were classically associated with invasive diseases like epiglottitis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old male software engineer presents with 6 months of intermittent epigastric burning pain, worse at night and often relieved by meals. Last week he noticed dark, tarry stools and one episode of lightheadedness on standing. He takes occasional over-the-counter aspirin for tension headaches and drinks coffee daily.

He was born and raised in a crowded household in Southeast Asia and emigrated at age 12. No chronic medical conditions, no regular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug prescriptions, no prior endoscopies, and no recent courses of antibiotics. No alcohol excess and no known liver disease.
Haemoglobin 104 g/L, MCV 74 fL, white cell count 6.4 × 10^9/L, ferritin 8 µg/L. Two separate stool guaiac tests were positive. Serum C-reactive protein 2 mg/L.

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrates a single 15 mm anterior duodenal ulcer with a clean base and surrounding mucosal erythema; multiple gastric and duodenal biopsy specimens were obtained at the procedure.

A rapid urease test on a gastric biopsy turned positive within minutes. He was treated with a proton-pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics for 14 days; at 8-week follow-up his epigastric pain had resolved and a urea breath test was negative.

explanation: This case represents active Helicobacter pylori infection causing a duodenal ulcer with associated iron deficiency anemia and occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Chronic epigastric pain worse at night and relieved by meals, endoscopic identification of a duodenal ulcer, a positive rapid urease test on biopsy, and positive stool guaiac with low ferritin point to H. pylori as the causal factor rather than simple NSAID injury alone. H. pylori produces abundant urease which raises local pH and underlies diagnostic tests such as the rapid urease and urea breath tests that detect active infection.

hints.text: A 22-year-old university student presents to urgent care with 4 days of fever to 38.9°C, severe throat pain and difficulty swallowing. He has drooling and has eaten very little; on inspection there are numerous painful multiple small ulcers on the anterior gingiva and buccal mucosa and erythematous, swollen lips. He has tender bilateral submandibular lymphadenopathy and appears mildly dehydrated.

No chronic illnesses and not on medications. He reports no prior episodes like this. Two weeks earlier he kissed a new partner who had a crusted vesicle at the lip margin; he recalls the partner’s lesion appeared shortly before they met. No recent travel, no sexual symptoms elsewhere.

Full blood count: white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L with a normal neutrophil predominance; C-reactive protein 24 mg/L. A scraping from an oral lesion stained on-site showed epithelial cells with multinucleation and nuclear changes consistent with a viral cytopathic effect.

Close oral-photograph by the clinician demonstrates multiple small, shallow ulcers clustered on the attached gingiva and inner lower lip mucosa with surrounding erythema and a yellowish fibrinous base; no single large necrotic lesion.

Empiric oral antiviral therapy was started; within 48 hours his fever resolved, oral pain decreased and ulcers began to crust. A PCR assay of a lesion swab later returned positive for an enveloped, linear double-stranded DNA virus that produced the multinucleated epithelial cells seen on scraping.

explanation: The diagnosis is Herpes simplex virus 1. The acute onset of numerous small painful ulcers on the gingiva after exposure to a partner with a lip lesion, the presence of multinucleated epithelial cells on lesion scraping, positive PCR for an enveloped double stranded DNA virus, and rapid clinical response to antivirals all support HSV-1 over aphthous stomatitis or enteroviral herpangina. HSV-1 is an enveloped double stranded DNA virus that produces multinucleated giant cells on cytology and then establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion, which predisposes to recurrent cold sores.

hints.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with 3 days of progressive left eye pain, photophobia, tearing and blurred vision. She notes foreign-body sensation and worsening pain with bright light. Visual acuity in the affected eye has fallen from baseline; there is unilateral ciliary injection but no systemic fever.

She is otherwise healthy, uses soft contact lenses intermittently and admits to wearing them overnight the night before symptom onset. She also reports recurrent painful vesicular lesions at the left lip margin during prior febrile illnesses, last episode several months ago. No diabetes or immunosuppression.

Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining reveals a branching, linear epithelial defect on the corneal surface with terminal bulb-like endings; there is minimal stromal infiltration and no hypopyon.
Corneal scrapings were obtained. Light microscopy showed multinucleated epithelial cells; bacterial cultures remained sterile. PCR of the corneal swab detected an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus.

Topical antiviral therapy was initiated promptly; within 48–72 hours pain and photophobia improved and the epithelial defect began to epithelialize. No response was seen to initial empirical antibacterial drops prior to antiviral initiation.

explanation: The diagnosis is Herpes simplex virus 1. The classic branching linear corneal epithelial defect with terminal bulbs on fluorescein staining, multinucleated epithelial cells on microscopy, PCR detection of an enveloped double stranded DNA virus, and prior orolabial herpetic lesions point to HSV-1 rather than bacterial contact lens keratitis or other viral causes. HSV-1 establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion and recurrent reactivation at the cornea is a leading infectious cause of corneal scarring and vision loss.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency clinic with 72 hours of severe vulvar pain, burning dysuria and a fever of 38.2 °C. Examination shows multiple small, clustered clear vesicles on an erythematous base over the labia majora and introitus with bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy; she is unable to sit comfortably because of the pain.

She reports this is the first time she has had genital lesions. No chronic medical conditions, not pregnant, no routine medications, and HIV test two years ago was negative. She describes a systemic prodrome (malaise, low-grade fever) that began 24 hours before the skin lesions appeared.

Complete blood count shows leukocytes 12.4 × 10^9/L. Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Microscopy from a lesion scrape demonstrates multinucleated epidermal giant cells; nucleic-acid amplification from a vesicle swab detects viral DNA of an enveloped double-stranded DNA pathogen that preferentially infects mucocutaneous epithelium.

Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound performed to exclude a deeper pelvic process shows normal adnexa and no fluid collections; inflammatory change is limited to superficial vulvar soft tissues on clinical correlation.

On further questioning she reports a new male sexual partner 12 days before symptom onset; he later told her he had a brief episode of painful penile blisters around that time which he described as resolving after a few days.

explanation: The diagnosis is Herpes simplex virus 2. The acute onset of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base with fever, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, multinucleated giant cells on lesion scrape, and a recent sexual exposure to a partner with penile blisters strongly support HSV-2 over alternatives such as syphilis or bacterial vulvovaginitis. Primary genital HSV infections often cause systemic prodrome and more extensive symptoms with higher viral shedding, which increases the risk of transmission to sexual partners and neonates.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man presents to the sexual health clinic with a 48-hour history of painful grouped vesicles on the dorsal glans and proximal shaft. He reports a tingling prodrome 12–24 hours prior to lesion appearance and a tender ipsilateral inguinal lymph node.

Patient is otherwise healthy, HIV-negative, and reports similar outbreaks twice in the past 12 months that resolved over about a week. Episodes are now occurring more frequently and are preceded by the same local paresthesia.

White cell count 7.8 × 10^9/L. Swab of an intact vesicle sent for nucleic-acid amplification returns positive for viral DNA from an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus commonly recovered from genital mucosa; type-specific serology demonstrates IgG against the genital-associated glycoprotein antigen, consistent with prior exposure.
Targeted ultrasound of the penis to exclude a subcutaneous collection shows only superficial mucocutaneous inflammation without abscess or vascular abnormality.

He is started on oral acyclovir and reports marked reduction in pain and cessation of new vesicle formation within 48 hours; lesions crust and begin to heal over the next 5 days with no bacterial superinfection.

explanation: The diagnosis is Herpes simplex virus 2. Recurrent, short lived episodes preceded by local tingling, a positive nucleic acid test for an enveloped double stranded DNA virus from a genital vesicle, and type specific IgG indicating prior exposure distinguish recurrent HSV-2 from first episode genital ulcers or nonviral causes. HSV-2 establishes latency in sacral sensory ganglia so recurrences are common and are often heralded by localized paresthesia or tingling at the lesion site.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously healthy man presents to urgent care with 10 days of fevers, sore throat, diffuse non‑pruritic maculopapular rash on trunk and proximal limbs, myalgias and tender posterior cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Temperature 38.8°C and pulse 110/min; he has several small painless oral ulcers but no respiratory distress.

No chronic medical conditions and no regular medications. He had routine STI screening 3 months ago that was negative. He reports a single new sexual partner about 4 weeks before presentation. Denies recent travel, blood transfusion or injection drug use.

CBC: leukocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.6 × 10^9/L. ALT 98 U/L. Heterophile antibody (monospot) negative. A combination antigen–antibody screening assay returned reactive; plasma viral RNA measured by nucleic acid amplification was 5.2 × 10^7 copies/L.
Neck ultrasound demonstrated multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes (largest 2.2 cm) with preserved fatty hilum and increased vascularity. Chest radiograph was normal.

On further questioning he acknowledges unprotected receptive anal intercourse with the new partner three weeks before symptom onset; that partner later developed a febrile illness and tested positive on the same combination antigen–antibody screening assay.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human immunodeficiency virus 1. The constellation of fever, sore throat, diffuse maculopapular rash, tender generalized lymphadenopathy after recent high risk exposure, a very high HIV RNA level, and a reactive fourth generation assay fit acute HIV infection and help exclude other causes such as infectious mononucleosis which had a negative heterophile test. Fourth generation HIV assays detect p24 antigen and antibodies and can become positive during the acute phase when plasma viral RNA is often extremely high, making early detection possible before full seroconversion.

hints.text: A 42-year-old woman is admitted with 3 months of progressive weight loss (≈8 kg), night sweats, nonproductive cough and increasing exertional dyspnoea. She has painful white pseudomembranous plaques on the buccal mucosa and multiple violaceous papules on the trunk. Temp 37.8°C, respiratory rate 22/min and SpO2 94% on room air.

History notable for type 2 diabetes on metformin and a 10 pack‑year smoking history. She reports multiple sexual partners over the past decade and has not had regular primary care for several years. No recent travel or blood product exposure reported.

Hemoglobin 95 g/L, leukocytes 4.1 × 10^9/L. CD4 lymphocyte count 85 × 10^6/L. C‑reactive protein 58 mg/L. A combination antigen–antibody screening assay was reactive and plasma viral RNA by nucleic acid amplification was 6.5 × 10^7 copies/L.
High‑resolution CT chest showed diffuse bilateral ground‑glass opacities with perihilar predominance and several small cavitating nodules in the upper lobes.

She was started on empiric trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole for suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia and, after counselling, commenced combination antiretroviral therapy. At 3 weeks her oral candidiasis had improved and plasma viral RNA fell to 3.9 × 10^4 copies/L with subjective improvement in appetite and energy.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human immunodeficiency virus 1. A reactive combined antigen–antibody assay with a very high plasma viral RNA and a CD4 count of 85 cells/μL establish HIV-1 with severe immunodeficiency, the diffuse perihilar ground-glass changes on CT and clinical response to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole point to Pneumocystis pneumonia, and the white pseudomembranes and violaceous papules are classic for oral candidiasis and Kaposi sarcoma in advanced HIV. HIV-1 is a lentivirus that targets CD4 T cells and a CD4 count below 200 cells/μL greatly increases risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii, oral thrush and Kaposi sarcoma.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to a primary-care clinic with 3 months of intermittent postcoital spotting and an increase in malodorous vaginal discharge. She is otherwise well; pelvic examination reveals multiple small, friable, exophytic papular lesions at the cervical os and mild cervical ectropion.

She reports a new sexual partner 6 months ago, inconsistent condom use, smokes 5–10 cigarettes per day, and has never received the recommended adolescent viral vaccination. No history of immunosuppression or prior abnormal cervical cytology.

Liquid-based cervical cytology shows high-grade squamous epithelial abnormalities and numerous squamous cells with perinuclear clearing and irregular nuclear contours. A nucleic acid amplification test on the cervical swab detects high-risk viral DNA sequences (type-specific assay reported as positive for high-risk groups).

Colposcopic inspection demonstrates acetowhite change at the transformation zone with a mosaic vascular pattern and small punctation areas; directed biopsy was taken from the most abnormal area for histology.

On further questioning she acknowledges that her new partner has persistent, flesh–colored papular lesions on the external genitalia and declined evaluation; she has had unprotected intercourse with him since their relationship began.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human papillomavirus. The cytology shows high-grade squamous abnormalities with perinuclear clearing consistent with HPV effect, the NAAT is positive for high-risk HPV DNA, and the colposcopic acetowhite change with mosaic vascularity corresponds to areas of dysplasia rather than simple benign ectropion or low-risk condyloma. Oncogenic HPV types integrate viral DNA and express E6 and E7 oncoproteins that inactivate p53 and Rb, which is why persistent infection with high‑risk types can progress to cervical cancer and is preventable by vaccination.

hints.text: A 24-year-old kindergarten teacher presents to urgent care in midwinter with abrupt onset of high fever, severe myalgias and headache that began 12 hours earlier; she reports dry cough and marked malaise and is unable to work. On exam T 39.4 °C, pulse 110/min, RR 18/min; pharynx mildly erythematous and lungs clear to auscultation without focal crackles.

She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, does not smoke, and has no recent travel. She reports she did not receive this season’s respiratory virus immunisation. Symptoms progressed rapidly from feeling well to bedridden over half a day. No prior antibiotic treatment.
A portable chest radiograph obtained in clinic shows clear lung fields without lobar consolidation or effusion.

Because of the rapid onset and severity, oral antiviral therapy was started within 36 hours of symptom onset. Within 24 hours of treatment the patient’s fever and myalgias abated and she reported marked improvement in cough and energy level.

A nasopharyngeal swab tested by reverse-transcription PCR returned positive for a single-stranded, negative-sense, segmented RNA respiratory virus that bears haemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface glycoproteins; laboratory subtyping reported the strain to be the type responsible for seasonal human epidemics and known to undergo antigenic shift.

explanation: The diagnosis is Influenza A virus. The sudden high fever, marked myalgias and rapid progression in midwinter are typical for influenza, and RT‑PCR demonstrating a segmented negative‑sense RNA virus with haemagglutinin and neuraminidase that is a seasonal subtype confirms influenza A; the prompt clinical improvement after antiviral therapy given early is also characteristic of treated influenza. Influenza A has a segmented genome that allows reassortment of gene segments between strains, producing antigenic shift that can give rise to novel pandemic viruses.

hints.text: An 78-year-old woman from a long-term residential facility is brought in with 36 hours of fever, rigors, lower abdominal discomfort and new confusion. She has a Foley catheter in place after recent hip surgery; physical exam shows suprapubic tenderness and blood pressure 95/60 mmHg.

Her medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and limited mobility after a fractured femur. The indwelling urinary catheter was placed three weeks earlier for urinary retention; she has had a urinary tract infection treated as an outpatient 10 months ago.
Non-contrast CT of the pelvis and lower abdomen demonstrates gas within the bladder wall and lumen consistent with emphysematous cystitis; no obstructing ureteric stone is seen.

Intravenous fluids and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics were started and the Foley catheter was exchanged. Her blood pressure and mental status partially improved over 24 hours, but fever and marked pyuria persisted, prompting urine culture and susceptibility testing.

Urine microscopy: many leucocytes and numerous gram-negative bacilli. Urine culture grows mucoid colonies that ferment lactose (pink on MacConkey), are oxidase negative and non-motile; the isolate reduces nitrate and demonstrates intrinsic resistance to ampicillin.

explanation: This is a catheter-associated urinary tract infection with emphysematous cystitis and probable bacteremia due to Klebsiella pneumoniae. An elderly diabetic with an indwelling Foley is at high risk for gas-forming urinary infections, and the urine culture grew mucoid, lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, nonmotile gram-negative bacilli that are intrinsically ampicillin resistant, a profile typical of Klebsiella pneumoniae rather than other Enterobacterales. Klebsiella’s prominent polysaccharide capsule produces mucoid colonies and is a key virulence factor, and some strains frequently acquire ESBL or carbapenemase genes that complicate therapy.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 72 hours of fever (peak 39.6°C), productive cough, progressive dyspnoea and two watery bowel motions. He is a current 40-pack-year smoker; on arrival he was confused, tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 28/min and oxygen saturation 88% on room air.

Past medical history notable for COPD treated with inhaled bronchodilators and low-dose oral prednisone for the past month after an acute exacerbation; type 2 diabetes controlled with metformin. No recent antibiotics prior to presentation.

Serum sodium 124 mmol/L, leukocyte count 11.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, CRP 265 mg/L, ALT 78 U/L. Sputum Gram stain showed few neutrophils and no predominant organisms; blood cultures pending.
Chest radiograph demonstrated dense patchy consolidation of the right lower lobe. Chest CT confirmed lobar consolidation with a small right pleural effusion and no cavitation.

He returned three days before symptom onset from a city conference where he stayed at a downtown hotel and used the indoor spa. Hotel management later contacted guests reporting several other attendees with febrile respiratory illness. A urine antigen test returned positive for a single respiratory pathogen; culture of respiratory secretions later grew a fastidious gram-negative bacillus on buffered charcoal yeast extract medium.

explanation: This presentation is Legionnaires disease due to Legionella pneumophila causing severe community-acquired lobar pneumonia with systemic and gastrointestinal features. The epidemiologic link to a hotel spa with other cases, hyponatraemia, prominent GI symptoms and confusion, a sputum Gram stain with few organisms, a positive urine antigen and growth on buffered charcoal yeast extract all point to Legionella rather than typical extracellular bacteria. These findings together identify a fastidious intracellular gram-negative bacillus that often evades routine sputum culture and Gram stain. Legionella stains poorly by Gram stain and is best detected by urine antigen or culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract, and it classically causes hyponatraemia and extrapulmonary GI or neurologic symptoms from its intracellular infection.

hints.text: A 55-year-old woman presented with 4 days of high fevers (up to 40°C), dry cough, myalgia, and several watery bowel movements; family noted new confusion at home. She was tachycardic and hypoxaemic with oxygen saturation 90% on room air and required admission for oxygen therapy.

She had returned 6 days earlier from a 7-day Mediterranean cruise during which she frequently used the ship’s indoor whirlpool and swimming pool; several other passengers reported respiratory illness during the voyage and the vessel reported mid-voyage maintenance on potable water tanks.

Serum sodium 121 mmol/L, leukocyte count 13.0 × 10^9/L, CRP 310 mg/L, AST 92 U/L, ALT 104 U/L. Routine sputum culture was non-diagnostic; urine antigen test was positive for a single respiratory pathogen.
Chest x-ray revealed dense consolidation of the right middle lobe with a small pleural effusion; CT chest confirmed lobar consolidation without cavitation.

She received empirical intravenous amoxicillin/clavulanate on admission but remained febrile and more hypoxaemic at 48 hours. After switching to intravenous levofloxacin she defervesced over the next 24–48 hours and oxygen requirement fell; urine antigen later confirmed the same pathogen.

explanation: This is Legionnaires disease caused by Legionella pneumophila presenting as severe lobar pneumonia associated with an outbreak after cruise ship water exposure. Recent cruise ship whirlpool and water-tank maintenance with multiple ill passengers, marked hyponatraemia and transaminitis, non-diagnostic routine sputum culture, positive urine antigen and rapid clinical response only after switching to a fluoroquinolone all support Legionella rather than common bacterial pneumonias. The pattern of systemic symptoms, paucity of organisms on Gram stain and epidemiologic exposure to aerosolized water are characteristic for this fastidious organism. The urine antigen test mainly detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 and Legionella prefers warm aquatic environments where it is transmitted in aerosolized water from sources such as whirlpools and air conditioning systems.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-week history of a single enlarging ulcer on his left forearm. The lesion began as a small papule after an insect bite while he was backpacking; it is now roughly 2.5 cm in diameter with a raised indurated border and central granulation tissue. He is afebrile, otherwise well, and topical antibiotic courses prescribed abroad produced no improvement.

He returned 3 weeks ago from a 10-week trip to rural northern Brazil, where he camped in forested areas and slept in hammocks. He has no chronic medical conditions, is not on immunosuppressants, and reports multiple nocturnal bites that acquaintance locals described as 'tiny, itchy' insects. No bleeding disorders, no prior similar lesions.

High-frequency ultrasound of the lesion shows focal dermal and subcutaneous hypoechoic inflammatory thickening extending to but not involving the deep fascia; there is increased vascularity on colour Doppler but no discrete abscess cavity or underlying osteomyelitis.

On direct questioning he emphasizes that bites occurred at night while sleeping without bed netting; a fellow traveller developed multiple papules that resolved slowly. Local health posts in the villages he visited frequently manage chronic skin ulcers after river-side camping.

A punch biopsy touch-prep stained with Giemsa shows numerous intracellular round bodies within macrophages; each body has a distinct rod-shaped kinetoplast adjacent to a nucleus. Culture incubated at ambient laboratory temperature yielded flagellated promastigote forms after several days.

explanation: This is cutaneous leishmaniasis due to Leishmania species causing a single chronic ulcerated skin lesion after travel to an endemic area. The history of nocturnal insect bites in rural Brazil, a slowly enlarging indurated ulcer, Giemsa-stained macrophages containing intracellular round bodies with a rod-shaped kinetoplast, and culture yielding flagellated promastigotes at ambient temperature distinguish Leishmania from bacterial or fungal skin infections. Those distinctive intracellular amastigotes and the promastigote culture form confirm a kinetoplastid protozoan rather than other parasitic or infectious causes of chronic ulcers. Leishmania has two diagnostic life stages with intracellular amastigotes bearing a kinetoplast in mammalian tissue and extracellular promastigotes in culture, and it is transmitted by nocturnal phlebotomine sandflies.

hints.text: A 72‑year‑old woman presents with 48 hours of progressive headache, fever to 38.4°C, confusion and new right‑sided facial weakness; she has lethargy, vomiting and nuchal rigidity on examination and a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13.

Medical history notable for seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with oral prednisone 10 mg daily for the past 6 months. She lives independently, has no recent travel, and had no preceding significant respiratory or urinary symptoms.

Blood: WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 95 mg/L. Lumbar puncture: CSF WBC 1.5 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, protein 2.8 g/L, glucose 1.8 mmol/L (concurrent plasma glucose 6.3 mmol/L). Initial CSF Gram stain shows small Gram‑positive rod forms.

MRI brain with contrast demonstrates T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and patchy enhancement in the pontine and medullary tegmentum with relative sparing of the cerebellar hemispheres, findings most in keeping with brainstem encephalitis.

She was started on empiric ceftriaxone plus vancomycin but showed no clinical improvement after 48 hours; blood and CSF cultures subsequently grew small Gram‑positive bacilli and high‑dose intravenous ampicillin was added, after which the patient defervesced and cognitive function began to recover over the next 72 hours.

explanation: This is Listeria monocytogenes meningitis with brainstem encephalitis in an elderly immunosuppressed patient. An older patient on chronic prednisone presented with fever, meningism and new cranial nerve or facial weakness with MRI brainstem involvement, CSF showing neutrophilic meningitis and Gram-positive small rods, and cultures yielding small gram-positive bacilli with clinical improvement only after adding ampicillin, all of which point to Listeria rather than other common causes of bacterial meningitis. The combination of risk factors, brainstem tropism and small rod morphology on CSF are characteristic for Listeria. Listeria is an intracellular, tumbling motile Gram-positive bacillus that commonly causes meningitis in neonates, the elderly, pregnant people and immunocompromised hosts and is not reliably covered by third-generation cephalosporins.

hints.text: A 4-year-old previously well boy presents to the emergency department with 72 hours of high fever (max 40.0 °C), cough, coryza and red, tearing eyes. His parents report noticing tiny white spots on the buccal mucosa this morning; a confluent erythematous maculopapular rash began at the hairline and face and is spreading downward. He attends a community daycare and looks uncomfortable but not toxic.

Family declines routine childhood vaccinations; the child received no scheduled live childhood immunisations. Several classmates developed febrile rash illness earlier in the week. No recent travel, no chronic conditions, and no hospitalisations.

Chest radiograph shows perihilar peribronchial cuffing with patchy air‑space opacities in the right middle lobe and perihilar regions, appearances most consistent with viral bronchiolitis/early viral pneumonia.

Supportive care including antipyretics, oral rehydration and two doses of oral vitamin A were given. Over 48 hours the fever and conjunctivitis improved and the rash evolved in a cephalocaudal pattern, beginning to desquamate as lesions faded.

Nasopharyngeal swab PCR detected an enveloped, single‑stranded, negative‑sense RNA virus. Paired sera demonstrated seroconversion with virus‑specific IgM present in convalescent sample, confirming recent infection.

explanation: The diagnosis is Measles virus. The triad of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots, cephalocaudal spread of an erythematous maculopapular rash, a daycare outbreak, and PCR plus IgM seroconversion for an enveloped negative sense RNA virus pinpoint measles rather than other viral exanthems. Measles is an enveloped negative sense paramyxovirus that is extremely contagious by respiratory droplets and causes transient immunosuppression that increases the risk of secondary infections such as pneumonia.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation presents with 4 days of fever to 38.8 °C, sore throat, and a severe dry cough. Over the prior 48 hours she developed red eyes and a confluent erythematous maculopapular rash that began at the forehead and behind the ears and is spreading to the trunk. On examination small whitish flecks are visible on the buccal mucosa.

She emigrated from Eastern Europe six months prior and cannot locate childhood immunisation records; she does not recall receiving two doses of a childhood combined live viral vaccine. Her pregnancy until now has been uncomplicated.

She works as a clinician in a community refugee health clinic. Ten days before symptom onset she assessed a febrile toddler with a generalized rash who was later admitted to hospital with progressive illness.

Because of increasing cough and breathlessness, a CT chest was performed and shows multifocal ground‑glass opacities and bronchovascular thickening without lobar consolidation, appearances compatible with viral pneumonitis.

Throat swab PCR identified an enveloped, single‑stranded, negative‑sense RNA virus. Acute serum was negative but convalescent serum 10 days later showed high‑titre virus‑specific IgM, consistent with recent primary infection.

explanation: The diagnosis is Measles virus. Her fever, sore throat, cough, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a confluent cephalocaudal maculopapular rash after occupational exposure, together with identification of an enveloped negative sense RNA virus and seroconversion, distinguish measles from other pregnancy-associated rashes. Measles in pregnancy can cause severe maternal pneumonitis and is associated with higher risk of pregnancy loss and preterm delivery, so verifying immunity before pregnancy is important.

hints.text: A 21-year-old male university student presents with 48 hours of progressive painful swelling in the left preauricular region, fever to 38.9 °C, trismus and difficulty chewing. On examination there is a firm, tender swelling over the angle of the mandible extending to the submandibular area; Stensen’s duct appears nonpurulent.

He returned 5 days ago from an inter‑university rowing regatta. He lives in a crowded dormitory with five roommates. Childhood vaccination records are unavailable and he does not recall receiving an adolescent booster. He denies recent dental work or trauma.
Complete blood count: white cell count 7.2 × 10^9/L. CRP 36 mg/L. Serum amylase is elevated at 880 U/L (reference 25–125 U/L). Throat swab sent for routine bacterial culture; blood cultures obtained.
Ultrasound of the left parotid gland shows enlargement with heterogeneous echotexture and increased Doppler flow; there is no intraglandular stone and no abscess cavity identified.

Campus health notified the ward that several students who attended the same regatta developed febrile parotid swelling over the past 2 weeks; the cluster began with a single student who had acute salivary‑gland swelling followed days later by similar cases among close contacts.

explanation: The diagnosis is Mumps virus. The painful preauricular swelling with trismus, markedly elevated serum amylase, nonpurulent Stensen duct, ultrasound showing diffuse gland enlargement without abscess, and a cluster among close contacts in a communal setting with uncertain vaccination indicate mumps rather than bacterial sialadenitis. Mumps is an RNA paramyxovirus spread by respiratory droplets that commonly causes salivary gland swelling and can lead to complications such as orchitis and aseptic meningitis, especially in incompletely vaccinated populations.

hints.text: A 32-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 6-month history of slowly progressive numbness of the right hand and intermittent painless ulcers on the plantar surface of his left foot. Examination shows two well-demarcated hypopigmented macules on the dorsal right hand with loss of light touch and pinprick, weakness of right finger abduction, and a visibly thickened, tender right ulnar nerve palpable at the elbow.

He emigrated from a rural district in eastern India 18 months ago. He has no diabetes, is HIV-negative by prior testing, takes no immunosuppressive medications, and reports that the sensory symptoms began insidiously after he finished agricultural work; symptoms have progressed despite topical emollients. He recalls his mother having long-standing skin plaques when he was a child.

Skin biopsy of a hypopigmented patch shows a granulomatous infiltrate on haematoxylin–eosin stain; Fite-Faraco stain demonstrates numerous acid-fast bacilli within cutaneous nerves. Slit-skin smear returns a bacteriologic index reported as +3. Full blood count is unremarkable (WBC 6.4 × 10^9/L), CRP 2 mg/L.

High-resolution ultrasound of the right ulnar nerve demonstrates focal enlargement with hypoechoic change and increased intraneural blood flow consistent with active neuritis; chest radiograph is normal.

He spent his first 30 years in a district where the condition remains endemic and lived in the same household as his mother, who had untreated chronic nodular skin disease for decades; he reports prolonged, close household contact during childhood and early adulthood.

explanation: This is multibacillary leprosy due to Mycobacterium leprae presenting with chronic hypopigmented anesthetic skin patches and progressive peripheral neuropathy. The combination of long standing hypopigmented sensory patches, focal ulnar nerve thickening and ultrasound evidence of neuritis, endemic household exposure, and biopsy demonstrating numerous acid fast bacilli with a bacteriologic index of +3 confirms M. leprae infection rather than other neuropathies or dermatoses. Mycobacterium leprae prefers cooler skin and peripheral nerves, cannot be grown on routine culture media, and diagnosis relies on clinical signs plus slit-skin smear or biopsy, with armadillos serving as a zoonotic reservoir in some areas.

hints.text: A 34-year-old male presents to an urban clinic with a 3-month history of productive cough, drenching night sweats and progressive weight loss of 6 kg. He reports intermittent streaks of blood in sputum over the last 2 weeks and low-grade fevers. On exam he is thin, afebrile, with dullness and bronchial breath sounds at the right upper chest.

He emigrated from South Asia 18 months ago and works at a large homeless shelter. Past medical history notable for poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (most recent HbA1c 8.9%). No known HIV risk factors; rapid HIV test in clinic was negative.

Posterior–anterior chest radiograph shows a cavitary consolidation in the right upper lobe with adjacent patchy nodular opacities and volume loss. No acute cardiopulmonary oedema; small calcified granuloma is noted in the left hilum.

Colleagues at the shelter report a recent outbreak of chronic cough among clients; one resident had been diagnosed with a smear-positive pulmonary infection three months earlier but left the facility before treatment completion.

Three sputum samples: Ziehl–Neelsen stain shows numerous acid-fast bacilli; culture on egg-based medium produced rough, buff colonies after approximately 3 weeks. A nucleic acid amplification assay targeting a species-specific genomic region returned positive; phenotypic susceptibility testing showed susceptibility to isoniazid and rifampicin.

explanation: This presentation is active pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, manifesting as reactivation cavitary disease in the right upper lobe. Chronic constitutional symptoms, haemoptysis, an upper‑lobe cavitary consolidation on chest radiograph, numerous acid‑fast bacilli on Ziehl–Neelsen stain and growth of slow, rough buff colonies on egg medium with a species‑specific NAAT together point to M. tuberculosis rather than non‑tuberculous mycobacteria or common bacterial pneumonias, and the epidemiologic exposure and smear‑positive contact support recent transmission and reactivation risk. M. tuberculosis is a slow growing acid‑fast bacillus that commonly reactivates in high oxygen tension areas such as the upper lobes and forms cavitary lesions that promote contagion.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman reports 4 months of progressively worsening lower back pain radiating to the left flank, night sweats and a 7-kg weight loss. Over the past 3 weeks she developed bilateral leg weakness and difficulty walking. On examination she has focal midline tenderness at the thoracolumbar junction and reduced hip flexion strength.

She has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (most recent HbA1c 9.6%), lives in a multi-generational household and recalls prolonged household exposure years earlier to a relative treated for pulmonary infection. No history of intravenous drug use; no recent surgery.

MRI of the spine demonstrates collapse of the L1 vertebral body with destruction of adjacent endplates, a large anterior paravertebral fluid collection tracking along the psoas muscle and an epidural collection causing spinal canal stenosis and cord compression.

Family members describe that an elderly household contact had a chronic cough and weight loss 8–10 years ago and completed a course of therapy; the patient herself has spent most of her adult life in a region with high prevalence of pulmonary mycobacterial disease.

CT-guided core biopsy of the vertebral lesion showed necrotising granulomatous inflammation; Ziehl–Neelsen stain identified acid-fast bacilli. Culture from the biopsy yielded slow-growing, non-pigmented colonies on egg-based medium after 3–6 weeks; a molecular assay targeting an organism-specific genetic element was positive and baseline susceptibility testing showed sensitivity to first-line agents.

explanation: This is tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with vertebral body collapse, paravertebral psoas abscess and epidural extension causing cord compression due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The subacute progressive back pain, systemic symptoms, MRI showing anterior vertebral destruction with a psoas collection and epidural mass, necrotising granulomas with acid‑fast bacilli on biopsy and slow growth on egg medium with a positive molecular assay all distinguish M. tuberculosis from pyogenic bacteria and from non‑tuberculous mycobacterial causes. Spinal tuberculosis classically produces anterior vertebral body destruction with contiguous spread, forming paravertebral and psoas abscesses and causing slowly progressive neurologic deficits from epidural extension.

hints.text: A 19-year-old woman who lives in a university dormitory presents with a 10-day history of gradually worsening dry cough, sore throat, headache and malaise. She reports low‑grade fevers to 38.2°C and intermittent chest discomfort but no dyspnoea at rest. On examination she is alert, T 38.0°C, SpO2 97% on room air; pharynx is erythematous and there are scattered fine inspiratory crackles at the right mid‑lung.

She shares a room with two classmates who developed coughs approximately two weeks earlier. She is otherwise healthy, a non‑smoker, received seasonal influenza vaccine, and was given oral amoxicillin by her general practitioner three days ago with no improvement in symptoms.
Frontal chest radiograph demonstrates patchy, bilateral perihilar and peribronchial interstitial opacities more on the right; there is no dense lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

Peripheral blood: WBC 8.1 × 10^9/L with relative lymphocytosis; CRP 20 mg/L. Cold agglutinin titre 1:128. Enzyme immunoassay returned elevated specific IgM directed against an atypical respiratory pathogen.

Amoxicillin was stopped and oral azithromycin started; fever abated and the cough markedly improved within 48 hours. Clinical follow‑up showed progressive resolution of symptoms and radiographic clearing over the next few weeks.

explanation: This is atypical community acquired pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, the classic 'walking pneumonia' seen in young adults in congregate settings. A subacute dry cough in a college dorm outbreak, bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates on chest radiograph, a positive cold agglutinin test and specific IgM for an atypical pathogen, together with lack of response to a beta‑lactam and rapid improvement after macrolide therapy, point to M. pneumoniae rather than typical lobar bacterial pneumonias. Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall so it does not respond to beta‑lactam antibiotics and can trigger cold agglutinin IgM antibodies that transiently agglutinate red cells.

hints.text: A 28-year-old male recruit from a military training camp presents with a 12-day history of persistent dry cough and progressive fatigue, now noting dark urine and yellowing of the eyes. Temperatures up to 38.5°C; he denies chest pain or significant shortness of breath. On examination he is jaundiced, pulse 108/min, lungs with scattered wheeze and a few crackles, SpO2 96% on room air.

He lives in crowded barracks; multiple platoon members have had prolonged coughs over the past three weeks. No prior medical conditions, not on medications, no recent travel, and no known sick contacts outside the camp.

Haemoglobin 88 g/L with elevated reticulocyte count; LDH 520 U/L, total bilirubin 62 μmol/L with indirect predominance, and low haptoglobin. Direct antiglobulin test positive for complement only; cold agglutinin titre >1:256.
Chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy peribronchial and perihilar reticulonodular infiltrates, greater on the left, without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

He was started on oral doxycycline and measures to keep warm; over several days the urine colour and jaundice improved and haemoglobin stabilised while the cough abated. Clinicians noted the combination of atypical pneumonia, high cold agglutinins and a barracks outbreak when formulating their working diagnosis.

explanation: This is Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection presenting as atypical pneumonia complicated by cold agglutinin mediated autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The crowded barracks outbreak, prolonged dry cough with patchy interstitial infiltrates, very high cold agglutinin titre, laboratory evidence of hemolysis and a direct antiglobulin test positive for complement only are characteristic of M. pneumoniae provoking complement‑fixing IgM antibodies and distinguish it from other respiratory pathogens. Cold agglutinin antibodies in Mycoplasma infection are usually IgM that bind red cells at low temperatures and cause complement mediated hemolysis, often giving a DAT positive for C3 only.

hints.text: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of rapidly worsening frontal headache, fever to 39.5°C, photophobia and neck stiffness. Friends report progressive confusion and one episode of vomiting; on arrival he is febrile, tachycardic, GCS 13, and has marked nuchal rigidity with a subtle left upper‑limb pronator drift.

Previously healthy, no chronic illness, not on immunosuppressive medication, up to date with routine vaccinations. Symptoms began as malaise 3 days earlier and progressed quickly; no recent sinus or neurosurgical procedures and no known sick contacts.

Blood: leukocytes 16.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 330 mm H2O; CSF WBC 2.3 × 10^9/L with 92% neutrophils, glucose 1.3 mmol/L (paired serum 5.6 mmol/L), protein 3.0 g/L. CSF Gram stain shows no organisms; routine bacterial cultures pending.

MRI brain performed the day after admission shows diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and cortical swelling, greatest in the frontal lobes, with abnormal T2 signal tracking along the cribriform region and olfactory bulbs.

On re-questioning he reports swimming and repeatedly diving under the surface of a warm inland lake on the weekend before symptom onset. A concentrated CSF wet mount examination demonstrates rapidly motile, uninucleate trophozoite forms; CSF bacterial cultures remain sterile after 48 hours.

explanation: This presentation represents acute primary amoebic meningoencephalitis due to Naegleria fowleri following freshwater exposure. The clinical picture is fulminant meningoencephalitis with high intracranial pressure and rapid decline in an otherwise healthy young adult. The combination of rapid onset severe meningitis with olfactory/cribriform region MRI changes, a history of diving in warm lake water, neutrophil-predominant CSF with very low glucose and high protein, and motile uninucleate trophozoites on a fresh CSF wet mount points to Naegleria fowleri rather than bacterial meningitis or other free-living amoebae which have more indolent courses or different patient profiles. The sterile bacterial cultures and the visualization of rapidly motile amoebae in CSF are the decisive diagnostic clues. Naegleria fowleri is a thermophilic free-living amoeba that enters via the nasal mucosa and olfactory nerves after freshwater exposure and causes a rapidly progressive, often fatal meningoencephalitis with trophozoites visible on fresh CSF wet mount.

hints.text: A 56-year-old woman presents with 72 hours of severe bifrontal headache, fever to 38.9°C, nausea and two brief episodes of confusion; family witnessed a single generalized tonic–clonic seizure at home. On exam she is drowsy, oriented only to person, has neck stiffness and early papilledema.

Medical history notable for well‑controlled type 2 diabetes (metformin only) and chronic allergic rhinitis managed with daily nasal saline rinses for years. She has no known immunosuppression and no recent dental or ENT procedures. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin were started in the emergency department for presumed bacterial meningitis.

Blood: leukocytes 12.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 90 mg/L, serum glucose 6.7 mmol/L. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 280 mm H2O; CSF WBC 3.0 × 10^9/L with 85% neutrophils, glucose 0.9 mmol/L (paired serum 6.7 mmol/L), protein 4.5 g/L. CSF Gram stain negative; bacterial PCR and viral PCR panels pending.

After 24 hours of empiric antibacterial therapy the patient’s level of consciousness declined, requiring intubation for airway protection. Given concern for a non‑bacterial etiology, clinicians added intravenous amphotericin B and an oral azole; intracranial pressure rose despite hyperosmolar therapy and she showed only transient improvement in fever over the next 48 hours.

Family reports she rinsed her nasal passages with unboiled well water six days before symptom onset. Repeat CSF microscopy using a fresh, centrifuged wet mount now shows rapidly motile, uninucleate trophozoites; bacterial and viral studies remain negative.

explanation: This is primary amoebic meningoencephalitis from Naegleria fowleri associated with nasal exposure to contaminated well water during saline rinses. The illness is an acute, rapidly progressive meningoencephalitis in a previously immunocompetent adult. The neutrophil-predominant, high‑pressure CSF with very low glucose and high protein that is culture negative, the clinical deterioration despite antibacterial therapy, the history of nasal irrigation with unboiled well water, and demonstration of rapidly motile uninucleate trophozoites on fresh CSF wet mount together point to Naegleria fowleri rather than bacterial, viral, or chronic amoebic causes such as Acanthamoeba. Naegleria fowleri infections classically follow forceful nasal exposure to warm freshwater or contaminated irrigation fluids and evolve over days, so diagnosis is most rapidly made by observing motile trophozoites on a fresh CSF wet mount.

hints.text: A 24-year-old male cacao farm worker presents with 6 months of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea; he reports intermittent crampy abdominal pain and noticed pruritic erythematous papules on the soles of his feet. On examination he is pale, heart rate 110 min−1, and has faint conjunctival pallor without jaundice or hepatosplenomegaly.

He was raised and continues to work in a rural coastal community in northeastern Brazil, habitually barefoot while tending wet soil and irrigation furrows. He completed a short over-the-counter iron course with minimal improvement and has no prior transfusions or chronic medical conditions.

Haemoglobin 72 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 62 fL, ferritin 7 µg/L; eosinophils 2.4 × 10^9/L. Stool guaiac positive and direct faecal microscopy shows numerous oval thin‑shelled eggs with morulated embryos compatible with a strongyliform nematode.

Chest radiograph obtained for intermittent dry cough several weeks earlier showed patchy perihilar air‑space opacities; repeat film 3 weeks later demonstrated near‑complete clearance of those faint infiltrates.

The patient received a single 400 mg oral dose of albendazole; within 48 hours several thin live nematodes were observed in the stool. Light microscopy of recovered adult worms showed lengths near 8–10 mm and buccal cutting plates without visible teeth. After deworming plus oral iron his symptoms and haemoglobin progressively improved.

explanation: This patient has chronic hookworm infection due to Necator americanus causing significant iron deficiency anemia. The syndrome reflects blood loss from intestinal attachment combined with larval skin penetration and pulmonary migration. The epidemiology of barefoot agricultural work in wet tropical soil, pruritic plantar papules, progressive microcytic anemia with low ferritin, transient pulmonary infiltrates, stool eggs consistent with a strongyliform nematode, and recovery of 8–10 mm adults with buccal cutting plates without teeth distinguish Necator americanus from other helminths including Ancylostoma duodenale which has teeth. Necator americanus adults use buccal cutting plates to feed on intestinal mucosa, leading to chronic blood loss and iron deficiency, and recovery of adults after albendazole with characteristic cutting plates helps species identification.

hints.text: A 22-year-old woman presents to the sexual health clinic with a 3-day history of purulent vaginal discharge, dysuria, and mild lower abdominal cramping. She is afebrile. On speculum examination there is mucopurulent cervical discharge and mild cervical friability; bimanual exam elicits minimal cervical motion tenderness.

She reports a new male sexual partner 10 days ago and condomless vaginal intercourse. She had an uncomplicated chlamydia infection 18 months earlier that was treated. The partner described an episode of urethral discharge one week before she became symptomatic.
Transvaginal ultrasound shows normal-appearing ovaries, no tubo-ovarian abscess, and no hydrosalpinx. There is minimal free fluid in the pelvis but no adnexal mass or other focal pathology.

When contacted, the recent partner confirms he sought urgent care for profuse urethral discharge and received a single intramuscular dose of a third‑generation cephalosporin the week prior to the patient’s presentation.

Nucleic acid amplification test (endocervical swab) returned positive for a bacterial sexually transmitted pathogen. Gram stain of cervical discharge shows abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes and numerous intracellular gram‑negative diplococci within epithelial cells.

explanation: This is acute mucopurulent cervicitis due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The clinical and laboratory findings indicate an active gonococcal cervical infection in a sexually exposed young woman. The acute purulent cervical discharge after recent unprotected intercourse with a symptomatic partner, a positive NAAT from endocervical swab, and the Gram stain showing abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes with numerous intracellular gram-negative diplococci within epithelial cells are highly specific for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and distinguish it from causes like Chlamydia which do not show intracellular gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain. Finding intracellular gram-negative diplococci in polymorphonuclear cells on a cervical Gram stain is a rapid and specific clue to gonorrhea and often correlates with a positive NAAT pending confirmatory testing.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man is seen in the emergency department with a 5-day history of fever, migratory arthralgias and an acutely painful swollen right wrist. He also has several small pustular lesions on the dorsal hands and fingers and pain along the flexor tendon sheath of the right wrist that limits active motion.

He reports a brief episode of urethral burning and scant clear discharge about 10 days earlier that resolved without treatment. He had unprotected sex with a new partner two weeks ago and has no other chronic medical conditions.

Blood tests show WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 11.0 × 10^9/L and C‑reactive protein 110 mg/L. Blood cultures at 48 hours remain negative. Synovial aspiration from the wrist yields turbid fluid with markedly elevated neutrophils; Gram stain shows few organisms and routine synovial fluid cultures are sterile so far.

Point‑of‑care ultrasound of the wrist demonstrates a radiocarpal joint effusion with distension of the extensor and flexor tendon sheaths consistent with tenosynovitis; plain radiographs show no joint space narrowing or bony destruction.
He was started empirically on intravenous ceftriaxone. Within 48 hours his fever abated, the pustular lesions began crusting, and wrist pain and range of motion improved substantially.

explanation: This presentation is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection manifesting with migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions progressing to septic arthritis of the wrist. The brief antecedent urethritis, recent unprotected sexual exposure, sterile blood and joint cultures, and the triad of migratory arthralgias plus tenosynovitis with pustular dermatitis point to Neisseria gonorrhoeae rather than typical pyogenic organisms, which usually cause an isolated, culture-positive purulent monoarthritis without the characteristic skin lesions and tendon sheath involvement. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an intracellular gram negative diplococcus that often causes a syndrome of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and migratory arthralgias and may yield negative blood or synovial cultures, so mucosal NAAT or special culture techniques are more sensitive for diagnosis.

hints.text: A 42-year-old woman presents to clinic with 6 weeks of worsening cough, daily wheeze and intermittent expectoration of thick brownish plugs. She reports reduced exercise tolerance and two prior courses of oral antibiotics over the past year for presumed chest infections without sustained improvement.

Longstanding moderate asthma diagnosed in childhood, uses inhaled corticosteroid intermittently. Atopic dermatitis since adolescence. No systemic immunosuppression. Works part time at a municipal composting facility and recalls heavy dust exposure from decaying leaves last month.
Peripheral eosinophil count 1.6 × 10^9/L. Total IgE 2 200 kU/L. Sputum Gram stain showed no predominant bacterial pathogen. Serum C-reactive protein 18 mg/L.

High resolution CT chest shows central bronchiectasis most pronounced in the upper lobes, with branching mucus-filled bronchi producing a finger-in-glove appearance. No nodules or cavities identified.

Expectorated mucus plug submitted for mycology grew a thermotolerant mould on culture at 37 °C. Microscopy from the colony revealed septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. Serum and sputum specific IgE to the isolated mould were markedly elevated.

explanation: This constellation of asthma, central bronchiectasis, high total IgE, eosinophilia and brown mucus plugs is consistent with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis due to Aspergillus fumigatus. Longstanding asthma with worsening cough and expectoration of brownish plugs, markedly elevated total and specific IgE to the cultured thermotolerant mold, peripheral eosinophilia, and upper‑lobe central bronchiectasis with a finger‑in‑glove appearance distinguish ABPA from simple asthma or bacterial bronchiectasis and point specifically to hypersensitivity to Aspergillus rather than invasive fungal disease. ABPA is an allergic hypersensitivity to Aspergillus that occurs in atopic asthmatics and is characterized by central bronchiectasis and very high IgE levels, while the organism shows septate hyphae with acute angle branching in culture and microscopy.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man is admitted with fever and pleuritic left-sided chest pain that began on day 12 after induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia. He has a non-productive cough and a single episode of haemoptysis.

He received cytarabine and daunorubicin 2 weeks ago. For 9 days he has been neutropenic with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.05 × 10^9/L. He received prophylactic antibacterial agents but no mould-active prophylaxis.

C-reactive protein 220 mg/L. Blood cultures remain negative after 48 hours. Serum galactomannan index 1.8. Bronchoalveolar lavage was performed because fever persisted despite broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Contrast CT chest shows multiple peripheral nodules in the left lower lobe. Several nodules have surrounding ground-glass attenuation consistent with a halo sign. One focus shows early cavitation.

Patient did not improve on antibacterial therapy. Intravenous voriconazole was started empirically. Within 72 hours fever and pleuritic pain diminished. BAL culture later grew a thermotolerant mould demonstrating septate hyphae with acute-angle branching.

explanation: This clinical picture indicates invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in a profoundly neutropenic host caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. Prolonged severe neutropenia after induction chemotherapy, fever with pleuritic pain, CT nodules with surrounding ground glass halo sign, elevated serum galactomannan, and recovery of a thermotolerant mold with septate acute‑angle branching hyphae point to invasive Aspergillus rather than bacterial or non‑Aspergillus fungal infections. Aspergillus spp. characteristically produce septate hyphae with acute angle branching and cause angioinvasive disease in neutropenic patients, with the halo sign on CT reflecting hemorrhagic infarction from vascular invasion and galactomannan serving as a useful serum biomarker.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presents with 6 weeks of productive cough, intermittent fevers, night sweats, and a 5 kg weight loss. He also has two enlarging verrucous plaques, one on the left forearm and one on the cheek. He works outdoors as a river restoration technician and reports increasing dyspnea on exertion.

He is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, is HIV negative by recent testing, and has received no immunosuppressive therapy. He completed two courses of oral antibiotics for presumed bacterial pneumonia without clinical improvement.

Blood leukocyte count 14.2 × 10^9/L, neutrophil predominant. C-reactive protein 94 mg/L. Sputum AFB smears negative. Punch biopsy of a skin lesion shows granulomatous inflammation and numerous large yeast forms on PAS stain with broad-based budding.

Chest radiograph shows patchy consolidation in the right upper lobe and multiple bilateral nodular opacities, one with a 2.5 cm cavitary change. CT chest confirms right upper lobe consolidation with scattered nodules.

On further questioning he reports that three weeks before symptoms began he spent several days clearing driftwood and rebuilding a beaver dam along a nearby river valley, frequently disturbing damp soil and rotting wood.

explanation: This is pulmonary blastomycosis with cutaneous dissemination due to Blastomyces dermatitidis. The subacute pulmonary syndrome following soil and rotting wood exposure in a river valley, failure to improve with antibiotics, and biopsy showing granulomas with large yeast forms that demonstrate broad based budding are diagnostic for Blastomyces rather than Histoplasma or Cryptococcus, which have different yeast morphologies and epidemiology. Blastomyces dermatitidis is a dimorphic fungus that grows as a mold in the environment and as broad‑based budding yeast in tissue, and it commonly causes pulmonary infection that can disseminate to skin and bone even in immunocompetent hosts.

hints.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to primary care with three days of intense vulvar pruritus and a thick white vaginal discharge. Symptoms began two days after she completed a 10-day course of oral amoxicillin for sinusitis. She reports burning on urination and discomfort with intercourse. On examination the labia are erythematous and there are adherent white curd-like plaques in the vaginal vestibule.

Her medical history is unremarkable. She is not diabetic and not pregnant. She uses combined oral contraceptives. She has had no new sexual partners and no prior similar episodes requiring systemic therapy.

Vaginal pH measured at 4.3. Wet mount with 10% KOH preparation shows numerous budding yeast forms and pseudohyphae. Gram stain does not show clue cells and bacterial culture returned without pathogenic growth.
Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound was performed to exclude anatomic causes. The uterus and adnexa have normal appearance. No fluid collection or tubo-ovarian abnormality is identified.

She received a single 150 mg oral dose of an azole antifungal. Within 48 hours pruritus and dysuria were markedly reduced. At one-week follow-up the discharge and vulvar erythema were nearly resolved.

explanation: This presentation is acute vulvovaginal candidiasis due to Candida albicans causing intense vulvar pruritus and adherent curd-like vaginal discharge. The classic combination of recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use, normal vaginal pH, adherent white curd-like plaques, and KOH demonstrating budding yeast and pseudohyphae with no clue cells or pathogenic bacteria points to Candida rather than bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis. Vulvovaginal candidiasis typically occurs at a normal acidic vaginal pH and is characterized microscopically by budding yeasts and pseudohyphae, which helps distinguish it from BV and trichomonas.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman from coastal Massachusetts presents to clinic with 6 days of fever, drenching night sweats and dark urine. She reports temperatures up to 39.0 °C. On examination she is icteric and has a palpable spleen 2 cm below the left costal margin.

She is otherwise healthy. She recalls an attached tick after a day hike on Nantucket 12 days before onset. She has not travelled outside New England and has no history of blood transfusion or chronic illness.

Hb 82 g/L, reticulocyte count 8%, WBC 6.4 × 10^9/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L. Bilirubin 60 μmol/L, LDH 980 U/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/L. Peripheral blood smear shows intraerythrocytic ring forms with an estimated parasitaemia of 3%. Rapid malaria antigen test is negative.
Abdominal ultrasound shows a spleen length of 14 cm without focal lesion. No hepatomegaly is seen.
Oral atovaquone plus azithromycin was started. Fevers resolved within 48 hours and repeat smear showed parasitaemia <0.5% at 72 hours. PCR for an intraerythrocytic protozoan returned positive.

explanation: This is acute babesiosis from Babesia microti manifesting as febrile hemolytic anemia following a tick exposure in an endemic area. The history of an attached tick in New England, fever with splenomegaly, laboratory evidence of hemolysis, intraerythrocytic ring forms on smear, and a negative malaria antigen test strongly favor Babesia over Plasmodium or bacterial causes of hemolysis. Babesia microti is transmitted by Ixodes ticks and may show intraerythrocytic ring forms and the pathognomonic Maltese cross tetrads on smear, which help distinguish it from malaria.

hints.text: A 69-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 5 days of fever, fatigue and dark urine. Symptoms began three weeks after he received packed red blood cells during a hip replacement. On arrival he is tachycardic and icteric.
His medical history is notable for traumatic splenectomy, hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He lives in a rural area and denies recent travel outside the region.

Hb 75 g/L, reticulocyte count 12%, WBC 7.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 95 × 10^9/L. Bilirubin 120 μmol/L, LDH 1450 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable. Peripheral smear shows intraerythrocytic ring forms and red cell fragmentation with estimated parasitaemia 12%.
Chest radiograph shows no acute airspace consolidation. Abdominal CT demonstrates postsplenectomy anatomy without abscess or other acute intra-abdominal process.

Because of high parasitaemia and asplenia he underwent urgent red cell exchange and was started on intravenous clindamycin plus quinine. Parasitaemia fell to 3% within 24 hours and he became afebrile. PCR for an intraerythrocytic protozoan returned positive.

explanation: This is severe, transfusion-associated babesiosis with high-level parasitemia and hemolytic anemia in an asplenic patient. Onset after a blood transfusion, marked hemolysis, very high intraerythrocytic parasitemia, and the absence of a spleen explain the severe presentation and point to Babesia microti rather than other post-transfusion hemolytic processes. Asplenic or immunocompromised patients are at risk for fulminant babesiosis with high parasitemia, so rapid parasite reduction is often required to prevent life-threatening hemolysis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old woman presents to clinic with a two-month history of chronic cough, occasional blood-streaked sputum, low-grade night sweats and 4 kg weight loss. She is a current smoker and reports persistent right upper chest discomfort but no severe dyspnoea.

She is otherwise well, takes no immunosuppressive medications, and tested HIV negative three months ago. She recently cleaned a large backyard pigeon coop and reports heavy pigeon droppings there for several years.

Peripheral blood count shows WBC 8.9 × 10^9/L, CRP 24 mg/L. Sputum AFB smears and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis are negative. Routine bacterial cultures grow oral flora only. Cytology of induced sputum shows occasional extracellular round yeast forms.
Chest computed tomography demonstrates a solitary 2.6 cm cavitary nodule in the right upper lobe with surrounding ground-glass change and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

A CT-guided core biopsy was performed. Histology showed round yeasts with a prominent mucopolysaccharide capsule highlighted by mucicarmine stain. Culture of tissue on Sabouraud medium produced mucoid colonies and the isolate was urease positive. She improved clinically on oral fluconazole after partial wedge resection.

explanation: This case represents pulmonary cryptococcosis caused by Cryptococcus neoformans presenting as a cavitary pulmonary nodule after heavy pigeon droppings exposure. Chronic upper-lobe cavitary nodule in a patient with significant pigeon exposure plus biopsy showing round yeasts with a mucopolysaccharide capsule on mucicarmine stain, mucoid urease-positive colonies, and negative TB testing are diagnostic for Cryptococcus rather than other fungal or mycobacterial causes. Cryptococcus neoformans has a prominent polysaccharide capsule visible with mucicarmine or India ink and is urease positive, and it can cause isolated pulmonary nodules even in immunocompetent hosts.

hints.text: An 86-year-old woman from a residential care home is brought to hospital with 48 hours of fever, rigors, and new confusion. She reports acute dysuria. Blood pressure 90/60 mmHg and heart rate 110/min. She has an indwelling urinary catheter placed 10 days earlier after a hip fracture.

Her past medical history includes hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and recurrent urinary tract infections. Two weeks ago she completed a 10-day course of ceftriaxone for a presumed chest infection.

Urinalysis shows pyuria and is nitrite negative. Urine culture yields small, non-haemolytic colonies of Gram-positive cocci. Admission blood cultures grew the same Gram-positive cocci in chains at about 28 hours. White blood cell count 14.8 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine 160 μmol/L.
Renal ultrasound demonstrates normal renal size without hydronephrosis. The urinary catheter tip projects within the bladder and there is no evidence of perinephric fluid collection or abscess.

Empiric piperacillin-tazobactam was started. After culture and susceptibility results the team switched to intravenous ampicillin. She defervesced within 48 hours and repeat blood cultures became sterile. The isolate was reported resistant to cephalosporins but susceptible to ampicillin.

explanation: This is catheter-associated urinary tract infection with secondary bacteremia due to Enterococcus faecalis. An elderly patient with an indwelling urinary catheter, nitrite-negative pyuria, and matching small non‑hemolytic Gram‑positive cocci in chains from urine and blood that are cephalosporin‑resistant but ampicillin‑susceptible fits Enterococcus rather than staphylococci or streptococci. The organism's propensity to cause nosocomial UTIs and to seed the bloodstream explains the clinical picture of sepsis and confusion. Enterococci are gut commensals that commonly form biofilms on urinary catheters, are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, and frequently retain susceptibility to ampicillin.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to clinic with 2 weeks of progressive fatigue, anorexia, nausea, dark urine and yellowing of the eyes. He reports mild right upper quadrant discomfort and a low-grade fever. On exam he is jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant. He mentions a new sexual partner about 6 weeks ago and says he did not receive childhood immunisation for the relevant infection.

No prior liver disease. Denies intravenous drug use, recent tattoos, travel outside the country, or heavy alcohol intake. No regular medications and denies acetaminophen overdose. HIV test last year was negative.

Abdominal ultrasound shows an enlarged liver with preserved echotexture, no focal hepatic lesions, and no biliary dilatation. Portal and hepatic vein flow appear normal. No gallstones or cholecystitis.

Serum ALT 1 920 U/L, AST 1 080 U/L, total bilirubin 85 µmol/L, INR 1.4, WBC 6.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 230 × 10^9/L. Serum PCR detects viral DNA at 6.2 × 10^7 IU/mL. IgM antibody directed against a viral core antigen is present.
