Oral nucleotide analogue therapy was started given symptomatic acute liver injury and high viraemia. Within 3 weeks the patient reports improved appetite and decreasing jaundice. Repeat serum viral DNA decreased by >3 log10 to 4.1 × 10^4 IU/mL and ALT is falling toward the reference range.

explanation: The diagnosis is Hepatitis B virus. The incubation timing after a new sexual exposure, very high HBV DNA levels, and presence of IgM antibody to the core antigen together identify acute hepatitis B as the cause of the marked transaminase elevation rather than another viral or toxic hepatitis. Hepatitis B is a partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus that replicates via reverse transcription and can integrate into host DNA, predisposing to chronic infection and hepatocellular carcinoma.

hints.text: A 62-year-old retired poultry farmer presents with 3 months of productive cough, intermittent haemoptysis and an 8 kg unintentional weight loss. He reports night sweats and reduced exercise tolerance. He has a 30 pack-year smoking history. On exam he appears thin with localized coarse crackles over the right upper chest.
Known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with inhaled bronchodilators. No prior diagnosis of tuberculosis. HIV test negative. No systemic immunosuppressive drugs.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 105 g/L, WBC 8.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 240 × 10^9/L. ESR 78 mm/h. Three sputum samples negative for acid-fast bacilli by smear and NAAT. Sputum fungal stain reveals small intracellular yeast forms within alveolar macrophages.
Chest CT shows a 4.2 cm thin-walled cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe with surrounding fibrotic scarring. Multiple calcified hilar lymph nodes are present.

He has lived his whole life in a river basin region endemic for cave and bird roost exposures. He routinely cleaned an old chicken coop and the attic of a barn where heavy bird droppings accumulated. Respiratory cultures later grew a dimorphic fungus.

explanation: This is chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis due to Histoplasma capsulatum, likely related to environmental exposure to bird droppings. The epidemiologic history of bird and bat guano exposure, an upper‑lobe cavitary lesion with systemic symptoms, and identification of small intracellular yeasts within macrophages on sputum point to Histoplasma rather than tuberculosis or common molds, and subsequent growth of a dimorphic fungus confirms the diagnosis. Histoplasma is a dimorphic fungus that appears as small intracellular yeasts in tissue and as a mold with microconidia in the environment, and antigen testing of urine or serum is useful in disseminated disease.

hints.text: A 46-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with a 6-week history of progressive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, night sweats, and a 6 kg weight loss. He reports low-grade fevers and increasing exertional breathlessness. On exam he is afebrile with oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Chest auscultation reveals reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles localized to the right upper lung field.

Past medical history notable only for type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, recent HbA1c 9.2%. He is a current smoker, 20 pack-years. He completed a short course of oral amoxicillin prescribed by his general practitioner 3 weeks ago with no clinical improvement. He denies known HIV, haematologic malignancy, chronic corticosteroid use, or previous tuberculosis.

Blood tests show WBC 12.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.5 × 10^9/L. CRP 92 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures are sterile. Sputum bacterial culture shows normal respiratory flora. Three induced sputum smears for acid fast bacilli are negative. Routine renal and liver function are within reference ranges.

Chest CT demonstrates a 4.5 cm thin-walled cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe with adjacent patchy nodular consolidation and several small peribronchial nodules in the same lobe. No pleural effusion. Mediastinal lymph nodes are mildly enlarged. A comparison chest radiograph from 8 weeks earlier had shown only a small right apical scarring.

He reports a 10-day work assignment two months before symptom onset grading unpaved roads in the San Joaquin Valley. During that period a windstorm produced heavy dust clouds. Two co-workers developed febrile respiratory illnesses. A CT-guided core biopsy of the cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathology shows large nonbudding spherical structures 20–60 μm in diameter filled with numerous uniform endospores.

explanation: The diagnosis is Coccidioides species. The history of working in the San Joaquin Valley with a dust storm, subacute constitutional and pulmonary symptoms, and histopathology showing large spherules 20 to 60 μm filled with endospores are diagnostic of Coccidioides and distinguish it from other dimorphic fungi and mycobacterial disease. Coccidioides forms large nonbudding spherules containing endospores in tissue while producing infectious arthroconidia in soil, and culturing the organism poses a significant laboratory biosafety risk.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man on hospital day 21 presents with a 7-day history of low-grade fevers up to 38.1°C and new pruritic, finely scaly, hypopigmented macules across the upper chest and back. He reports the rash started gradually and is worse with heat. On exam there are multiple 1–3 cm flaky macules and a few tender erythematous papules on the anterior chest. A tunneled central venous catheter is in place.

Three weeks earlier he underwent emergency small bowel resection for mesenteric ischemia and now has short bowel syndrome. He has been receiving total parenteral nutrition including an intravenous lipid emulsion for 18 days. He completed a 10-day course of broad-spectrum antibiotics for intra-abdominal contamination and received a short course of systemic corticosteroids for bronchospasm while in the ICU.

Admission labs show WBC 11.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 145 mg/L, platelets 98 × 10^9/L. Paired peripheral and catheter blood cultures were reported as positive for small budding yeast forms on Gram stain in 3/3 sets. Subculture on routine media produced no colonies. When an agar overlaid with olive oil was used, smooth creamy colonies grew within 48 hours. Scale from the chest on KOH preparation revealed round yeast forms with short hyphae.

Point-of-care ultrasound of the catheter showed echogenic material adherent to the distal lumen suggestive of intraluminal thrombus. Chest radiograph showed a correctly positioned catheter tip and no focal pulmonary consolidation. No intra-abdominal collections were identified on bedside ultrasound.

The catheter was removed and the lipid component of parenteral nutrition was stopped. Fever resolved within 36 hours and repeat blood cultures were sterile at 48 hours. The organism retrieved from the lipid-supplemented culture matched the yeast forms seen on the skin KOH.

explanation: This case represents catheter-related fungemia with concomitant tinea versicolor caused by Malassezia furfur in the setting of prolonged total parenteral nutrition with lipid emulsion. The organism was a small budding yeast seen on blood Gram stain that failed to grow on routine media but produced smooth colonies only on lipid‑supplemented agar, and the skin KOH showing round yeasts with short hyphae matches Malassezia; the presence of a tunneled catheter, intraluminal thrombus and lipid infusion with rapid clearance after catheter removal and stopping lipids clinch a catheter-associated lipid‑dependent fungemia. Malassezia species are lipophilic yeasts that often cause tinea versicolor on skin and can cause catheter or TPN‑associated bloodstream infections because they require lipid supplementation to grow in culture.

hints.text: A 19-year-old male university student presents to the emergency department 12 hours after onset of fever and severe bifrontal headache. He reports vomiting, photophobia and neck stiffness. During triage he developed scattered petechial lesions on his trunk and lower limbs. Temperature 39.7°C, heart rate 125/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 14.

Previously healthy, no history of splenectomy or immunodeficiency. He smokes lightly and recalls not having received the adolescent conjugate meningococcal vaccine. Symptoms progressed from malaise to severe headache and rash over a single day.

Bloods show white cell count 18.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, platelets 45 × 10^9/L, CRP 320 mg/L and INR 1.8. Lumbar puncture after CT had opening pressure 28 cm H2O. CSF was turbid with leucocytes 2100 × 10^6/L (predominantly neutrophils), protein 2.5 g/L and glucose 0.8 mmol/L with concurrent serum glucose 6.2 mmol/L. Gram stain of CSF demonstrated Gram-negative diplococci.

Contrast CT abdomen performed for ongoing hypotension shows bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with peripheral high attenuation and central low attenuation, consistent with acute bilateral adrenal haemorrhage.

He shares a 12-person hall of residence. Public health were notified and identified multiple close contacts; single-dose oral fluoroquinolone prophylaxis was given to exposed housemates. Nasopharyngeal PCRs from two roommates were positive for an oxidase-positive, maltose-fermenting Gram-negative diplococcus.

explanation: This presentation is fulminant meningococcal meningitis with meningococcemia complicated by bilateral adrenal hemorrhage consistent with Waterhouse‑Friderichsen syndrome. Rapidly progressive fever, neck stiffness and a petechial purpuric rash with hypotension and DIC plus CSF neutrophilic meningitis and Gram‑negative kidney‑shaped diplococci that are oxidase positive and maltose fermenting point to Neisseria meningitidis, and nasopharyngeal positives in close contacts support a transmissible carriage source. Neisseria meningitidis colonizes the nasopharynx and spreads by respiratory droplets, with capsular serogroups determining invasive potential and targeted vaccine strategies.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 18 hours of abdominal cramps, profuse watery diarrhoea 8 times, nausea and two episodes of vomiting. She reported a fever at home of 38.9°C and felt light-headed when standing. On arrival she was febrile 38.7°C, heart rate 108 bpm, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, and had dry mucous membranes and diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs.

She is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, is not pregnant and has no history of chronic gastrointestinal disease. She had not taken antibiotics or acid-suppressing drugs in the prior month and had no recent international travel. She works in childcare and had no known animal exposures at home.

Blood tests showed leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 11.0 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 78 mg/L. Creatinine 120 μmol/L consistent with mild pre-renal azotaemia. Stool microscopy positive for fecal leukocytes and faint occult blood. Initial stool culture returned growth of a motile, oxidase-negative, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus that produces hydrogen sulphide on triple sugar iron agar.

CT abdomen and pelvis with oral and IV contrast performed for persistent pain showed circumferential mucosal thickening of the terminal ileum and several mildly enlarged adjacent mesenteric lymph nodes. No perforation or bowel obstruction was identified.

On targeted questioning she disclosed attending a family gathering 36 hours before illness, where multiple attendees ate a homemade chicken liver pâté and several developed similar diarrhoeal illness. Public health cultures later recovered the same motile, hydrogen sulphide–producing, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacillus from both the leftover pâté and stool samples from affected contacts.

explanation: The diagnosis is Non-typhoidal Salmonella. The clinical picture of acute diarrheal illness following a common exposure, stool fecal leukocytes and occult blood, and isolation of a motile oxidase‑negative non‑lactose fermenting Gram‑negative bacillus that produces hydrogen sulfide on TSI are classic for non‑typhoidal Salmonella and match the organism recovered from the implicated food. Non‑typhoidal Salmonella typically causes self‑limited diarrheal disease after poultry or egg exposure and can invade ileal Peyer patches causing terminal ileitis; H2S production on culture helps distinguish Salmonella from Shigella.

hints.text: A 42-year-old primary school teacher presents with 3 days of nasal congestion and hoarseness followed by 24 hours of a harsh 'barking' cough. He has low-grade fever to 38.0°C and progressive noisy breathing, worse at night. On examination he has biphasic stridor at rest, mild intercostal retractions, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.

Past medical history notable only for well controlled asthma treated with a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. He received this season's influenza vaccine. He reports being otherwise well until this illness and has had no recent intubation, facial trauma, or dental procedure.

Blood count shows WBC 7.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 4.8 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 1.9 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. Rapid influenza antigen and respiratory syncytial virus PCR are negative. Throat bacterial culture pending. A nasopharyngeal multiplex PCR has been sent.

Anteroposterior neck radiograph obtained because of persistent stridor shows subglottic narrowing producing a focal tapering of the upper trachea consistent with laryngotracheobronchitis. Frontal chest radiograph is clear without focal consolidation.

Occupational review reveals a small cluster of children at a nearby preschool had abrupt onset barking cough over the prior week and two of his teacher colleagues developed similar symptoms. Subsequent testing of several exposed children identified an enveloped negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus that agglutinates red blood cells and produces syncytia in cell culture. The patient's nasopharyngeal PCR returned positive for the same agent.

explanation: The diagnosis is Parainfluenza virus. The acute onset of hoarseness, nocturnal barking cough and biphasic stridor with radiographic subglottic tapering, an epidemiologic cluster in preschool contacts, and detection of an enveloped negative‑sense RNA virus that agglutinates red cells and forms syncytia on culture point to parainfluenza as the etiologic agent. Human parainfluenza viruses are a leading cause of croup because their hemagglutinin‑neuraminidase and fusion proteins promote upper airway infection and cell‑to‑cell fusion, which produces the characteristic airway inflammation and obstruction.

hints.text: A 28-year-old primigravida at 22 weeks' gestation presents to the antenatal clinic with 5 days of low-grade fever and new symmetric joint pain in her wrists and proximal interphalangeal joints. She notes mild facial flushing but no pruritus. She teaches in a primary school. Fetal movements are reported as normal. On examination temperature is 37.8°C and the rest of the maternal exam is unremarkable.

No chronic medical conditions, no known haemoglobinopathy, and no recent transfusions. Pregnancy to date had been uncomplicated with normal first trimester screens. She is not on immunosuppressive medication and has no history of frequent infections.

Maternal blood tests show haemoglobin 98 g/L, white cell count 6.5 × 10^9/L, platelets 220 × 10^9/L. Reticulocyte percentage is 0.4%. C-reactive protein 3 mg/L. Liver transaminases are within reference limits. Routine prenatal serology pending.

Targeted obstetric ultrasound demonstrates fetal ascites, scalp oedema and a moderate pericardial effusion consistent with hydrops fetalis. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is 1.8 multiples of median for gestation, consistent with moderate to severe fetal anaemia.

Public health follow up reveals an outbreak in her class the previous week, several pupils had abrupt onset facial erythema described by parents as 'slapped cheeks' followed by a reticular truncal rash. Maternal serology later returned positive IgM and PCR on amniotic fluid detected high copy numbers of a small single-stranded DNA virus known to infect erythroid precursors.

explanation: This is acute maternal Parvovirus B19 infection with transplacental fetal infection causing severe fetal anemia and nonimmune hydrops fetalis. Symmetric adult arthralgia after exposure to schoolchildren with 'slapped cheek' illness, maternal IgM positivity, low reticulocyte percentage suggesting marrow suppression, and ultrasound with fetal ascites, scalp edema and elevated MCA velocity together with high-copy PCR of a small single-stranded DNA virus in amniotic fluid point specifically to parvovirus B19 infecting fetal erythroid precursors rather than other vertically transmitted agents. Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid precursor cells via the P antigen and can cause profound fetal anemia and hydrops when maternal infection occurs in the second trimester.

hints.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of high fevers, severe frontal headache, and vomiting. She reports dark urine and increasing lethargy. On arrival she is febrile 39.5°C, tachycardic 120/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, mildly jaundiced, and intermittently disoriented to time.

No chronic medical conditions except elective splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision five years ago. She is not pregnant. She left work early because of progressive weakness over two days, and had no recent antibiotics. She has no known allergies and takes no routine medications.

Laboratory results show haemoglobin 68 g/L, white cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 38 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 68 µmol/L, creatinine 150 µmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, and LDH 980 U/L. Peripheral blood film reported marked haemolysis and frequent red cell inclusions; urgent parasitological studies were requested.
Non-contrast CT head shows mild diffuse cerebral oedema without discrete focal infarct or intracranial haemorrhage. Abdominal ultrasound confirms absence of spleen and mild hepatomegaly.

She returned nine days ago from a two-week visit to relatives in coastal West Africa where she slept without bed netting and did not take any chemoprophylaxis. Thick and thin blood films prepared in the ED show high-level intraerythrocytic parasitaemia measured at 12%, numerous small ring forms with multiple rings in single erythrocytes, and crescent-shaped sexual stages on the thin film.

explanation: This presentation is severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria with high parasitemia causing hemolytic anemia, metabolic disturbance and signs of cerebral involvement. Recent travel to West Africa without prophylaxis, very high parasitemia of 12 percent, numerous small ring forms with multiple rings per erythrocyte and crescent shaped gametocytes on thin film are characteristic for P. falciparum and distinguish it from other Plasmodium species and nonmalarial causes of hemolysis; prior splenectomy further explains the fulminant course. P. falciparum produces high level and often multi-infected erythrocyte parasitemia with sequestration that underlies severe complications and the distinctive banana shaped gametocytes on thin smear.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency clinic with a 2-week history of progressive exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He reports low-grade fevers and a 1.5 kg weight loss. On arrival SpO2 is 89% on room air, respiratory rate 22/min. Chest auscultation reveals fine bilateral crackles, no wheeze, no peripheral oedema.

He has known HIV infection diagnosed 2 years earlier but reports stopping antiretroviral therapy 3 months ago after relocating. He has not been taking any prophylactic antibiotics. Six months ago his CD4 count was 120 × 10^6/L. He smokes 5 cigarettes daily and has no recent travel or occupational inhalational exposures.

Arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 7.0 kPa. Serum lactate dehydrogenase 820 U/L. White cell count 4.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 35 mg/L. Routine sputum cultures and a nasal viral PCR are negative.

High-resolution chest CT shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass attenuation, greatest centrally with relative subpleural sparing. There is mild interlobular septal thickening and no pleural effusion or lobar consolidation.

Empiric high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with adjunctive oral corticosteroids was started for presumed opportunistic pneumonia. Over 72 hours his PaO2 rose to 10.8 kPa and dyspnea improved. Bronchoalveolar lavage subsequently yielded foamy proteinaceous material and organisms visualised on methenamine silver stain.

explanation: This is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia causing progressive hypoxemic interstitial lung disease in an untreated patient with advanced HIV. The history of stopping antiretroviral therapy with low CD4 risk, subacute exertional dyspnea and dry cough, profound hypoxemia with disproportionately elevated LDH, diffuse central ground glass opacities with subpleural sparing on CT, and foamy material with organisms on methenamine silver stain from BAL are diagnostic for Pneumocystis rather than bacterial or typical viral pneumonia. Pneumocystis jirovecii is not readily cultured and is diagnosed by microscopic identification on induced sputum or BAL, and it commonly causes severe hypoxemia with diffuse ground glass opacities in patients with impaired cellular immunity.

hints.text: An 18-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of progressive weakness in his right leg. Two days before the weakness he had fever and sore throat. On exam he is afebrile, alert, with flaccid paresis of the right lower limb, reduced tone, absent deep tendon reflexes on the right, preserved pinprick and light touch, and no sensory level.

He is a university student with no chronic illnesses. Childhood immunisations were incomplete; he received only two infant doses of the standard paralytic disease vaccine series and no later booster. He reports no recent vaccinations since childhood, no intravenous drug use, and no preceding trauma.

CSF shows 40 × 10^6/L leucocytes with 80% lymphocytes, protein 0.8 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L with paired serum glucose 5.0 mmol/L. Bacterial culture of CSF is sterile. Routine blood count is 9.8 × 10^9/L with normal differential. PCR panel for herpesviruses in CSF is negative. Nerve conduction studies show reduced compound muscle action potentials in the affected limb with preserved sensory nerve action potentials.

MRI of the spine demonstrates T2 hyperintense signal and restricted diffusion confined to the anterior horn cell region of the lumbar enlargement, without a compressive lesion or meningeal enhancement.

Two weeks before illness he spent 10 days volunteering at a refugee camp where local public health reported multiple recent cases of acute flaccid paralysis in children. Stool testing from that cluster yielded a small, non-enveloped single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus that matched one of the three serotypes targeted by routine inactivated and oral childhood immunisation regimens.

explanation: This case represents acute flaccid paralysis from poliovirus infection with selective anterior horn cell involvement in an under-immunized individual. A preceding febrile prodrome followed by asymmetric flaccid weakness with preserved sensation, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, MRI changes confined to anterior horn cells, electrophysiology showing reduced motor amplitudes with preserved sensory responses, and stool confirmation of a poliovirus serotype in a setting of incomplete vaccination and exposure at a camp all point to poliovirus rather than other enteroviruses or Guillain Barré syndrome. Poliovirus is a non-enveloped positive sense RNA enterovirus that destroys anterior horn motor neurons and is largely controlled by routine childhood vaccination, so outbreaks occur primarily in under-immunized populations.

hints.text: A 66-year-old man presents to the emergency clinic with 10 days of left ear pain, progressive hearing loss, and purulent, malodorous discharge. He is febrile to 38.3°C. On examination the external auditory canal is erythematous and tender, with friable granulation tissue deep in the canal and severe pain on manipulation of the tragus.

He has a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes with poor control, recent HbA1c 9.0%. He reports cleaning his ear with cotton buds and had been swimming daily at a local hotel pool for the week before symptoms began. He used over-the-counter topical drops without improvement.

Blood tests show white cell count 15.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 112 mg/L. Capillary glucose is 16 mmol/L. Gram stain of canal discharge demonstrates gram-negative rods. Routine blood cultures remain negative at 48 hours.

Contrast CT of the temporal bones shows focal erosion of the posterolateral external auditory canal with soft tissue extension into the adjacent temporal bone and early medially directed bone involvement, findings concerning for skull base osteomyelitis.

Environmental cultures were obtained from the hotel pool and the patient’s home shower. Isolates from the ear discharge and from the pool grew an oxidase positive, non-fermenting gram-negative rod that produced blue-green pigment, emitted a distinct fruity odour on culture plates, and grew at 42°C.

explanation: This presentation is malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa with contiguous skull base osteomyelitis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The classic diabetic risk factor, severe external ear pain with granulation tissue and CT evidence of temporal bone erosion point to malignant otitis externa, and the organism from ear and pool cultures is an oxidase positive non‑fermenting gram negative rod that produces a blue‑green pigment, emits a fruity odour and grows at 42°C, findings that identify Pseudomonas aeruginosa rather than other gram negative rods. Pseudomonas makes the pigment pyocyanin that gives colonies a blue‑green colour and promotes tissue damage, and its thermotolerance, biofilm formation and intrinsic antibiotic resistance help explain its persistence in water sources and chronic wound or device related infections.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by family with 4 days of fever, malaise, and headache followed by 24 hours of increasing anxiety, confusion, and agitation. He has intermittent choking and gagging when offered water and appears to drool more than usual. On arrival he is febrile 38.6 °C, tachycardic, diaphoretic, and intermittently disoriented to time. A small healed puncture wound is visible on the dorsum of his right hand.

He returned 3 weeks ago from visiting rural villages where he slept in simple wooden houses. He recalls being awakened one night by something landing on his hand but did not seek care because the wound bled little and healed. He has no relevant chronic medical conditions and reports no recent vaccinations before travel and no wound care or immunisations after the incident.

Admission blood count shows leukocytosis 13.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance. Lumbar puncture on day 1 of neurologic decline: opening pressure normal, CSF white cell count 72 × 10^6/L with 88% lymphocytes, protein 0.95 g/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L. Gram stain and routine bacterial cultures of CSF are negative. PCR assays for herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses are negative.

Brain MRI performed on hospital day 2 shows bilateral hyperintense signal on T2/FLAIR within the hippocampi and dorsal medulla. There is no focal mass lesion and no abnormal parenchymal enhancement after contrast. Findings are most prominent in limbic structures and the brainstem.

On further questioning the family confirm that the nocturnal contact three weeks earlier was with a small sleeping mammal that fell onto his hand while he slept; they later found the animal dead in the corner of the room and describe it as bat-sized. No post-exposure prophylaxis or immunisations were obtained after that event.

explanation: The diagnosis is Rabies virus. The three week incubation after nocturnal contact with a small bat, the evolving anxiety, dysphagia and hypersalivation, lymphocytic CSF with negative bacterial and HSV tests, and MRI changes in limbic and brainstem structures all fit rabies virus rather than other causes of encephalitis. Rabies is a bullet shaped rhabdovirus that travels centripetally in peripheral nerves to the central nervous system and is almost always fatal once clinical neurologic symptoms appear, which is why timely post‑exposure prophylaxis before symptom onset is critically protective.

hints.text: A 68-year-old retired preschool teacher presents to the emergency department with 7 days of progressive dyspnoea and dry cough following a brief runny nose. She reports increased work of breathing and new wheeze. On arrival she is tachypnoeic, uses accessory muscles, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air, falling to 86% with minimal exertion. Past medical history includes COPD and compensated heart failure.

Two weeks before presentation she completed a short course of oral corticosteroids for a COPD flare. Family history on review reveals that a 7-month-old grandchild stayed in the house during the previous week and was admitted to hospital with bronchiolitis two days before the patient's symptoms began.

Blood tests show white cell count 6.1 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.8 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 4.7 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. Blood cultures and sputum cultures show no growth after 48 hours. A nasopharyngeal viral PCR panel was submitted on admission and remained pending at 36 hours.

Chest CT without contrast demonstrates diffuse peribronchial thickening, small scattered centrilobular nodules, patchy peribronchial ground-glass opacities and minimal subsegmental atelectasis. There is no focal lobar consolidation to suggest bacterial lobar pneumonia.

Infection‑control flagged a paediatric cluster earlier that week. The grandchild's nasopharyngeal PCR returned positive for the same virus identified by the hospital's paediatric lab. The patient's nasopharyngeal PCR subsequently returned positive for that single pathogen, the same virus for which palivizumab is used as prophylaxis in high‑risk infants.

explanation: The diagnosis is Respiratory syncytial virus. Her illness followed household exposure to an infant with the same virus, the PCR identified the single pathogen for which palivizumab is used in infants, and the imaging and lack of bacterial growth are typical for viral bronchiolitis caused by RSV rather than bacterial pneumonia. RSV is an enveloped paramyxovirus that uses its F protein to drive syncytium formation, and monoclonal antibody prophylaxis against the F protein is used in selected high risk infants while older adults with COPD remain vulnerable to severe RSV disease.

hints.text: A 34-year-old female preschool teacher presents in early autumn with 4 days of nasal congestion, clear rhinorrhoea, sore throat and daytime cough. Over the last 24 hours she developed increased wheeze and dyspnoea on minimal exertion. She reports no high fevers. On examination temperature 37.8 °C, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. There is diffuse expiratory wheeze and nasal mucosal oedema.

She has atopic asthma since childhood, on inhaled corticosteroid and short acting bronchodilator. No systemic corticosteroids in the past year. Non-smoker. Influenza vaccination this season. Takes no other regular medicines. She works in a nursery caring for 2–5 year olds. No recent travel, no known sick contacts at home.

Full blood count WBC 7.1 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 4.3 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 2.0 × 10^9/L, eosinophils 0.3 × 10^9/L. CRP 6 mg/L. Multiplex nasopharyngeal PCR negative for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, metapneumovirus, adenovirus and seasonal coronaviruses. A single positive PCR signal was detected for a small non-enveloped positive-sense single-stranded RNA respiratory virus. Viral culture from the same swab produced cytopathic effect when incubated at 33 °C but no growth at 37 °C.

Chest radiograph shows peribronchial cuffing and no focal lobar consolidation. Peak expiratory flow measured in clinic 240 L/min, down from her personal best of 420 L/min. No radiographic evidence to suggest bacterial pneumonia.

Nursery records show a cluster of brief upper respiratory illnesses among children 48–72 hours before the teacher became symptomatic. Parents reported runny nose and sneezing without significant fever and rapid recovery. The combination of an adult with asthma exacerbation following a preschool outbreak, a single positive respiratory PCR for a small non-enveloped ssRNA virus, and culture growth only at cooler incubation temperature points to the responsible pathogen.

explanation: This is a rhinovirus upper respiratory infection that precipitated an asthma exacerbation in an adult with atopic asthma. The epidemiology of a preschool outbreak, mild upper respiratory prodrome without high fever, a single PCR signal for a small non‑enveloped positive sense ssRNA virus, and viral culture that grows at 33 °C but not 37 °C all point to rhinovirus rather than other respiratory viruses. Rhinoviruses are picornaviruses with many serotypes that replicate best at cooler temperatures of the nasal mucosa and commonly bind ICAM‑1, which helps explain frequent reinfections and why they are major triggers of asthma exacerbations.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency clinic with 8 days of progressive left-sided facial pain, nasal congestion, and purulent nasal discharge. Over 48 hours he developed increasing periorbital swelling and left-sided facial numbness. He reports low-grade fevers and difficulty chewing because of pain. On examination he has left periorbital oedema, reduced sensation over the maxillary distribution, and mild proptosis with preserved extraocular movements.

He has transfusion dependent haemoglobinopathy and receives regular red cell transfusions. He has been on iron chelation therapy with an injectable iron chelator for the last 9 months. He denies diabetes, corticosteroid use, recent travel, and HIV risk factors. He had a dental extraction on the same side 3 weeks ago without immediate complications.

Contrast CT of the paranasal sinuses shows opacification of the left maxillary and ethmoid sinuses with irregular erosion of the medial maxillary wall and extension of soft tissue into the inferomedial orbit. There is suggestion of cisternal enhancement along the skull base but no discrete abscess.
He works part time as a community gardener. In the week before symptom onset he spent several days turning an old compost pile and clearing rotting vegetation at a community allotment.

At endoscopic sinus debridement tissue was sent for histology and culture. Routine blood tests showed haemoglobin 72 g/L and white cell count 9.6 × 10^9/L. Histology of necrotic sinus mucosa demonstrates broad, ribbonlike hyphae, largely without septa, branching at irregular, wide angles and invading vessel walls. Fungal culture grew a rapidly expanding woolly colony within 48 hours.

explanation: Invasive rhinocerebral mucormycosis due to Rhizopus species causing necrotizing sinusitis with orbital and skull base extension. The histology shows broad, ribbonlike nonseptate hyphae with wide-angle branching and angioinvasion, and culture grew a rapidly expanding woolly mold; these features together with soil and decaying vegetation exposure, recent dental manipulation, and iron chelation therapy point to mucorales rather than septate molds like Aspergillus. Mucorales are highly angioinvasive fungi that exploit high free iron states, so iron overload and certain iron chelators markedly increase susceptibility to rapidly progressive disease.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented in late June with 4 days of high fever to 39.6°C, frontal headache, severe myalgias and progressive rash. The rash began 2 days after fever onset on his wrists and ankles and has spread centrally to involve the forearms and palms. He reports nausea and photophobia. On examination he is febrile 39.2°C, heart rate 110 min−1, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and has a maculopapular eruption with several petechial lesions on the wrists and palms.

He is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, and works on a forestry crew. Symptoms progressed despite 48 hours of outpatient symptomatic treatment and a single prescription for amoxicillin. He has no recent international travel and no known sick contacts. He does not recall any recent vaccinations beyond childhood schedule.

Routine blood tests show white blood cell count 8.5 × 10^9/L, platelet count 72 × 10^9/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, AST 156 U/L, ALT 98 U/L, and C-reactive protein 118 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures drawn on admission remain sterile at 24 hours. Prothrombin time is within reference range.

Chest radiograph is clear. Non-contrast CT of the head performed for severe headache shows no acute intracranial abnormality. Photographs of the rash taken on admission show early petechial change most prominent at distal extremities.

He remembered removing an attached tick from his right ankle five days before fever onset after an overnight camping trip in a wooded area of the southeastern United States. The rash began at the wrists and ankles within days of the bite and progressed to involve the palms and soles.

explanation: Rocky Mountain spotted fever from Rickettsia rickettsii, presenting with febrile illness, myalgias, and a centripetal maculopapular to petechial rash. A tick exposure in wooded habitat followed by a rash beginning on the wrists and ankles that progressed centrally to involve the palms and soles, together with thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and transaminitis, is classic for RMSF and distinguishes it from viral exanthems or bacterial sepsis. Rickettsia rickettsii infects vascular endothelium causing a vasculitic petechial rash that often starts on distal extremities and can become severe within days of symptom onset.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man five months after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation presents with four weeks of high-volume watery diarrhoea, up to eight watery stools daily, with crampy periumbilical pain and 4 kg weight loss. He is afebrile, mildly tachycardic, and exam shows dry mucous membranes and diffusely soft, non-tender abdomen without organomegaly.

Immunosuppression includes tacrolimus and low-dose prednisone for chronic graft-versus-host disease. He has not received recent broad-spectrum antibiotics and denies recent travel. He lives with his partner and a 2-year-old child who had an episode of profuse vomiting followed by watery diarrhoea two weeks before the patient's symptoms began.

Blood tests show lymphopenia 0.4 × 10^9/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, creatinine 120 µmol/L and C-reactive protein 18 mg/L. Repeated stool studies are negative for bacterial culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin. Multiplex stool PCR returned positive for a non-enveloped, segmented double-stranded RNA virus commonly included on paediatric viral gastroenteritis panels.

Contrast CT abdomen shows diffuse small-bowel wall thickening and luminal fluid without colonic wall thickening, no free air, and only small mesenteric lymph nodes. Findings were felt more consistent with small-intestinal enteritis than with predominant colonic graft-versus-host disease.

The household 2-year-old was unvaccinated for the routine infant vaccine that prevents this pathogen. The toddler's clinic performed a rapid stool enzyme immunoassay which was strongly positive for the same viral antigen detected on the patient's multiplex PCR, and sequencing showed identical viral genotype in both stools.

explanation: Protracted rotavirus small-intestinal enteritis in an immunocompromised adult with household transmission from an unvaccinated toddler. Stool multiplex PCR detected a non-enveloped segmented double-stranded RNA virus with identical genotype to the symptomatic child, imaging showed small-bowel predominant enteritis, and bacterial and C. difficile studies were negative, supporting rotavirus rather than bacterial causes or graft-versus-host disease. Rotavirus is a segmented dsRNA member of the Reoviridae family that commonly causes severe pediatric gastroenteritis and can produce prolonged shedding and more persistent illness in immunocompromised hosts.

hints.text: A 29-year-old primigravida presents to the antenatal clinic with 48 hours of low-grade fever, sore throat, conjunctival injection and a faint erythematous maculopapular rash that began on the trunk and limbs. She is at estimated 9 weeks' gestation and reports new stiffness and aching in the small joints of both hands.

She has no chronic medical problems. She emigrated from Eastern Europe at age 16 and is unsure of childhood booster vaccines. First-trimester antenatal records contain no documented serology proving immunity to the relevant vaccine-preventable exanthems.

Complete blood count shows WBC 3.9 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 5 mg/L. Maternal serum returned positive for virus-specific IgM with low-avidity IgG, a pattern consistent with recent primary infection on acute and convalescent serology.

Targeted fetal ultrasound at 13 weeks demonstrates bilateral lens opacities suspicious for cataracts and a prominent arterial duct with abnormal flow pattern. Fetal biometric measurements are at the 10th centile for gestational age.

On review of contacts she reports caring for an unvaccinated 3-year-old niece two weeks before symptom onset. The child had fever and a rash that began on the face and was noted to have enlarged postauricular nodes. Local public health later confirmed the child had a positive PCR for the same RNA virus implicated in the maternal serology.

explanation: The diagnosis is Rubella virus. The maternal prodrome of low fever, conjunctivitis, rash and arthralgia, documented rubella IgM with low-avidity IgG indicating recent primary infection, and fetal ultrasound showing cataracts and a persistent ductus arteriosus point to rubella rather than other childhood exanthems. Rubella is a togavirus that is highly teratogenic in early pregnancy and classically causes the triad of cataracts, congenital heart defects and sensorineural deafness in affected fetuses.

hints.text: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 7 days of fever, frontal headache, diffuse abdominal pain and constipation. He reports dry cough and anorexia. Temperature 39.0°C with pulse 78 beats per minute. Examination shows a coated tongue and mild right lower quadrant tenderness without peritonism.

He returned 10 days before presentation from a 3-week visit to relatives in South Asia. He has no chronic medical conditions, is not immunosuppressed and declined pretravel immunisations. He took no antibiotics while abroad.

Blood tests show white cell count 3.4 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 110 g/L, platelets 140 × 10^9/L, CRP 86 mg/L and ALT 78 U/L. Blood cultures drawn on admission became positive at 48 hours for a motile, oxidase-negative Gram-negative bacillus that produced hydrogen sulphide on selective media.
Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrates circumferential thickening of the terminal ileum and ileocaecal valve with several enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. There is no free air or focal abscess.

During travel he frequently ate street-vendor food including raw salads and ice made with tap water. A household contact in the town works as a food handler and had an episode of febrile gastroenteritis months earlier followed by intermittent diarrhoea.

explanation: The diagnosis is Salmonella typhi. The prolonged stepwise fever, frontal headache, coated tongue, relative bradycardia, constipation, cytopenias and mildly elevated liver enzymes fit typhoid, and blood cultures yielding a motile, oxidase negative gram negative bacillus that produces hydrogen sulfide plus CT showing terminal ileum and ileocaecal inflammation point to S. Typhi rather than non-typhoidal Salmonella or other enteric pathogens. The travel history with exposure to potentially contaminated food and a local food handler with prior gastroenteritis further supports acquisition and the known foodborne or carrier-mediated transmission of S. Typhi. S. Typhi often causes systemic febrile illness with terminal ileum and Peyer patch involvement and can be carried chronically in the gallbladder of convalescent carriers, which sustains transmission in endemic settings.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began three hours earlier. He reports a preceding 10-day history of low-grade fever, dry cough and malaise. On arrival he is tachycardic at 112/min, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 89% on room air and temperature 37.9°C. Lung auscultation is unremarkable and there is no unilateral leg swelling.

Medical history notable only for well controlled hypertension. He works in an office. He visited his mother in an assisted living facility 7 days before presentation where several residents developed respiratory symptoms. He completed a two-dose primary vaccine series with an mRNA platform about 10 months ago and has not received a recent booster.

Blood tests show lymphocyte count 0.8 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 5.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 220 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 120 mg/L, ferritin 450 µg/L, D-dimer 3.4 mg/L FEU. Arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 7.8 kPa. High-sensitivity troponin is within reference range.

CT pulmonary angiography demonstrates bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. The study also shows multifocal, bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities with posterior and lower-lobe predominance, without lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

Public health testing at the assisted living facility identified a cluster of residents with sudden loss of smell and taste and positive real-time reverse transcription PCR for the pandemic single-stranded RNA respiratory virus that emerged in 2019. The patient’s nasopharyngeal swab later returned positive by the same RT-PCR assay with a low cycle threshold, consistent with high viral load.

explanation: This is COVID-19 pneumonia due to SARS-CoV-2 complicated by a prothrombotic state with bilateral pulmonary emboli during acute infection. A 10 day prodrome of dry cough, recent exposure to a cluster with anosmia and positive RT-PCR with low cycle threshold explain active SARS-CoV-2 infection, while the peripheral bilateral ground glass opacities, lymphopenia, high inflammatory markers and markedly elevated D-dimer, together with CTPA-confirmed segmental emboli, indicate viral pneumonitis accompanied by COVID-19 associated coagulopathy rather than an isolated community acquired bacterial pneumonia or noninfectious cause. The lack of unilateral leg swelling does not exclude pulmonary embolism in the setting of systemic viral endothelial injury and inflammation. SARS-CoV-2 is a single stranded RNA betacoronavirus that commonly produces peripheral ground glass opacities on imaging and triggers endothelial inflammation that increases thrombotic risk even in patients who have completed a primary vaccine series months earlier.

hints.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with 48 hours of fever to 39.0°C, crampy lower abdominal pain, urgent sensation with frequent small-volume bowel movements and tenesmus. Parents report 8 to 12 stools since symptoms began, described as bloody and mucoid. On exam he is febrile, mildly tachycardic, has dry mucous membranes and focal tenderness over the left lower quadrant without peritonism.

Previously healthy, developmentally normal, fully immunised, no chronic illness and no recent antibiotics. He attends a community daycare where three other children in his class have been absent this week with diarrhoea. There was no recent travel and no family members with a similar illness until his symptoms began.

Blood tests show white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 68 mg/L. Serum sodium 133 mmol/L. Stool microscopy shows numerous neutrophils and gross blood. Multiplex PCR panel for common viral enteropathogens is negative. Stool culture was requested and processing is underway.

Abdominal ultrasound is obtained because of persistent pain, and shows segmental thickening of the rectosigmoid colon with preserved peristalsis and no free fluid. Findings were reported as consistent with acute colitis, most marked in the distal colon.

Stool culture from the patient and two symptomatic classmates grew a non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative gram-negative bacillus. Biochemical testing showed absence of hydrogen sulfide production and the isolate was non-motile on motility medium. The public health team notes a high attack rate among toddlers in the same classroom, consistent with person-to-person transmission in a daycare setting.

explanation: This child has bacillary dysentery consistent with Shigella species causing acute invasive colitis in a daycare outbreak. The abrupt onset of high frequency, small volume bloody and mucoid stools with tenesmus, left lower quadrant colonic wall thickening, neutrophil‑rich stool and an epidemiologic high attack rate in a daycare point to Shigella rather than viral gastroenteritis or noninvasive bacterial enteritis, and the laboratory profile of a non-lactose fermenting, oxidase negative, non‑motile gram negative bacillus that does not produce hydrogen sulfide is classic for Shigella species as opposed to Salmonella or E. coli. Shigella requires only a very low infectious dose and spreads efficiently by direct person to person contact, which explains rapid outbreaks in daycare and household settings.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presents to a general medicine clinic with a 9-month history of intermittent watery diarrhoea and crampy abdominal pain. He reports 7 kg weight loss and episodic pruritus around the buttocks and perianal region. For the last 3 weeks he has had a dry cough and low-grade fevers. On exam he appears thin, temperature 37.8°C, abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness, and there is faint erythema with excoriation in the perianal area.

Medical history notable for type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and inhaled corticosteroid for asthma. He received a 7-day course of oral corticosteroids 8 weeks ago for an exacerbation. He was born and raised in a rural province of Southeast Asia and worked barefoot in rice paddies until emigrating 18 years ago. He recalls similar mild gastrointestinal complaints intermittently over many years.

Complete blood count shows white cell count 13.6 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 3.2 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 6 mg/L. Three separate standard stool microscopy examinations for ova and cysts were reported as negative.

Chest radiograph obtained for cough shows patchy bilateral peripheral air‑space opacities that are not lobar and appear migratory on comparison with imaging performed 2 weeks earlier. CT thorax demonstrates small bilateral ground-glass nodules without consolidation.

Given eosinophilia, chronic GI symptoms and migratory pulmonary findings, he received a course of antihelmintic therapy with ivermectin. Within 10 days his diarrhoea and cough resolved, eosinophil count fell to 0.2 × 10^9/L, and an agar-plate stool culture obtained after treatment demonstrated motile larvae identified on microscopy consistent with rhabditiform larvae; repeat stool testing became negative.

explanation: This clinical picture represents chronic strongyloidiasis due to Strongyloides stercoralis with pulmonary migration and autoinfection, unmasked by recent corticosteroid exposure and confirmed by post‑treatment detection of rhabditiform larvae on agar‑plate culture. Longstanding intermittent gastrointestinal symptoms, perianal pruritus, marked eosinophilia, migratory pulmonary infiltrates and a history of barefoot exposure in an endemic area are typical for S. stercoralis, and the frequent false negative routine stool microscopy followed by recovery of motile larvae on agar plate culture after empirical therapy distinguishes strongyloidiasis from other parasitic or eosinophilic disorders. The clinical course and response to antihelminthic therapy with normalization of eosinophils supports active helminth infection with autoinfection rather than a transient exposure. Strongyloides can persist for decades through an autoinfection cycle and standard stool microscopy has low sensitivity, so specialized techniques or serology are often needed to detect chronic infection.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presents to clinic with a 5-week history of a slowly enlarging papule on the dorsal aspect of her right index finger that ulcerated and intermittently drains serous fluid. Over the past 10 days she noticed two tender subcutaneous nodules ascending the forearm. She has no fever and is otherwise well.

She is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, and is not diabetic. Primary care treated the finger lesion with two courses of oral beta-lactam antibiotics without improvement. Symptoms progressed despite wound care, and she denies recent travel or known insect bites.

Blood tests show white blood cell count 7.6 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 4 mg/L. Bacterial swab and routine cultures from the finger are sterile. Punch biopsy of the primary lesion shows chronic granulomatous inflammation with occasional small yeastlike structures on periodic acid Schiff and silver stains; fungal culture was submitted and is pending.

Ultrasound of the forearm demonstrates multiple small, well defined, hypoechoic subcutaneous nodules in a linear arrangement following the superficial lymphatic distribution from the hand toward the elbow. There is no fluid collection and no involvement of tendon sheaths.

On further questioning she recalls a puncture to the right finger from a rose thorn while pruning at the plant nursery where she works about two weeks before the lesion appeared. After 7 days of incubation at 25 °C submitted fungal culture produced mouldy colonies; subculture at 37 °C converted to yeast. Microscopy of the mould phase showed slender septate hyphae with conidia borne in rosettelike clusters.

explanation: This presentation is cutaneous sporotrichosis with characteristic nodular lymphangitic spread caused by Sporothrix schenckii infection of the skin and superficial lymphatics. The history of a rose thorn puncture followed by an ulcerated papule and ascending tender subcutaneous nodules along lymphatic channels, sterile bacterial cultures, granulomatous inflammation with small yeastlike forms on fungal stains, and a mould-to-yeast thermal conversion with rosette conidia together point to Sporothrix rather than common bacterial cellulitis, Nocardia, or mycobacterial infection. Sporothrix schenckii is a thermally dimorphic fungus classically acquired from plant material and causes ‘rose gardener’s disease’ with lymphatic nodules; the mould phase shows rosette clusters of conidia and the yeast phase is seen in tissue.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after two witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizures in 48 hours. She reports three months of progressively worse frontal headaches and intermittent confusion. No prior seizure history. On arrival she is afebrile, oriented but slow to respond, and has no focal motor deficit.

Born and raised in a rural Andean community, emigrated 6 years ago and works as a school kitchen assistant. No chronic medical problems and no immunosuppressive therapy. Family members report one relative had intermittent diarrhoea during the past year. She denies recent international travel and has never been treated for intestinal parasites.

Full blood count: WBC 8.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.35 × 10^9/L. CRP normal. HIV antigen/antibody negative. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 18 cm H2O, CSF leucocytes 22 × 10^6/L with lymphocyte predominance, protein 0.8 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L. Single stool microscopy for ova and parasites reported as negative.

Non-contrast CT of the head shows multiple small cortical calcifications. Contrast MRI demonstrates numerous parenchymal and some subarachnoid cystic lesions at different stages, with several ring-enhancing lesions and surrounding vasogenic oedema.

Household review revealed that a close relative returned from seasonal work on a pig farm several months before the patient’s symptoms and later noted passage of long, white, ribbon-like segments in stool. The patient frequently ate home-prepared pork dishes at family gatherings and no household member received anti-parasitic treatment.

explanation: This is neurocysticercosis from Taenia solium, producing multiple parenchymal and subarachnoid cysts at different stages and seizures from intracranial involvement. The imaging pattern of numerous cystic lesions with ring enhancement and cortical calcifications at different stages, together with household exposure to a relative who passed tapeworm segments, fits T. solium cysticercosis rather than other parasitic or neoplastic causes, because cysticercosis results from ingestion of eggs from a human tapeworm carrier and can present with varied lesion stages on MRI. Neurocysticercosis results from ingesting T. solium eggs shed by human carriers rather than from eating undercooked pork, and lesions often coexist at different stages including viable cysts, enhancing lesions, and calcified granulomas.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented with three weeks of progressive, dull bifrontal headache, episodic confusion, and new right-sided weakness. He had persistent low-grade fevers to 38.2°C and became increasingly disoriented with impaired attention during the prior week. He is six months after a deceased-donor renal transplant and was brought by his partner for acute deterioration.

Maintenance immunosuppression consists of tacrolimus and mycophenolate. He received basiliximab at transplant and a brief prednisone taper. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis was stopped three months ago after a hypersensitivity rash. He has no history of malignancy and no recent travel beyond the region.

Blood tests showed leucocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L with absolute lymphopenia 0.7 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein was 28 mg/L. Cerebrospinal fluid had 20 × 10^6/L mononuclear cells, protein 1.1 g/L, and glucose 3.2 mmol/L with paired serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L. CSF bacterial cultures and a multiplex viral PCR panel were negative.

MRI brain with gadolinium showed three ring-enhancing lesions measuring 1.5–3.2 cm. Lesions were centred in the basal ganglia and at the corticomedullary junction with surrounding vasogenic oedema and mild mass effect. There was no diffuse meningeal enhancement.

On focused exposure history he reported gardening in a shared allotment where a neighbour had recently added cat faeces to the compost. He also ate undercooked lamb at a family meal about four weeks before symptom onset.

explanation: This clinical picture is most consistent with cerebral toxoplasmosis from Toxoplasma gondii reactivation in a heavily immunosuppressed solid organ transplant recipient. Multiple ring-enhancing lesions centered in the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction in a patient with recent discontinuation of TMP-SMX prophylaxis, significant lymphopenia on maintenance immunosuppression, exposure to cat feces, and negative bacterial and viral studies strongly favor toxoplasmosis over bacterial abscess or metastatic disease. Toxoplasma commonly causes multiple contrast-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia in immunocompromised hosts and reactivation is prevented by TMP-SMX prophylaxis in many transplant protocols.

hints.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats, frontal headache, and progressive fatigue. She returned 6 weeks ago from six months of community health work in rural eastern Indonesia. On examination she is febrile to 38.8 °C, tachycardic, pale, and has a spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

She recalls a similar self-limited febrile illness at the same site about five months before presentation that resolved without medical care. She used mosquito nets inconsistently and missed several weeks of the oral prophylaxis she had been prescribed while in the field. She has no chronic medical conditions and is not pregnant.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 86 g/L and platelets 78 × 10^9/L. Total bilirubin 48 μmol/L and lactate dehydrogenase 520 U/L, consistent with haemolysis. Blood cultures are sterile. A point-of-care malaria antigen test is positive for the pan-malarial antigen and negative for the falciparum-specific antigen. Initial thin smear describes low parasitaemia with occasional trophozoites.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms splenomegaly with a splenic length of 14.5 cm. The liver is normal in size and echotexture. No focal hepatic or splenic lesions are identified.

During her deployment she spent long periods at lowland and mid-altitude sites in eastern Indonesia where she was bitten frequently. After receiving an initial blood-stage antimalarial locally she experienced recurrent febrile episodes recurring on an approximate 48-hour rhythm. She was advised that a separate course to eradicate dormant liver stages would be needed but could not start it until screening for a relevant enzyme deficiency was performed.

explanation: This is relapsing Plasmodium vivax malaria causing cyclical fevers, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and splenomegaly after travel to an endemic area. The travel history to eastern Indonesia, pan-malarial antigen positive with negative falciparum-specific antigen, 48-hour periodic fever pattern, prior similar illness months earlier, low peripheral parasitemia, and splenomegaly point to P. vivax rather than P. falciparum or non-malarial febrile illnesses because vivax forms dormant liver hypnozoites that cause relapse. P. vivax and P. ovale can form dormant liver hypnozoites that cause relapses and require specific anti-hypnozoite therapy, which is typically given only after screening for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man attends the clinic with a 3-month history of intermittent painless visible haematuria and increased urinary frequency. Episodes produce small clots but no fever. He reports occasional right flank discomfort but denies dysuria. He is a current smoker with a 10 pack-year history. Vital signs are normal and abdominal examination is unremarkable.

Symptoms began insidiously after multiple courses of oral antibiotics for presumed urinary infection that gave transient relief. He has no history of pelvic irradiation, no known bleeding disorder, and is not immunosuppressed. He works in construction and has not had recent urologic procedures.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 116 g/L, white blood cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.3 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine 88 μmol/L. Urine dipstick positive for blood and protein, nitrite negative. Midstream urine culture yields no growth on two separate samples. Urine cytology shows no malignant cells.

Renal and bladder ultrasound demonstrates irregular nodular thickening of the posterior bladder wall with punctate and linear echogenic foci consistent with calcification. There is mild right-sided hydronephrosis without an obvious intraluminal stone.

On further questioning he says that from age 8 until age 15 he regularly swam and worked in irrigation canals and a seasonal reservoir in the Nile delta region during school holidays. He recalls episodes of an itchy rash after entering the water as a child.

explanation: This presentation is classic urinary schistosomiasis from Schistosoma haematobium causing chronic cystitis with bladder wall calcification and obstructive uropathy manifesting as painless visible haematuria. Painless terminal haematuria, a history of freshwater exposure in the Nile delta, peripheral eosinophilia, negative urine cultures, and ultrasound showing posterior bladder wall nodularity with calcification point to S. haematobium rather than bacterial cystitis or malignancy. The geography and the parasite's predilection for the pelvic venous plexus distinguish S. haematobium from intestinal schistosomes. Schistosoma haematobium eggs have a characteristic terminal spine and lodge in the vesical venous plexus, producing granulomatous inflammation and bladder wall calcification and carrying a long term risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man is referred to hepatology for 3 months of progressive abdominal distension and early satiety. He describes increasing left upper quadrant fullness and fatigue. He reports occasional small-volume bright red rectal bleeding for several months but denies fever, night sweats, or overt jaundice. On exam he has tense ascites and a firm spleen palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin. He has no spider naevi or palmar erythema.

He emigrated 18 months ago. Childhood history includes recurrent bouts of diarrhoea in adolescence managed as community disease. He drinks alcohol only rarely and has no history of intravenous drug use or blood transfusion. He is HIV negative and otherwise immunocompetent. He reports prior treatment for an unspecified intestinal parasite as a child but has no records.

CBC shows haemoglobin 108 g/L, MCV 76 fL, white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.5 × 10^9/L, platelets 90 × 10^9/L. Liver tests show ALT 32 U/L, AST 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 18 µmol/L, albumin 40 g/L, INR 1.0. Serologies for hepatitis B and C are negative. Three separate stool ova and parasite examinations were reported negative.

Ultrasound and contrast CT show marked splenomegaly, large volume ascites, and echogenic linear thickening along portal tracts producing a pipe-stem appearance of the periportal regions. Hepatic contour is smooth, hepatic veins are patent, and there is prominent portosystemic collateralisation. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrates large oesophageal varices.

On targeted questioning he recalls growing up in a riverside village in north-eastern Brazil, where he swam and fished in slow-moving freshwater canals throughout childhood. A rectal mucosal biopsy obtained during colonoscopy showed granulomatous inflammation surrounding ovoid eggs about 140 µm in length with a single prominent lateral spine on light microscopy.

explanation: This is hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni causing presinusoidal portal hypertension with massive splenomegaly and variceal bleeding risk despite preserved hepatic synthetic function. The combination of large splenomegaly, ascites, periportal 'pipe-stem' fibrosis on imaging, preserved liver function tests, a history of childhood freshwater exposure in Brazil, and rectal biopsy showing ovoid eggs with a lateral spine is diagnostic of S. mansoni rather than viral or alcoholic cirrhosis. Stool tests are often falsely negative in chronic disease while tissue biopsy can reveal the characteristic lateral-spined eggs. Schistosoma mansoni eggs measure about 140 µm and have a lateral spine, and granulomatous reaction to trapped eggs in periportal areas drives presinusoidal portal hypertension while the hepatic parenchyma remains relatively preserved.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents with six days of fever and progressive, severe muscle pain. He describes diffuse myalgias worst in the thighs and shoulders, new exertional dyspnoea, and intermittent palpitations. He had a brief self-limited episode of diarrhoea about eleven days before presentation. On examination temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 110/min, there is proximal muscle tenderness and mild facial puffiness, but no focal neurological deficit.

Previously well chef, non-smoker, takes no regular medications. He stayed in his home region and reports no recent travel abroad. Symptoms began about eleven days after attending a private weekend gathering. No known sick contacts. No recent procedures or transfusions. He denies intravenous drug use.

Full blood count shows leukocytes 16.8 × 10^9/L with absolute eosinophils 3.6 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein 92 mg/L. Serum creatine kinase 2,400 U/L. High-sensitivity troponin I 280 ng/L. ALT 128 U/L, AST 162 U/L.

Cardiac MRI demonstrates patchy midwall late gadolinium enhancement and mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, consistent with myocarditis. MRI of the thighs shows diffuse T2 hyperintensity and contrast enhancement of proximal muscle groups, compatible with active myositis.

On targeted questioning he recalls sharing homemade cured sausages made from wild boar at the gathering three weeks earlier, some slices chewed but not fully cooked. Because symptoms progressed a percutaneous thigh muscle biopsy was obtained. Histology shows coiled larvae located within striated muscle fibres, each larva surrounded by a thin inflammatory capsule.

explanation: This is acute trichinellosis from Trichinella spiralis, producing systemic illness with myositis and myocarditis after ingestion of undercooked wild boar products. The sequence of transient diarrhoea followed by fever, severe proximal myalgias, marked eosinophilia, greatly elevated creatine kinase and troponin, recent consumption of raw cured wild boar, and muscle biopsy showing coiled larvae within striated muscle fibers are pathognomonic for Trichinella infection. The biopsy finding of encysted larvae in muscle distinguishes this from other parasitic myositides. Trichinella larvae invade and encyst within skeletal muscle forming a nurse cell complex, and human infection is acquired by eating raw or undercooked pork and wild game that contain encysted larvae.

hints.text: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with 6 months of progressive fatigue and exertional breathlessness, intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain, and 3 to 4 loose stools daily that sometimes contain fresh blood and mucus. She reports an 8 kg weight loss. On examination she is pale, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, BMI 19 kg/m2, and there is mild perianal excoriation but no fever or organomegaly.

She was raised and still lives in a rural provincial town in Southeast Asia and works as a primary-school teacher. She describes limited latrine availability at the school, frequent contact with children who play in bare soil, and new-onset pica, specifically clay ingestion, developing over the last 4 months. She takes no immunosuppressants and has not received routine mass deworming in recent years.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy performed to evaluate chronic rectal bleeding shows patchy mucosal erythema and friability of the rectum and distal sigmoid. Several slender, white filamentous organisms are seen with their anterior ends embedded in the rectal mucosa, surrounded by mucous and petechiae.

When asked about exposures she notes that many pupils at her school have persistent diarrhoea and that open defecation near the school playground is common. She frequently washes soiled clothes by hand and sometimes handles soil and faecally contaminated material without gloves while supervising play.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 68 fL, white cell count 7.5 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.2 × 10^9/L. Concentrated stool microscopy demonstrates brown, barrel-shaped ova approximately 50–55 µm long with clear polar plugs at both ends.

explanation: This is heavy Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) infection causing chronic bloody diarrhoea, mucosal inflammation, and iron deficiency anemia from ongoing colonic blood loss. Endemic rural exposure with contact with contaminated soil and children, colonoscopic visualization of slender worms with anterior ends embedded in the rectal mucosa, and stool microscopy showing characteristic brown, barrel shaped eggs with biopolar clear plugs confirm Trichuris trichiura rather than bacterial colitis or inflammatory bowel disease. The attached anterior end and the bipolar-plug eggs are diagnostic features that separate whipworm from other soil transmitted helminths. Trichuris adults anchor their narrow anterior ends in the mucosa causing chronic blood loss, and their eggs are passed unembryonated and require several weeks in soil to become infective to new hosts.

hints.text: A 59-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with abrupt onset of right arm weakness and slurred speech over 8 hours. She described a lancinating left-sided frontal headache and scalp tenderness that began 6 days earlier, and low grade fever since onset of the headache. On arrival she was afebrile, blood pressure 150/86 mmHg, and examination showed right arm drift and mild expressive dysphasia. No skin lesions were seen on the trunk or limbs on initial exam.

Medical history notable for type 2 diabetes and polymyalgia rheumatica treated with prednisone 10 mg daily for 3 months. She recalled having a febrile vesicular illness in childhood but could not remember the exact year. No recent travel, no known cohabitants with chronic illness, and no recent vaccinations.

Initial blood tests showed white blood cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 18 mg/L. Lumbar puncture on day 2 demonstrated cerebrospinal fluid white cell count 120 × 10^6/L with 80% lymphocytes, protein 1.2 g/L, and glucose 3.4 mmol/L with contemporaneous serum glucose 6.2 mmol/L. CSF bacterial cultures were sterile.

MRI brain on day 3 showed multiple acute cortical and subcortical infarcts in the left temporal and parietal lobes. MR angiography demonstrated segmental narrowing of branches of the left middle cerebral artery. Contrast-enhanced vessel wall imaging showed focal enhancement of the affected arterial segments.

On further questioning the patient reported that her 6-year-old grandchild developed fever and a widespread vesicular rash two weeks before her headache began. The grandchild was cared for in the home during the period immediately preceding the patient’s illness.

explanation: The diagnosis is Varicella-zoster virus. The prodrome of lancinating headache and scalp tenderness after household exposure to a child with varicella, chronic corticosteroid use, lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, and MRI showing segmental arterial narrowing with vessel wall enhancement point to VZV-related granulomatous vasculitis rather than thromboembolism or bacterial infection. VZV can reactivate decades after primary infection and cause cerebral vasculopathy; CSF PCR is often insensitive for this complication and detection of intrathecal anti-VZV IgG increases diagnostic yield.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 18 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea and repeated vomiting. She reports passing large volumes of pale, watery stool described by family as 'rice-water' in appearance. On arrival she is tachycardic at 120 min−1, blood pressure 85/50 mmHg, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, and reduced skin turgor.

She returned 48 hours ago from a one-week visit to a coastal region after volunteer work following recent seasonal flooding. She has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications, did not receive antibiotics during travel, and reports no blood in the stool or abdominal pain beyond mild cramping.

Initial blood tests show haemoconcentration with haemoglobin 185 g/L, WBC 7.2 × 10^9/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 2.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, creatinine 220 µmol/L. Stool microscopy shows large volumes of watery fluid and mucus but no fecal leukocytes. Stool culture pending.

Contrast CT abdomen performed to evaluate persistent oliguria shows markedly fluid-filled small-bowel loops without wall thickening, no colonic mucosal enhancement or mesenteric fat stranding, and no evidence of obstruction or abscess.

During travel she repeatedly drank untreated well and bottled water from street vendors and ate raw shellfish from a flooded estuary. Local public health notices described a cluster of severe watery diarrhoea among residents after the same exposures. Regional laboratories reported isolation from stool of oxidase-positive, comma-shaped gram-negative bacilli that produce yellow colonies on sucrose-containing selective medium.

explanation: This is classic cholera due to Vibrio cholerae producing profuse secretory 'rice-water' diarrhea with severe hypovolemia. Profuse watery stools without fecal leukocytes following ingestion of untreated water and raw shellfish in a flooded coastal area, rapid dehydration with metabolic derangements, and isolation of an oxidase-positive comma-shaped gram-negative bacillus forming yellow colonies on sucrose selective medium fit V. cholerae rather than an invasive bacterial enteritis. Cholera toxin permanently activates Gs proteins to elevate adenylate cyclase and intestinal cAMP, causing massive chloride and water secretion, and V. cholerae grows well on alkaline, sucrose-containing media producing characteristic yellow colonies.

hints.text: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of fever and abdominal pain. Pain began as periumbilical cramping then localized to the right lower quadrant. She reports three watery bowel movements, one with streaks of blood. On exam temperature is 38.4°C, pulse 98/min, there is focal tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritoneal rebound. Pelvic exam is unremarkable.

She is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, and has no history of haemochromatosis or chronic liver disease. She has not received recent blood transfusions or iron supplements. She denies recent travel, antibiotic use, or new sexual partners. Symptoms developed abruptly while she was otherwise well.

Blood tests show white blood cells 12.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 10.4 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 72 mg/L. Stool microscopy shows fecal leukocytes. Routine stool culture grew small colonies of a gram-negative coccobacillus. Laboratory notes that yield increased after cold enrichment at about 4°C.

Contrast CT abdomen demonstrates concentric thickening of the terminal ileum and multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes up to 2.1 cm. The appendix appears normal. No free fluid or abscess is identified.

History obtained later disclosed attendance at a local market three days before symptom onset, where she ate undercooked pork sausages. A younger sibling who shared the meal had a brief, self-limited diarrhoeal illness the next day.

explanation: This case represents Yersinia enterocolitica infection causing terminal ileitis and mesenteric adenitis that can mimic acute appendicitis. The evolution from periumbilical pain to right lower quadrant tenderness, CT showing terminal ileal thickening with enlarged mesenteric nodes and a normal appendix, stool leukocytes and a small gram-negative coccobacillus that grows better after cold enrichment, and recent consumption of undercooked pork point to Y. enterocolitica rather than typical enteric pathogens. Yersinia enterocolitica is notable for its ability to grow at low temperatures, is classically associated with pork products, and can trigger postinfectious complications such as reactive arthritis.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of progressive, dull bifrontal headache, intermittent confusion, and new right upper‑limb weakness. He reports low-grade fevers and increasing gait instability.
