She is otherwise well, afebrile with normal vital signs, and pelvic examination showed thin, non-bloody discharge coating the vaginal vault with minimal vulvovaginal erythema and no cervical motion tenderness.

She reports a new sexual partner three weeks ago and used a commercial intravaginal cleansing wash twice in the past fortnight. She had self-treated once with an over-the-counter topical antifungal without improvement and takes no regular medications; pregnancy test in clinic was negative.

Wet mount microscopy of vaginal fluid showed numerous epithelial cells with small bacteria adherent to their borders, obscuring cell margins. Gram stain revealed mixed polymicrobial flora with small Gram-variable coccobacillary forms predominant. Vaginal pH measured at 5.5 and a complete blood count was 6.2 × 10^9/L with normal differential.
Transvaginal ultrasound performed to exclude pelvic inflammatory disease and abscess was unremarkable with normal-appearing uterus and adnexa and no free fluid.

She confirms recent intravaginal douching and new sexual contact but no history of intrauterine device insertion, recent systemic antibiotics, or systemic symptoms. A clinic test using 10% potassium hydroxide produced a pronounced amine odour when mixed with her vaginal secretions.

explanation: This clinical picture is bacterial vaginosis, most consistent with Gardnerella vaginalis overgrowth rather than a vulvovaginal candidiasis or pelvic inflammatory disease. The thin, noninflammatory discharge, positive amine test on KOH, vaginal pH above 4.5, and wet mount showing clue cells with mixed polymicrobial flora are classic for bacterial vaginosis and help distinguish it from yeast infection and cervicitis. Bacterial vaginosis results from loss of hydrogen peroxide producing lactobacilli and an overgrowth of Gardnerella and anaerobes, and practices like douching and new sexual partners increase risk and recurrence.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously well man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of fever, diffuse myalgia, and progressive shortness of breath. He was ambulatory until the past 24 hours, and on arrival he is febrile at 38.6°C, tachycardic at 112 beats/min, tachypnoeic at 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air; examination shows bilateral fine crackles at the lung bases.

He has no chronic medical conditions and does not smoke. The illness began with high fever and severe muscle aches, followed on day 2 by nausea and two episodes of non-bloody vomiting; his GP started a short course of oral antibiotics for presumed bronchitis without improvement. He works as a field ecologist and spent several days on a remote mountain research trip three weeks before presentation.

Initial blood tests show leukocytosis 16.0 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 65 × 10^9/L, and haemoconcentration with haematocrit 0.54 L/L. Serum creatinine is 140 µmol/L, C-reactive protein 140 mg/L. Arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 7.0 kPa with mild metabolic acidaemia and lactate 2.5 mmol/L.

Portable chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral, patchy interstitial and alveolar opacities most prominent in the mid and lower zones, with small bilateral pleural effusions and a normal cardiac silhouette. A repeat film six hours later shows interval progression of the airspace opacities.

On further questioning he recalls cleaning out an old field research cabin about 18 days before becoming ill, sweeping up a large amount of dry rodent faeces and nesting material without a mask. Several colleagues noted heavy mouse activity in the building around the same time.

explanation: This is hantavirus pulmonary syndrome following aerosolized exposure to rodent excreta, producing rapidly progressive noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. The prodrome of fever and myalgia, then swift deterioration to hypoxemic respiratory failure with bilateral interstitial and alveolar opacities, thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, and a history of cleaning a rodent-infested cabin are characteristic of hantavirus rather than typical community-acquired pneumonia or cardiogenic edema. Hantaviruses are transmitted by inhalation of aerosolized rodent urine or droppings and cause increased capillary permeability in the lungs, so a history of rodent exposure is a key diagnostic clue.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to primary care with three months of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and intermittent loose stools. She has lost 4 kg, reports mild paresthesias in her fingertips, and on examination is pale with conjunctival pallor and a heart rate of 102/min; abdominal examination shows mild diffuse tenderness without organomegaly.

She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and is not pregnant. She moved 18 months ago to a lakeside town and works part time at a community kitchen. She denies overt bleeding, heavy menses, recent antibiotics, or travel outside the country. She tried an over-the-counter iron preparation for six weeks with little change in symptoms.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 85 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 110 fL, leukocytes 5.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 210 × 10^9/L. Peripheral smear demonstrates macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum cobalamin is 95 pmol/L (reference 140–652). Serum ferritin is 120 μg/L. Fecal occult blood test is negative.

Video capsule endoscopy was performed because symptoms persisted and showed a 15–20 cm glistening, ribbonlike structure adherent to the mucosa of the proximal jejunum with mild adjacent erythema. No obstructing lesion was seen and the remainder of the small bowel mucosa appeared grossly normal.

When asked specifically about diet she reports frequent meals of cold-smoked and lightly cured lake trout prepared by a local vendor over the past year. She also recalls passing a long flat white segment in her stool about two weeks ago.

explanation: This is vitamin B12 deficiency megaloblastic anemia caused by intestinal infection with the fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum. The patient has macrocytic anemia with low serum cobalamin and hypersegmented neutrophils while ferritin and fecal occult blood are not consistent with blood loss, and the history of frequent cold-smoked freshwater trout plus capsule endoscopy showing a long ribbonlike mucosal worm and passage of a flat segment point specifically to Diphyllobothrium rather than nutritional or autoimmune causes. Diphyllobothrium latum is acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater fish and can competitively absorb host vitamin B12 in the small intestine, producing a characteristic megaloblastic anemia while the adult worm appears as a wide, flat, ribbonlike tapeworm.

hints.text: A 31-year-old previously well man presents to clinic with 10 days of progressive fatigue, anorexia, dark urine and yellowing of his eyes. He reports low-grade fevers and intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, temperature 37.8°C on arrival, scleral icterus and mild tender hepatomegaly on abdominal palpation.

He has no prior liver disease, drinks alcohol only occasionally, denies injection drug use and reports monogamous sexual activity. His childhood immunisations included vaccines for two common vaccine-preventable hepatitides and he takes no regular medications.

Blood tests show ALT 1 240 U/L, AST 920 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 160 U/L, total bilirubin 88 μmol/L and INR 1.1. A laboratory panel for common hepatotropic viruses and routine blood-borne pathogens was negative, and platelet count was 210 × 10^9/L.
Abdominal ultrasound shows a mildly enlarged liver without focal lesions, normal biliary calibre and no gallstones or bile duct dilation to suggest obstructive cholestasis.

Three weeks before symptom onset he had spent two weeks working in rural South Asia, during which he drank untreated well water and ate several dishes prepared from undercooked pork and pig liver at local markets.

explanation: This is acute viral hepatitis due to hepatitis E virus acquired during recent travel to an endemic region. Very high transaminases with jaundice and a negative panel for other common hepatotropic viruses, together with recent rural South Asia travel involving consumption of untreated water and undercooked pork or pig liver, point to HEV infection rather than hepatitis A, B, C or drug toxicity. Hepatitis E virus is an RNA virus transmitted fecal-orally with waterborne genotypes causing outbreaks in endemic regions and zoonotic genotypes linked to undercooked pork, and some genotypes can cause severe disease in vulnerable patients.

hints.text: A 32-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 6 days of fever, severe myalgias and progressive malaise. He says the myalgias are worst in his calves and now limit his ability to walk. On arrival he was febrile at 38.9°C, pulse 112/min and blood pressure 102/64 mmHg; examination showed mild scleral icterus, diffuse calf tenderness without focal erythema, and no focal neurological deficit.

He is a municipal sanitation worker, previously healthy, with no chronic liver disease and no regular medications. Symptoms began about four days after a week of heavy seasonal rains in the city. He denies recent international travel, illicit drug use, or animal bites, and reports self-treatment with ibuprofen for the first three days.

Laboratory tests show white blood cells 14.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 85 × 10^9/L, creatinine 180 µmol/L, total bilirubin 85 µmol/L, ALT 110 U/L and AST 145 U/L. Urinalysis demonstrates protein 2+ and microscopic hematuria. Two sets of blood cultures remain sterile at 24 hours.

Chest radiograph shows bilateral, patchy alveolar opacities with small bilateral pleural effusions but no lobar consolidation. Abdominal ultrasound shows mild hepatomegaly without biliary dilatation or obstructing lesion.

On further questioning he reports wading through knee-deep floodwater in the city while clearing storm drains three days before symptom onset, and he recalls a recent rat infestation in the area. He also had a superficial abrasion on his shin at that time that he did not clean thoroughly.

explanation: This presentation represents leptospirosis from Leptospira interrogans, complicated by hepatic dysfunction, acute kidney injury and pulmonary involvement consistent with severe disease. The classic severe calf myalgias, conjunctival icterus, thrombocytopenia, sterile cultures, recent wading through floodwater with rat exposure and a skin abrasion, plus renal proteinuria and diffuse alveolar infiltrates, fit leptospiral infection and Weil's disease rather than typical bacterial sepsis or viral hepatitis. Leptospira are thin motile spirochetes that enter through mucous membranes or skin breaks after contact with contaminated animal urine and can cause a biphasic illness that progresses to jaundice, renal failure and pulmonary hemorrhage in severe cases.

hints.text: A 49-year-old woman presented to neurology with three weeks of progressive right-sided clumsiness and difficulty reading that began insidiously. She described intermittent visual blurring and new falls. On examination she was afebrile, alert but slowed in speech, had a right homonymous hemianopia, 3/5 weakness of the right hand, and a broad-based ataxic gait.

She has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis and started monthly monoclonal antibody therapy 11 months ago. She has not recently received high-dose corticosteroid pulses. She takes no other chronic immunosuppressants and has no history of HIV infection.

CSF obtained on day 5 showed WBC 3 × 10^6/L, protein 0.85 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L. CSF bacterial Gram stain and fungal smear were negative and cultures remained sterile. Peripheral lymphocyte count was 0.9 × 10^9/L. Routine serum infection testing including HIV antibody was negative.

MRI brain with contrast demonstrated multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter of the left parietal and occipital lobes and the splenium. Lesions were non-enhancing after gadolinium and produced minimal mass effect.

Her last monoclonal antibody infusion was three weeks before symptom onset and she had received 11 monthly doses in total. CSF nucleic acid amplification returned positive for viral DNA consistent with the agent responsible for subacute demyelinating lesions in patients treated with this therapy.

explanation: This is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy due to JC virus reactivation in the setting of monoclonal antibody immunotherapy. Subacute focal neurologic deficits with nonenhancing multifocal T2/FLAIR white matter lesions causing minimal mass effect in a patient on prolonged monthly monoclonal antibody treatment, together with positive CSF viral DNA, are diagnostic of JC virus PML rather than an MS relapse or typical bacterial or fungal infection. JC virus is a ubiquitous polyomavirus that remains latent in most people and causes demyelination by infecting oligodendrocytes when cell mediated immunity is impaired, with markedly increased risk after therapies such as natalizumab.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to a clinic in the city with 3 weeks of jaundice, malaise and anorexia that began shortly after receiving a tattoo while traveling abroad. On exam she is afebrile, markedly jaundiced and tender in the right upper quadrant.

She reports no prior liver disease and had normal liver tests recorded two years earlier during antenatal care. She recalls the tattoo was performed with unregulated equipment and she had several unprotected sexual encounters during the same trip.

Laboratory testing shows ALT 1 900 U/L, AST 2 200 U/L, total bilirubin 150 µmol/L and INR 1.7. Newly positive hepatitis surface antigen is documented alongside negative results for other routine acute hepatitides.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the liver demonstrates diffuse hepatic enhancement without focal abscess or biliary obstruction, and no portal vein thrombosis. The overall appearance is consistent with acute hepatitis.

Acute serology showed IgM to a small circular RNA agent and PCR detected that agent's RNA in blood, in addition to the new surface antigen positivity. The pattern indicated simultaneous acquisition of the surface antigen and the dependent RNA agent.

explanation: This presentation represents acute hepatitis D virus infection acquired concurrently with hepatitis B virus, producing severe acute hepatitis. The simultaneous new HBsAg and detection of HDV IgM and RNA indicate HDV co-infection rather than isolated HBV. The key diagnostic clues are new HBsAg positivity together with IgM and PCR evidence of a small circular RNA agent, which defines HDV because it requires hepatitis B surface antigen for propagation; the marked transaminase elevations, hyperbilirubinaemia and coagulopathy reflect the severe acute liver injury typical of HDV co-infection. Hepatitis D virus is a defective circular single-stranded RNA satellite that depends on hepatitis B surface antigen for assembly and often produces more severe acute hepatitis than HBV alone.

hints.text: A 48-year-old woman presented to neurology clinic with an 8-month history of progressive stiffness and weakness in both legs. She reports increasing difficulty climbing stairs and getting up from a chair, plus new urinary urgency and occasional urge incontinence. On examination she has marked lower limb spasticity with brisk knee and ankle reflexes and bilateral extensor plantar responses, gait is spastic and scissoring. Vital signs are normal.

Her past medical history is otherwise unremarkable and she takes no regular medications. She had an eczematous rash two years ago that resolved with topical steroids. She denies trauma, no family history of similar neurological disease, no diabetes, and no immunosuppressive therapy. She reports no intravenous drug use and has a long-term monogamous partner.

Routine bloods are within reference limits with white cell count 6.3 × 10^9/L and serum calcium normal. HIV serology is negative. Lumbar puncture shows opening pressure 15 cm H2O, CSF white cell count 38 × 10^6/L with 90% lymphocytes, CSF protein 1.2 g/L, and normal CSF glucose.

MRI thoracic spine demonstrates diffuse thinning of the thoracic cord and longitudinal T2 hyperintensity most prominent in the lateral columns spanning multiple segments. There is no focal compressive lesion. MRI brain is unremarkable.
She was born and raised in rural Jamaica and emigrated 15 years ago. She reports being breastfed in infancy and having received a blood transfusion after childbirth about 30 years ago.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human T-lymphotropic virus 1. The combination of progressive bilateral lower limb spasticity and gait disturbance, longitudinal lateral column T2 hyperintensity on spinal MRI, lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis and epidemiologic risk from Jamaica with breastfeeding and transfusion exposures points to HTLV-1 rather than multiple sclerosis or compressive myelopathy. HTLV-1 is a retrovirus transmitted by breastfeeding, sexual contact and contaminated blood and it can cause a chronic myelopathy and, in a minority of patients, adult T cell leukemia.

hints.text: A 12-year-old boy presents to urgent care 48 hours after acute onset of fever, diffuse myalgias and dry cough. He reports bilateral calf pain that began this morning and makes walking downstairs difficult. Temperature 39.3°C, heart rate 110/min, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Pharynx is mildly erythematous without exudate, chest auscultation clear, and both calves are tender to palpation without swelling.

Previously healthy, no chronic respiratory disease or neuromuscular disorder, received the seasonal inactivated respiratory virus vaccine four months ago. His 8-year-old sister missed school yesterday with a febrile cough. No recent travel or animal exposures and no recent antibiotic use. He attends a local elementary school and was present in class through the day before presentation.

Complete blood count shows WBC 3.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 2.5 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.5 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 12 mg/L. Serum creatine kinase elevated at 820 U/L. Throat rapid streptococcal antigen negative and point-of-care antigen tests for respiratory syncytial virus and adenovirus were negative. A multiplex molecular respiratory panel was sent to the reference laboratory.

Frontal chest radiograph shows mild peribronchial cuffing and increased perihilar interstitial markings without focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Ultrasound of the calves shows no deep venous thrombosis and no soft-tissue fluid collection.

The regional public health service contacted the family to report an outbreak in the boy's classroom. Reference-lab reverse-transcription PCR on samples from multiple classmates detected a segmented negative-sense RNA virus in the Orthomyxoviridae family, described as a human-restricted seasonal lineage that lacks the antigenic-shift features seen in animal-to-human pandemic strains. The patient's nasopharyngeal RT-PCR returned positive for the same lineage.

explanation: The diagnosis is Influenza B virus. The acute febrile respiratory syndrome with a class outbreak, lymphopenia, substantially raised CK localized calf pain and a reference-lab RT-PCR showing a human-restricted segmented negative-sense RNA orthomyxovirus together distinguish influenza B and its recognized post-influenza myositis from other respiratory viruses. Influenza B circulates only in humans and lacks the animal reservoir driven antigenic shifts of influenza A, and children are particularly prone to transient post-influenza viral myositis affecting the calves.

hints.text: A 42-year-old man presents to clinic with 10 days of progressive jaundice, dark urine, pale stools and severe fatigue. He has right upper-quadrant discomfort, a low-grade fever of 37.8°C, scleral icterus and a tender liver edge palpated 3 cm below the costal margin; he stopped working because of weakness.

He emigrated from West Africa 12 years ago and reports he was told he had chronic viral hepatitis about a decade ago but received no follow-up or treatment. He denies heavy alcohol use, takes no regular medications, and reports a new sexual partner over the past 2 months; remote recreational injection drug use was many years earlier.

Laboratory tests show AST 2 100 U/L, ALT 1 900 U/L, total bilirubin 210 µmol/L, INR 1.7 and platelets 130 × 10^9/L. Prior hospital records note persistent positivity for a marker of chronic infection with a DNA hepatotropic virus and current nucleic-acid testing demonstrates a high circulating viral load of that DNA virus.

Abdominal ultrasound shows hepatomegaly with coarse echotexture, no intrahepatic or extrahepatic bile duct dilatation and patent portal and hepatic veins on Doppler. Small volume ascites is present and there is no focal hepatic lesion to suggest obstruction or vascular thrombosis.

He reports his new partner recently returned from his country of origin. Serum testing now detects a small circular single-stranded RNA molecule that appears only in patients who carry the chronic DNA-virus marker described in his records and that is linked to abrupt severe hepatitis on the background of chronic infection.

explanation: The diagnosis is Hepatitis D virus. The patient has longstanding markers of chronic HBV with high HBV DNA and now develops sudden severe transaminase elevation, jaundice and coagulopathy while testing positive for a small circular RNA molecule that appears only in HBsAg carriers, which is the pattern of HDV superinfection rather than isolated HBV flare. HDV superinfection of an HBV carrier typically causes more severe hepatitis and accelerates progression to cirrhosis because HDV requires hepatitis B surface antigen for packaging while driving liver injury.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 10 days of progressive jaundice, anorexia and new confusion. He has dark urine and daytime somnolence, temperature 38.2°C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, examination shows scleral icterus, tender hepatomegaly and asterixis.

He was diagnosed with chronic blood-borne viral hepatitis 18 years ago and has had intermittent follow-up, with no history of harmful alcohol use. He reports no recent travel, no new medications, and no intravenous drug use.

Laboratory tests show AST 1 050 U/L, ALT 880 U/L, total bilirubin 220 μmol/L, INR 2.3, ammonia 120 μmol/L and platelets 85 × 10^9/L. Serologic testing for acute antibody markers of the common RNA hepatotropic pathogens is negative.

Abdominal ultrasound shows a nodular liver contour with splenomegaly and patent portal and hepatic veins, without biliary dilatation. The appearance is consistent with underlying chronic liver disease with acute hepatic injury.

Molecular testing of serum returns positive for a small circular negative-sense RNA detected only in the context of the patient's preexisting chronic envelope-producing hepatotropic infection, and prior records confirm persistent envelope protein on prior assays. The laboratory reports that the detected agent is a defective satellite RNA that requires the envelope proteins of the chronic virus for propagation.

explanation: Acute hepatitis D virus superinfection causing acute on chronic liver failure in a patient with longstanding envelope-producing hepatotropic infection. The presentation is consistent with fulminant hepatic injury on a background of chronic liver disease. The detection of a small circular negative-sense RNA described as a defective satellite that requires the patient’s chronic virus envelope, together with negative serologies for other acute hepatotropic viruses and signs of chronic liver disease, point to hepatitis D virus rather than a primary hepatitis A, C, or E. The rapid biochemical collapse, high transaminases, rising bilirubin and encephalopathy fit HDV superinfection producing severe acute decompensation on chronic hepatitis B. Hepatitis D virus is a 1.7 kb circular negative-sense RNA satellite that requires hepatitis B surface antigen for packaging, and superinfection of chronic HBV typically causes more severe and rapidly progressive liver disease than HBV alone.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman who injects drugs presents with 6 days of dark urine, severe nausea and marked fatigue. She is febrile to 38.6°C, has jaundice and right upper quadrant tenderness but no encephalopathy.

She reports a diagnosis of chronic viral hepatitis after a transfusion in childhood, with low-level abnormal liver tests but no cirrhosis on prior imaging. She stopped regular clinic follow-up three years ago and has not received antiviral therapy.

AST 1 800 U/L, ALT 2 100 U/L, total bilirubin 180 μmol/L, INR 1.6 and C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. Screening tests for acute primary infection with the usual hepatotropic RNA viruses are negative, while baseline markers of her chronic infection remain detectable.

Transient elastography performed in clinic two years earlier recorded values compatible with minimal fibrosis and an ultrasound at presentation shows hepatomegaly without nodularity and no biliary obstruction.

A targeted PCR assay performed on serum identifies a 1.7 kb circular negative-sense RNA molecule and the laboratory notes replicative intermediates consistent with an RNA satellite dependent on the patient’s existing envelope-producing chronic virus. The finding explains the sudden severe hepatitis superimposed on chronic infection.

explanation: The diagnosis is Hepatitis D virus. Targeted PCR identified a 1.7 kb circular negative-sense RNA with replicative intermediates described as an RNA satellite dependent on the existing envelope-producing virus, which is diagnostic of HDV rather than primary infection by other hepatotropic RNA viruses that test negative. The clinical scenario of injection drug use and chronic viral carriage with abrupt severe hepatitis supports HDV superinfection. HDV requires the surface antigen of hepatitis B for assembly and release, so it only occurs in patients coinfected with or already chronically infected by HBV and often causes more intense liver injury after superinfection.

hints.text: A 61-year-old man on maintenance haemodialysis presents with three weeks of progressive pruritus, jaundice and weight loss. He is lethargic, has marked scleral icterus and mild peripheral oedema, blood pressure 125/78 mmHg and no fever.

He received multiple blood transfusions 30 years ago and was told he had a chronic viral hepatitis infection decades ago. He has been clinically stable with mild routine transaminitis until the current decline.

AST 760 U/L, ALT 690 U/L, total bilirubin 150 μmol/L, INR 1.9, albumin 28 g/L and platelets 92 × 10^9/L. Serologies for acute seroconversion to other common hepatotropic agents are negative and HIV screening is negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen shows a shrunken, nodular liver with moderate ascites and collateral vessels, without focal hepatic lesions or biliary obstruction. Findings are consistent with established cirrhosis and portal hypertension.

Specialised molecular testing detects a small circular, single-stranded negative-sense RNA in serum and the clinical laboratory comments that this RNA is a defective satellite which requires the envelope proteins of the patient’s chronic hepatotropic infection for its lifecycle. This explains the recent acute-on-chronic deterioration.

explanation: The diagnosis is Hepatitis D virus. Specialised testing identified a small circular single-stranded negative-sense RNA described as a defective satellite that requires the patient’s chronic virus envelope, which distinguishes HDV from other causes of decompensation given negative acute serologies. The pattern of prior transfusions, long-standing hepatitis and sudden worsening of liver function is classic for HDV superinfection driving rapid progression. Chronic HDV infection accelerates fibrosis and decompensation in patients with HBV because HDV depends on HBV surface antigen for its lifecycle and can persist as a destructive cofactor in chronic liver disease.

hints.text: A 42-year-old woman treated with high-dose corticosteroids for a flare of autoimmune disease presents with 2 weeks of jaundice, profound fatigue and right upper quadrant discomfort. On examination she is icteric, afebrile and mildly tachycardic, with no stigmata of chronic liver disease externally.

She has a remote diagnosis of chronic viral hepatitis identified during pre-employment screening 10 years earlier, with irregular follow-up. She recently received a pulse of immunosuppression and reports no travel or new sexual partners.

AST 1 320 U/L, ALT 1 100 U/L, total bilirubin 210 μmol/L, INR 2.0 and eosinophils 0.2 × 10^9/L. Autoimmune liver serologies are negative and tests for acute primary infection by common RNA hepatotropic pathogens are negative.
Liver elastography from last year suggested moderate fibrosis and current ultrasound shows mild surface irregularity but no biliary obstruction and minimal ascites. No hepatic mass is identified.

Serum PCR identifies a compact circular negative-sense RNA molecule and paired testing documents presence of the patient’s long-standing envelope-producing hepatotropic infection. The laboratory describes the finding as a defective satellite RNA requiring the chronic virus envelope for assembly and release.

explanation: The diagnosis is Hepatitis D virus. The serum PCR finding of a compact circular negative-sense RNA that is explicitly described as a defective satellite reliant on the existing envelope-producing virus, together with negative tests for other acute hepatotropic agents, identifies HDV rather than autoimmune or drug causes. The temporal link with immunosuppression and known chronic carriage supports HDV replication flaring and producing severe hepatic injury. Immunosuppression can precipitate increased replication or clinical activation of HDV in patients with chronic HBV because HDV requires HBV surface antigen to form infectious particles and may cause severe hepatitis when it proliferates.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man 21 days after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant for acute myeloid leukaemia was brought from the ward with 48 hours of progressive confusion and new anterograde memory loss. He was febrile to 38.7°C, alert but disoriented to time, and family reported a witnessed brief focal seizure this morning.

Conditioning included fludarabine and busulphan and he remains on tacrolimus for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis. He received aciclovir prophylaxis per protocol and has no prior central nervous system disease.

MRI brain performed urgently showed bilateral medial temporal lobe T2/FLAIR hyperintensity that was greater on the left, with minimal mass effect and no frank diffusion restriction or leptomeningeal enhancement.

Empirical intravenous aciclovir was started for presumed herpes encephalitis but there was no clinical improvement after 72 hours. After switching to intravenous foscarnet the patient had gradual recovery of orientation and memory over the next 7 days.

CSF PCR returned strongly positive with quantitative viral DNA >1.0 × 10^6 copies/mL. Peripheral blood PCR showed similar high levels, and hair‑follicle testing found no evidence of chromosomally integrated viral genome, indicating active reactivation rather than inherited integration.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 6. The post‑transplant timing, bilateral medial temporal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and very high CSF and blood HHV‑6 DNA identify HHV‑6 limbic encephalitis rather than HSV, and lack of response to aciclovir with subsequent clinical improvement on foscarnet supports HHV‑6 as the causative reactivated virus; hair‑follicle testing excluded chromosomal integration so the PCR reflects active replication. HHV‑6 commonly reactivates after stem cell transplant and causes limbic encephalitis that may not respond to aciclovir, and chromosomal integration can produce high blood DNA levels so testing nonblood tissues helps distinguish active infection from inherited integration.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presented with 6 days of fever, a spreading pruritic morbilliform eruption and progressive jaundice. On exam she had facial oedema, tender cervical lymphadenopathy and scleral icterus; temperature was 38.9°C and she was somnolent but rousable.

She had started allopurinol four weeks earlier for gout. There was no recent travel and no new herbal supplements. She had been started on high‑dose systemic corticosteroids by a local team three days prior for presumed severe drug reaction.

Complete blood count showed leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.8 × 10^9/L and platelets 110 × 10^9/L. Liver tests were markedly abnormal with ALT 860 U/L and total bilirubin 155 μmol/L. Bacterial cultures were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly without biliary obstruction. CT neck and chest showed widespread small lymph nodes and no focal abscess.

Skin biopsy taken for the eruption and quantitative PCR on peripheral blood mononuclear cells both returned with very high viral DNA levels consistent with active replication; hair‑bulb testing was negative for chromosomal integration. Clinical course had worsened after corticosteroids were started.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 6. The delayed onset after starting allopurinol with fever, facial edema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and severe hepatitis fits DRESS, and very high HHV‑6 DNA in blood and skin alongside clinical worsening after corticosteroids indicates viral reactivation amplifying the systemic inflammatory syndrome rather than drug effect alone. HHV‑6 reactivation is a well recognized accompaniment of DRESS and often coincides with delayed or worsening organ involvement, so viral testing can clarify the role of reactivation in severe presentations.

hints.text: A previously well 10-month-old infant was brought after 8 hours of febrile status epilepticus. Temperature on arrival was 40.1°C, the child was postictal and parents reported a faint pink macular rash that appeared as the fever fell.
The infant attends daycare and had a mild upper respiratory prodrome for two days before the seizure. There is no family history of epilepsy and the pregnancy and neonatal period were unremarkable.
Initial bloods showed WBC 9.4 × 10^9/L and CRP 7 mg/L. CSF cell count and chemistry were within reference intervals and HSV PCR was negative.
Head MRI performed after stabilization was unremarkable. EEG showed diffuse slowing without focal epileptiform discharges.

Quantitative PCR on whole blood reported persistently extremely high viral DNA >1.0 × 10^7 copies/mL. Identical high copy numbers were found in hair‑bulb and nail samples, consistent with an inherited chromosomally integrated viral genome rather than transient viraemia.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 6. The clinical syndrome is compatible with primary HHV‑6 infection but identical extremely high viral DNA in whole blood, hair and nail samples indicates inherited chromosomal integration, which produces uniformly high copy numbers across tissues and can mimic active infection on blood PCR. Approximately 1% of people carry chromosomally integrated HHV‑6, which yields very high DNA levels in blood and tissues and can confound PCR diagnostics unless nonblood samples or assays of viral transcription are used to demonstrate active replication.

hints.text: A 60-year-old woman six weeks after orthotopic liver transplant presented with progressive dyspnoea, non‑productive cough and fever for five days. On exam she was tachypnoeic, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, and had scattered crackles on lung auscultation.
Her immunosuppression regimen includes tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil. Valganciclovir prophylaxis had been stopped two weeks earlier because of worsening neutropenia.
CBC showed neutrophils 0.4 × 10^9/L and platelets 48 × 10^9/L. Blood and sputum cultures were negative and serum galactomannan was not elevated.
CT thorax demonstrated bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities and small areas of consolidation without cavitation. There was no pleural effusion.

Bronchoalveolar lavage PCR and a bone marrow aspirate both returned strongly positive for viral DNA at high copy number. After initiation of intravenous ganciclovir the patient had gradual improvement in respiratory status and a slow rise in neutrophil count over two weeks.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 6. The setting of profound immunosuppression after stopping antiviral prophylaxis, bilateral perihilar ground glass opacities, and high HHV‑6 DNA in bronchoalveolar lavage and bone marrow together with clinical and hematologic improvement on antiviral therapy point to HHV‑6 as the cause rather than bacterial or fungal infection. HHV‑6 can cause interstitial pneumonitis and direct marrow infection in transplant patients and may present with ground glass radiologic changes that mimic other viral pneumonias, so tissue or marrow PCR helps establish causality.

hints.text: A 37-year-old man presented to an urban clinic with an 8-week history of progressive non-tender skin lesions on both lower legs and new swelling of the right ankle that limited his walking. He reports 5 kg weight loss over two months and intermittent oral bleeding; on examination there are multiple flat brown-red papules on the shins and a 1 cm erythematous plaque on the hard palate, temperature 37.4°C, right ankle pitting oedema 2+.

He has known HIV infection diagnosed 6 years earlier but stopped antiretroviral therapy three months ago after moving between cities and reports inconsistent clinic follow-up. He is an MSM, takes no immunosuppressants, and has no recent travel outside the country.
Laboratory tests show CD4 count 0.12 × 10^9/L and HIV RNA 1.2 × 10^5 copies/mL, haemoglobin 95 g/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L and CRP 36 mg/L. A skin punch biopsy was obtained and sent to pathology.

Contrast CT of the chest shows multiple peribronchovascular nodules and small bilateral pleural effusions, without a dominant pulmonary mass; flexible nasopharyngoscopy notes mucosal erythema and a raised lesion on the posterior palate concordant with the oral plaque.

Histology of the skin lesion demonstrates a spindle-cell vascular proliferation with extravasated erythrocytes; immunohistochemistry stains positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen in lesional nuclei and quantitative PCR of plasma shows high copy number of the same viral DNA.

explanation: This presentation represents disseminated Kaposi sarcoma due to Human herpesvirus 8 with cutaneous, oral and probable pulmonary involvement in the setting of advanced untreated HIV/AIDS. The combination of violaceous papules on the shins and a palatal plaque, a spindle cell vascular proliferation with extravasated erythrocytes on histology, and lesional nuclei positive for the viral latent nuclear antigen with high plasma viral DNA identifies HHV-8 driven Kaposi sarcoma rather than other vascular lesions such as bacillary angiomatosis or nonviral vascular tumors. Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and is confirmed by LANA immunostaining or viral PCR, and visceral involvement such as pulmonary nodules or effusions indicates more widespread disease.

hints.text: A 78-year-old retired olive farmer presented with nine months of slowly progressive, non-painful nodules and thickening of the skin over the right lower leg, accompanied by chronic unilateral leg swelling that has increased his need for walking aids. He is afebrile, lesions are firm, dome-shaped nodules clustered over the anterior shin, and the leg shows chronic pitting oedema with skin hyperpigmentation.

He reports lifelong residence in a Mediterranean coastal region and no history of HIV risk behaviours or immunosuppressive medication. His past medical history includes well controlled hypertension and osteoarthritis; he denies systemic symptoms other than gradual mobility decline.

Routine bloodwork shows haemoglobin 120 g/L, white cell count 6.4 × 10^9/L, platelets 220 × 10^9/L and CRP 18 mg/L. An HIV test returned negative and a dermatology service obtained an excisional skin specimen.

Duplex ultrasound excludes deep venous thrombosis and CT of the pelvis and lower limbs demonstrates multiple subcutaneous nodular enhancing lesions and small ipsilateral inguinal lymph nodes but no deep soft tissue mass.

Excisional biopsy shows a vascular spindle-cell proliferation forming slit-like vascular channels; lesional cells stain positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen and tissue PCR demonstrates high copy number of the same viral DNA.

explanation: This is classic or Mediterranean Kaposi sarcoma caused by Human herpesvirus 8, presenting as a chronic indolent cutaneous vascular tumor of the lower leg in an older man. The slowly progressive, nonpainful nodules clustered on the anterior shin in an elderly Mediterranean man, together with spindle cell slit-like vascular channels on biopsy and positive viral latent nuclear antigen and PCR, point to HHV-8 associated Kaposi sarcoma rather than nonneoplastic causes of leg swelling or other cutaneous neoplasms. Classic Kaposi sarcoma typically affects older men from Mediterranean or eastern European backgrounds and often remains localized to the skin and subcutaneous tissue while being HHV-8 driven.

hints.text: A 50-year-old woman presented to clinic nine months after a kidney transplant with a three-week history of fevers, night sweats and new diffuse small red-purple papules on the trunk, together with increasing fatigue and reduced appetite. On examination she had generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy, palpable splenomegaly and multiple 2–5 mm erythematous papules over the chest and back; temperature 38.2°C.

She is maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil following a deceased-donor renal transplant and received basiliximab induction. CMV prophylaxis was completed three months earlier and she has not had known HIV exposure; graft function has been stable.

Blood tests reveal haemoglobin 80 g/L, albumin 25 g/L, platelets 90 × 10^9/L and CRP 120 mg/L. Liver and renal function are otherwise at baseline and a peripheral blood PCR assay for a DNA virus was requested.
Contrast CT shows widespread hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy above and below the diaphragm and splenomegaly without focal hepatic lesions; an excisional lymph node biopsy is planned.

Reduction of immunosuppression and a single course of rituximab were followed by rapid defervescence and clinical improvement; concurrent testing showed a marked fall in plasma viral DNA copies and lymph node histology demonstrated plasmacytic proliferation with cells positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen.

explanation: This clinical picture is Human herpesvirus 8 associated multicentric Castleman disease, presenting with systemic inflammatory symptoms, generalized lymphadenopathy and plasmacytic proliferation in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient. Fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias and plasmacytic lymph node histology with cells positive for the viral latent nuclear antigen and high plasma HHV-8 DNA are characteristic of KSHV/HHV-8 driven multicentric Castleman disease and distinguish it from other causes of posttransplant lymphoproliferation that lack LANA positivity and marked viral DNAemia. KSHV-MCD is driven by HHV-8 infected plasmablasts that provoke an IL-6 mediated inflammatory state and often shows rapid clinical improvement when the reservoir of infected B cells is reduced.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented with three weeks of progressive dyspnoea and pleuritic chest discomfort; he required therapeutic thoracentesis for a large right pleural effusion that recurred within days. He reports fatigue and night sweats, examination shows diminished breath sounds at the right base and oxygen saturation 94% on room air.

He was diagnosed with HIV infection several years ago and has had intermittent adherence to antiretroviral therapy; he denies intravenous drug use and has no known malignancy history. He had a recent community-acquired pneumonia treated with oral antibiotics two months earlier.

Pleural fluid is exudative and bloody with lactate dehydrogenase 580 IU/L, protein 48 g/L; cytology shows sheets of large plasmablastic cells that are negative for epithelial carcinoma markers and flow cytometry demonstrates a clonal plasma-cell phenotype. Peripheral blood CD4 count is 0.18 × 10^9/L.

Contrast-enhanced CT chest shows a large right pleural effusion without a discrete parenchymal or mediastinal mass and a small pericardial effusion; there is no significant lymphadenopathy to suggest systemic lymphoma.

PCR of the pleural fluid detected high copy numbers of viral DNA and immunohistochemical staining of the cell block was positive for a viral latent nuclear antigen within the atypical plasmablastic cells.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 8. A recurrent bloody pleural effusion composed of clonal plasmablastic cells that are negative for epithelial markers and positive for the viral latent nuclear antigen with high HHV-8 DNA is diagnostic of primary effusion lymphoma rather than metastatic carcinoma or conventional systemic lymphoma. Primary effusion lymphoma characteristically presents as malignant effusions without a solid tumor and is commonly associated with HHV-8 and often co-infected with Epstein Barr virus.

hints.text: A previously well 9-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. He had had 36 hours of high fever to 39.8 °C and was postictal for 20 minutes; on arrival he was afebrile and had no focal neurologic deficits.

Parents report the fever began abruptly with poor feeding and irritability. He attends a small home-based playgroup and an older sibling returned from daycare one week earlier after a short febrile illness.

Blood tests showed WBC 5.2 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 2.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 6 mg/L. Lumbar puncture revealed clear CSF with WBC 8 × 10^6/L (lymphocyte predominant), protein 0.22 g/L, glucose normal. A broad viral PCR panel on CSF detected viral DNA at 3.1 × 10^5 copies/mL, while bacterial cultures remained negative.
Non-contrast head CT was normal. EEG performed after the event showed generalized slowing without focal epileptiform discharges.

No antibacterial therapy was required. On day 4 of illness the child defervesced and developed a diffuse rose-pink maculopapular rash beginning on the trunk and spreading to the limbs, and no further seizures occurred.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 6. The classic picture of abrupt high fever in a 9-month-old followed by a rose-pink maculopapular rash as fever resolves, combined with lymphocytic CSF and a high HHV-6 DNA load in CSF, points to HHV-6 rather than bacterial meningitis or HSV encephalitis. HHV-6 is a common cause of roseola infantum and is a leading infectious cause of febrile seizures in infants, with the rash typically appearing as the fever subsides.

hints.text: A 49-year-old man 24 days after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant was admitted for progressive confusion and new complex partial seizures. Temperature was 38.3 °C and he was oriented only to person, with impaired short-term memory on examination.

Transplant conditioning included fludarabine and busulfan. He remains on tacrolimus and low-dose prednisone for graft‑versus‑host disease prophylaxis and receives standard antiviral prophylaxis that includes acyclovir.

CSF showed WBC 25 × 10^6/L with lymphocytic predominance, protein 0.70 g/L, glucose normal. A multiplex PCR panel returned negative for the usual acyclovir‑sensitive encephalitic viruses; quantitative CSF PCR identified 1.2 × 10^6 copies/mL of a large double‑stranded DNA virus. Serum quantitative PCR demonstrated a similar viral load.

Brain MRI showed bilateral T2 hyperintensity and restricted diffusion of the medial temporal lobes and hippocampi, left greater than right, without haemorrhage. No other focal lesions were identified.

Empirical IV acyclovir produced no clinical improvement and viral loads remained unchanged. After switching to IV foscarnet and later to IV ganciclovir the patient’s confusion and seizures abated over several days and serial PCR values fell substantially.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 6. Onset in the third to fourth week post-transplant with lymphocytic CSF, bilateral medial temporal lobe MRI abnormalities and high copies of a large double stranded DNA virus in CSF and serum, together with lack of response to acyclovir, is most consistent with HHV-6 rather than acyclovir‑sensitive viruses such as HSV. HHV-6 frequently reactivates after stem cell transplant to cause limbic encephalitis and is not reliably suppressed by acyclovir, often requiring agents such as ganciclovir or foscarnet.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the transplant clinic with 6 weeks of progressive, painless purple-brown plaques on the anterior left lower leg and several small raised lesions on the hard palate. He also reports a dry cough and mild exertional dyspnoea over the same interval. Temperature 36.8°C, SpO2 95% on room air. Lesions are non-tender, slightly firm, and do not blanch with pressure.

He received a deceased-donor renal transplant 20 months ago for diabetic nephropathy and remains on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and low-dose prednisone. He has had no acute rejection episodes and no recent travel. An HIV test performed for routine screening six months ago was negative.

Punch biopsy of a skin lesion was obtained. Histology shows a dermal spindle-cell proliferation with numerous small vascular channels and extravasated erythrocytes. Bacterial and fungal stains and cultures from the biopsy are negative. Routine bloods show haemoglobin 102 g/L, white cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 220 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 5 mg/L.

Contrast CT thorax demonstrates multiple bilateral peribronchovascular nodules and a small right pleural effusion. Bronchoscopy reveals several violaceous endobronchial nodules, and bronchoalveolar lavage cultures are sterile.

Review of donor records found the organ donor was born in sub-Saharan Africa and had documented chronic purple cutaneous lesions at procurement. Archived donor serum tested by PCR yielded viral DNA that matched sequences recovered from the patient’s skin lesion.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 8. The combination of violaceous non-blanching skin and oral lesions, spindle-cell vascular proliferation with extravasated erythrocytes on biopsy, sterile cultures, pulmonary nodules and matching viral DNA from the donor establish HHV-8 driven Kaposi sarcoma rather than a simple drug reaction or infectious vasculitis. HHV-8 is an oncogenic herpesvirus that infects endothelial lineage cells to cause Kaposi sarcoma and can be transmitted via organ transplantation from donors from endemic regions.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man admitted to the haematology ward develops progressive confusion and short-term memory loss over four days. He is febrile to 38.6°C and bedside examination shows disorientation with impaired recent memory but no focal motor deficit.

He underwent allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation 18 days earlier for acute myeloid leukaemia, with engraftment documented 12 days ago. He is maintained on tacrolimus and low-dose prednisone for graft-versus-host prophylaxis and received acyclovir prophylaxis through the peri-transplant period.

Lumbar puncture showed CSF leukocytes 48 × 10^6/L with 92% lymphocytes. CSF protein was 1.1 g/L and glucose 3.1 mmol/L. Gram stain and bacterial cultures were negative. Serum sodium was 128 mmol/L and neutrophils were 1.2 × 10^9/L on routine post-transplant blood counts.
Brain MRI demonstrates bilateral mesial temporal lobe T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, greater on the right, without diffusion restriction, haemorrhagic change, or substantial contrast enhancement.

Donor records note IgG seropositivity for a ubiquitous childhood virus that commonly causes a brief high-fever illness with a short diffuse rash in infancy. The timing of the recipient's encephalopathy about 2–3 weeks after transplant and donor serostatus raised concern for donor-derived reactivation of that latent virus.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 6. The timing about 2 to 3 weeks post-transplant, lymphocytic CSF, bilateral mesial temporal T2/FLAIR changes on MRI and donor seropositivity for the virus that causes roseola point to HHV-6 rather than bacterial causes or HSV. HHV-6 commonly reactivates in the early post-transplant period to cause limbic encephalitis and may not be prevented by acyclovir because the virus lacks the thymidine kinase targeted by that drug.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with five days of fever, dry cough and progressive shortness of breath. On arrival he was febrile to 38.9°C, tachypnoeic at 28/min and required 6 L/min oxygen by face mask to maintain SpO2 92%.

He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 3 chronic kidney disease, both stable on oral therapy. He reports malaise and two loose stools before respiratory symptoms, had completed a short course of oral amoxicillin prescribed in primary care without improvement, and is a non-smoker.

Blood tests showed WBC 3.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.6 × 10^9/L and platelets 120 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, ALT 86 U/L and creatinine 220 µmol/L (baseline 120 µmol/L). Rapid PCR for influenza A and B and respiratory syncytial virus was negative, initial bacterial blood cultures were pending and sputum cultures showed no growth.

Chest CT demonstrated bilateral, patchy ground-glass opacities and multifocal consolidation greater in the lower lobes, with small bilateral pleural effusions. The consolidation progressed on repeat chest radiograph 48 hours later, and he required transfer to high-dependency care for escalating oxygen requirements.

He returned 9 days before presentation from a 2-week work trip to Riyadh where he had direct contact with dromedary camels on a farm and drank unpasteurised camel milk; while there he visited a local hospital for an unrelated minor injury and learned colleagues had a cluster of febrile respiratory illness.

explanation: This presentation is severe MERS-CoV pneumonia causing progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure after recent travel to the Arabian Peninsula. Travel to Riyadh with direct dromedary contact, consumption of unpasteurised camel milk and exposure to a hospital cluster are classic epidemiologic clues for MERS-CoV, and the clinical picture of febrile viral pneumonia with lymphopenia, raised transaminases, negative influenza/RSV PCRs and rapidly progressive bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation fits MERS-CoV rather than routine community pathogens. MERS-CoV is a zoonotic betacoronavirus transmitted from dromedary camels that often causes lymphopenia and can produce severe pneumonia and acute kidney injury, with higher mortality in patients with underlying comorbidities.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with three days of progressive confusion, somnolence and two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. On arrival he is febrile to 38.2°C, Glasgow Coma Scale 12, and has new right-sided weakness with power 3/5.

He lives in a rural district of Sierra Leone and participated in last week's community mass drug distribution for a filarial control programme, receiving a single dose of an antiparasitic agent. For several months before that he had episodic pruritic swellings of the limbs but no diagnosed neurological disease.

Peripheral blood shows leukocytes 17.6 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.9 × 10^9/L. Community clinic records obtained on transfer document a daytime microfilarial density measured before treatment of 52 000 microfilariae per mL.

MRI brain demonstrates multiple small confluent hyperintense lesions on T2/FLAIR in the deep white matter with scattered areas of susceptibility consistent with petechial haemorrhage and focal restricted diffusion in some lesions.

His mental status deteriorated rapidly within 48 hours of the single-dose antiparasitic campaign drug, with recurrent seizures and coma. The timing of neurological decline together with the documented very high daytime microfilaremia supports an encephalopathic reaction to treatment of a filarial infection endemic to west-central Africa.

explanation: This is Loa loa encephalopathy due to rapid killing of very high microfilarial loads after mass antiparasitic administration. Living in an endemic area with prior episodic swellings, a documented daytime microfilarial density of 52 000/mL and the onset of seizures and coma within 48 hours of treatment are characteristic of post-treatment Loa loa neurologic complication rather than a primary bacterial or viral encephalitis. Extremely high Loa loa microfilarial densities, often above roughly 30 000/mL, predict a high risk of treatment-associated encephalopathy because dying microfilariae can obstruct cerebral microvasculature and trigger a severe inflammatory response.

hints.text: A 29-year-old primigravida at 24 weeks' gestation presents with several weeks of intermittent facial swelling and pruritus, plus a recent morning complaint of a moving sensation in her left eye. Vital signs are normal and obstetric examination shows a singleton pregnancy with fetal heart rate 140 bpm.

She immigrated from Cameroon six months ago and describes frequent daytime bites from large flies while working in irrigated fields. During the first trimester she had two brief episodes of limb swelling that resolved over 48 hours without specific therapy.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 110 g/L and eosinophils 2.5 × 10^9/L. Daytime peripheral blood smear sent from the antenatal clinic shows a low-density presence of microfilariae at approximately 800 per mL.

Slit-lamp examination documents a motile, slender white worm under the bulbar conjunctiva measuring about 2 cm; the parasite was removed intact at bedside with topical anaesthesia and the eye tolerated the procedure well.

She describes repeated daytime exposures to large, horsefly-like insects at the river margins in her home village, and several neighbours had similar transient swellings or ocular worms removed. The exposure history together with antenatal microfilaremia and extraction of an adult filarial worm confirm the diagnosis.

explanation: This is loiasis due to Loa loa with ocular migration of an adult worm in a pregnant woman who has low-level daytime microfilaremia. Her origin in Cameroon, daytime bites from large flies, transient limb swellings, daytime microfilariae on blood smear and the bedside extraction of a motile sub-bulbar conjunctival worm together confirm Loa loa rather than other filarial or allergic causes of swelling. Loa loa adults migrate through subcutaneous tissues and beneath the conjunctiva producing Calabar swellings and visible ocular worms, and microfilariae display diurnal periodicity with highest densities in daytime blood.

hints.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought by his parents with two months of episodic, non-pitting swellings of the limbs and intermittent pruritus. Today he also complains that something moved across his right eye this morning; he is afebrile and otherwise well on examination.

He spent the school holidays visiting relatives in southeastern Nigeria where he reports many daytime bites from large flies and was treated twice for presumed malaria. There was no screening or antiparasitic medication while he was there.

Full blood count shows leukocytes 15.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 3.6 × 10^9/L and normal platelets. External laboratory later reported a daytime peripheral smear demonstrating microfilariae at a density of 3 400 per mL.
Bedside orbital ultrasound with the eyelid everted reveals a 2.5–3.0 cm linear echogenic moving structure within the conjunctival sac, prompting urgent ophthalmology review.

During ophthalmic lid eversion a motile 3 cm adult filarial worm emerged and was removed intact; the child improved symptomatically after extraction and later daytime smears confirmed the microfilarial density. The clinical picture and extraction identify the causative filarial parasite.

explanation: This child has loiasis caused by Loa loa, confirmed by removal of an adult conjunctival worm and daytime microfilaremia. A history of travel to southeastern Nigeria with frequent daytime bites by large flies, episodic non-pitting swellings, eosinophilia and direct visualization and extraction of a motile 3 cm worm in the conjunctiva distinguish Loa loa from other causes of pruritus or swelling. In endemic areas children commonly present with Calabar swellings and ocular migration, and diagnosis is made by daytime blood smears or by direct extraction of the adult worm.

hints.text: A 34-year-old nurse presents with 3 months of intermittent, intensely pruritic swellings of the right forearm and two episodes of gritty foreign-body sensation in her left eye. Symptoms come and go over 1 to 3 days, leaving no permanent skin lesion. On exam she is afebrile, heart rate 82/min, and there is a 4 cm non-tender, tense subcutaneous fullness on the lateral forearm that softens between episodes.

She is otherwise healthy and not on regular medications. She reports the cutaneous events began while she was doing a 6-week nursing placement in rural clinical sites abroad six months earlier. She denies recent occupational chemical exposures or new topical products.
Full blood count shows leukocytes 12.1 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 3.6 × 10^9/L. Total IgE is 620 kU/L. Routine bacterial culture from the swollen area is sterile.

High-frequency ultrasound of the forearm swelling shows a 4.5 cm tubular, hyperechoic structure with intermittent longitudinal movement within the subcutaneous tissue. No abscess or fluid collection is identified.

On direct ophthalmic exam during a second episode the on-call clinician saw and removed a 5 cm motile, pale, slender worm crossing the bulbar conjunctiva. The patient recalls frequent painful daytime bites from deerfly-like insects while staying in rainforest villages in western Cameroon.

explanation: Loa loa filariasis causing intermittent migratory subcutaneous swellings (Calabar swellings) with ocular worm migration. The combination of transient pruritic subcutaneous swellings that move, marked eosinophilia and high IgE, a tubular moving structure on ultrasound, and a motile 5 cm worm visualized and removed from the conjunctiva after daytime deerfly bites in Cameroon is characteristic of Loa loa and excludes more common bacterial or nonfilarial causes. The daytime biting Chrysops exposure and the ocular passage of an adult worm are classic features that distinguish Loa loa from other filarial infections. Loa loa is transmitted by Chrysops deer flies in West and Central Africa, adult worms migrate in subcutaneous tissue and frequently cross the conjunctiva, and microfilariae show diurnal periodicity in peripheral blood.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with five days of fever, nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnoea. On arrival he was febrile at 39.2°C, tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 28/min and SpO2 88% on room air; bilateral basal crackles were heard and he required supplemental oxygen.

He has insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and obesity, with poor glycaemic control and an HbA1c last measured at 9.2%. He reported no recent antibiotic use, no known sick contacts at home, and had been working at a meat distribution warehouse during the preceding month.
Blood tests showed WBC 6.2 × 10^9/L with lymphopenia 0.7 × 10^9/L, CRP 192 mg/L, ALT 78 U/L and creatinine 135 μmol/L (baseline 90 μmol/L). Blood cultures remained negative after 48 hours.

Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral patchy air-space opacities greatest at the lung bases. Contrast CT showed multifocal consolidation and areas of ground-glass change predominantly in the lower lobes with a small bilateral pleural effusion.

He reported visiting a camel market during a business trip to the Arabian Peninsula 7 days before symptom onset. Tracheal aspirate real-time RT-PCR returned positive for an enveloped single-stranded RNA virus whose sequence matched strains from the recent Middle Eastern outbreak epidemiologically linked to camel exposure.

explanation: Severe MERS-CoV lower respiratory tract infection acquired after camel exposure resulting in hypoxemic pneumonia. Detection of an enveloped single-stranded RNA virus by RT-PCR with sequence identity to strains linked to camel exposure in the Arabian Peninsula together with lower lobe predominant consolidation, lymphopenia and systemic inflammation points to MERS-CoV rather than typical bacterial pneumonia or influenza. The epidemiologic link to a camel market and the molecular confirmation are decisive diagnostic clues. MERS-CoV is a zoonotic betacoronavirus associated with dromedary camels that often causes severe lower respiratory disease with lymphopenia and can lead to multiorgan dysfunction, especially in patients with diabetes.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation presented with three days of sore throat and fever after a day shift on a general medical ward. She was febrile to 38.6°C, tachycardic, and initially maintaining oxygen saturations of 94% on room air but developed increasing dyspnoea on day three of illness.

She is a hospital nurse with no chronic medical problems and had influenza vaccination in the previous season. Two days before symptom onset she had cared for an unwell patient recently returned from international travel; she reported wearing a surgical mask but recalls several prolonged close-care episodes.

Initial bloodwork showed WBC 4.0 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L and platelets 120 × 10^9/L, CRP 85 mg/L. Serial testing demonstrated rising oxygen requirement and a mild transaminitis with ALT 95 U/L.
Chest radiograph on day three showed bilateral patchy air-space consolidations, greater in the lower lobes. The team escalated her care to high-flow oxygen because of progressive hypoxaemia.

Infection control identified a small hospital cluster linked to the index patient who had recently returned from the Arabian Peninsula. Nasopharyngeal and tracheal aspirate RT-PCR were positive for the same single-stranded RNA virus matching sequences from the regional outbreak, implicating nosocomial transmission.

explanation: Nosocomial MERS-CoV infection causing progressive pneumonia in a pregnant healthcare worker. A small hospital cluster tied to an imported index case and positive RT-PCR matching the regional outbreak implicate nosocomial MERS-CoV rather than routine community respiratory viruses, and the clinical pattern of progressive hypoxaemia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis fits severe MERS. The occupational exposure during care of an internationally returned patient is the key epidemiologic discriminator. MERS-CoV transmits efficiently in healthcare settings and can cause severe disease in pregnant patients, so recognition of epidemiologic links is critical for diagnosis and infection control.

hints.text: A previously healthy 35-year-old man presented with six days of fever, myalgia and then progressive dyspnoea. He was febrile at 38.9°C, tachypnoeic, and had oxygen saturation 90% on room air with diffuse inspiratory crackles and subjective reduction in urine output.

He had returned to the country eight days earlier after a two-week work trip abroad. He reported an episode of transient diarrhoea during travel but denied chronic illness, immunosuppression or recent antibiotic exposure.

Blood tests revealed WBC 5.8 × 10^9/L with lymphopenia 0.5 × 10^9/L, CRP 210 mg/L and creatinine 220 μmol/L, up from a baseline of 80 μmol/L. Urinalysis showed proteinuria and microscopic haematuria; blood cultures were sterile.

Chest radiograph showed bilateral mid- and lower-zone air-space opacities. High-resolution CT demonstrated multifocal consolidations with surrounding ground-glass change, more pronounced in the dependent lung segments.

On further questioning he admitted visiting a camel market while abroad and having handled animals there. RT-PCR from nasopharyngeal and lower respiratory samples detected an enveloped single-stranded RNA virus whose sequence matched strains reported from the Arabian Peninsula outbreak linked to camel exposure.

explanation: MERS-CoV pneumonia acquired after camel exposure complicated by acute kidney injury. RT-PCR confirmation with sequences matching Arabian Peninsula strains together with a history of camel market exposure and lower-lobe predominant multifocal consolidation and ground-glass change point to MERS-CoV rather than other travel-associated pneumonias. The combination of lymphopenia, high inflammatory markers and rising creatinine with proteinuria is a recognized pattern in severe MERS infection. Beyond respiratory failure, MERS-CoV can involve the kidneys and cause proteinuria and acute kidney injury, reflecting its potential for systemic disease.

hints.text: A 54-year-old man presented with 7 days of fever, dry cough and progressive breathlessness. He arrived to the emergency ward with temperature 39.0 °C, respiratory rate 30/min and peripheral oxygen saturation 86% on room air, and bilateral inspiratory crackles on chest auscultation.

He has type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Two weeks before symptom onset he had returned from a 10-day trip to the Arabian Peninsula where he stayed with relatives, but he reports no known sick contacts during travel.

Blood tests showed lymphopenia 0.7 × 10^9/L, CRP 210 mg/L and serum creatinine rose from a baseline 150 µmol/L to 320 µmol/L. Nasopharyngeal PCR panels were negative for influenza A and B and for common respiratory syncytial viruses, blood cultures had no growth at 48 hours.

Chest CT demonstrated bilateral patchy ground glass opacities and multilobar consolidation, greater in the lower lobes, without cavitation. No localized lobar air bronchogram was seen and a small bilateral pleural effusion was present.

On further questioning he acknowledged visiting a camel farm and drinking unpasteurised camel milk during the trip. Lower respiratory PCR and subsequent sequencing returned positive for a novel enveloped single stranded RNA respiratory virus first reported from the Arabian Peninsula in 2012, and two dialysis staff who cared for him later developed febrile respiratory illness.

explanation: The diagnosis is MERS-CoV. The combination of recent travel to the Arabian Peninsula with camel exposure and raw camel milk, progressive lower respiratory failure with lymphopenia and acute kidney injury, negative tests for other respiratory viruses, and lower respiratory PCR and sequencing identifying the novel enveloped single stranded RNA virus first reported from that region point specifically to MERS‑CoV rather than a common community virus. MERS‑CoV is a zoonotic betacoronavirus associated with dromedary camels and is best detected by RT‑PCR of lower respiratory tract specimens because it often causes severe lower airway disease and can spread to close contacts and healthcare workers.

hints.text: A 68-year-old woman on chronic haemodialysis presented with 4 days of fever, malaise and new cough. On arrival she was febrile 38.7 °C, hypotensive 95/58 mmHg and required supplemental oxygen to maintain saturation above 92%.

Her comorbidities include ischaemic heart disease and end stage renal disease receiving thrice-weekly in-centre dialysis. During the prior week several other patients dialysing on the same shift had mild febrile illnesses but had been managed as outpatient.

Laboratory results showed lymphopenia 0.9 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 95 × 10^9/L and CRP 180 mg/L. Serial blood cultures remained negative and nasopharyngeal PCR was negative for influenza and common respiratory viruses.
Initial chest radiograph showed a right mid zone consolidation. Over 48 hours repeat radiograph revealed rapid progression to bilateral airspace opacities, consistent with evolving acute lung injury.

Infection control review identified an index patient recently transferred from a hospital in the Arabian Peninsula who attended the same dialysis shift. Respiratory samples from several patients and staff grew the same novel enveloped single stranded RNA virus first described in 2012 from that region.

explanation: The diagnosis is MERS-CoV. Epidemiology with an index case recently from the Arabian Peninsula linked to multiple cases on the same dialysis shift, clinical features of severe bilateral airspace disease with lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia, negative routine viral testing, and isolation of the novel enveloped single stranded RNA virus together confirm MERS‑CoV rather than typical influenza or other community respiratory pathogens. MERS‑CoV frequently causes severe disease in patients with comorbidities and has a propensity for healthcare associated transmission, particularly in crowded settings like dialysis units where close contact facilitates spread.

hints.text: A 33-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation presented with 5 days of fever, cough and worsening dyspnoea. She was tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 28/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air and decreased foetal movements reported by the patient.

She was previously healthy and had travelled abroad three weeks earlier to attend a large family celebration in the Gulf region. She denies known sick contacts at the event but recalls several animal stalls on the venue perimeter.
Bloods showed lymphopenia 0.6 × 10^9/L, ALT 140 U/L and AST 165 U/L. Urine output declined and serum creatinine increased from 60 µmol/L to 140 µmol/L over 48 hours. Influenza PCR was negative.

Chest radiograph revealed bilateral interstitial and alveolar infiltrates with more dense consolidation in the lower lobes. A bedside obstetric ultrasound showed reduced amniotic fluid and a non-reassuring foetal heart rate tracing prompting obstetric review.

Contact tracing identified that several attended stalls kept camels and sold raw camel milk at the celebration. Maternal lower respiratory samples were PCR positive and sequencing identified the same novel enveloped single stranded RNA respiratory virus first reported from the Arabian Peninsula in 2012.

explanation: The diagnosis is MERS-CoV. The combination of recent travel to camel‑exposed venues in the Gulf, progressive hypoxaemic pneumonia with lymphopenia and rising creatinine and transaminases, negative influenza testing, and lower respiratory PCR sequencing identifying the novel coronavirus supports MERS‑CoV as the specific cause rather than other respiratory infections. MERS‑CoV infection during pregnancy can be severe and is associated with maternal multi‑organ involvement and adverse pregnancy outcomes, and diagnostic yield is highest from lower respiratory tract specimens tested by RT‑PCR.

hints.text: A 41-year-old ICU nurse developed low grade fever and myalgia followed by progressive shortness of breath over 6 days. She required admission when oxygen saturation fell to 84% on room air and she became tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 32/min.

She had no chronic medical problems. Four days before her symptoms began she had participated in endotracheal intubation and non-invasive ventilation sessions for a patient transferred from overseas with severe pneumonia.
Laboratory tests showed lymphopenia 0.8 × 10^9/L, serum creatinine 220 µmol/L with a rising trend and CRP 240 mg/L. Initial bacterial cultures and standard viral PCR panel were negative.
High resolution chest CT showed diffuse bilateral ground glass attenuation with dependent consolidation and small bilateral pleural effusions. Findings were consistent with diffuse alveolar damage.

Occupational health noted that several colleagues who assisted during the same aerosol generating procedures developed febrile respiratory illness. Tracheal aspirate PCR and whole genome sequencing identified a novel enveloped single stranded RNA virus first described from the Arabian Peninsula in 2012, matching sequences from the index patient.

explanation: The diagnosis is MERS-CoV. The timing of symptoms after intubation of an index patient from the Arabian Peninsula, clusters of illness in colleagues involved in the same procedures, lymphopenia with severe hypoxaemic pneumonia, negative routine viral panels, and matching PCR sequencing to the index case point to MERS‑CoV rather than a common nosocomial bacterial or viral pathogen. MERS‑CoV can transmit during aerosol generating procedures and commonly causes diffuse alveolar damage; lower respiratory sampling yields the highest sensitivity for molecular diagnosis.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man presented to the dermatology clinic with a 3-month history of gradually increasing, painless red-purple papules on both forearms and the dorsum of his feet. He reported mild swelling of the right ankle and a 3 kg weight loss over two months, temperature 37.4°C, and otherwise normal cardiorespiratory examination.

He was diagnosed with HIV infection four years earlier and has had inconsistent adherence to antiretroviral therapy. He has sex with men, smokes cigarettes, and has no recent travel or animal exposures.
Plain radiographs of the affected foot showed soft tissue swelling without osseous lesion. A screening chest radiograph was normal.
Lesions were treated empirically with 10 days of oral erythromycin for presumed bacterial vascular lesion without clinical improvement; nodules continued to enlarge over the following month.

Punch biopsy of a forearm papule showed a dermal vascular proliferation composed of spindle-shaped cells and extravasated erythrocytes. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong nuclear staining of lesional cells for a viral latency-associated nuclear antigen and tissue PCR detected viral DNA.

explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 8. The chronic painless red-purple papules, HIV with inconsistent antiretroviral use, spindle-cell dermal vascular proliferation with extravasated erythrocytes on biopsy, and strong nuclear staining for the HHV-8 latency-associated nuclear antigen with PCR confirmation point to Kaposi sarcoma rather than bacterial lesions or other vascular tumors. HHV-8 is required for Kaposi sarcoma and is detected in lesional nuclei by LANA staining, with lesions often appearing as violaceous plaques or nodules on skin and mucosa and sometimes causing local lymphedema.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented with two weeks of progressive dyspnoea and nonproductive cough. On examination he was tachypnoeic with reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right hemithorax, and he required therapeutic thoracentesis for a large effusion.
He has a long history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with weekly methotrexate and low-dose prednisolone. He has no known malignancy and no recent international travel.
CT thorax demonstrated a large right-sided pleural effusion with mild loculation, no dominant pulmonary mass, and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
Repeated therapeutic thoracenteses transiently improved symptoms but the effusion reaccumulated within days despite diuretics and no radiographic parenchymal source was identified.

Pleural fluid cytology showed atypical plasmablastic lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemistry on cell block revealed nuclear staining for a viral latency-associated antigen and pleural fluid PCR detected viral DNA.
