explanation: The diagnosis is Human herpesvirus 8. A large recurrent pleural effusion containing atypical plasmablastic lymphoid cells in the setting of chronic immunosuppression, combined with nuclear LANA staining and HHV-8 DNA by PCR, is characteristic of HHV-8 primary effusion lymphoma rather than a benign effusion or metastatic epithelial malignancy. Primary effusion lymphoma is an HHV-8 driven B-cell lymphoma that typically presents as an effusion without a discrete mass and is most often seen with HIV or other profound immunosuppression.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to a dermatology clinic with a three-month history of multiple skin lesions on the lower abdomen, proximal thighs, and groin. He reports mild pruritus and says lesions interfere with shaving; he is afebrile and otherwise well. On examination there are dozens of discrete, firm, flesh-coloured dome-shaped papules 2–6 mm in diameter, some clustered, without surrounding erythema.

He has no chronic illnesses and takes no regular medication. He began applying a potent topical corticosteroid prescribed for presumed inflammatory folliculitis six weeks ago, and notes that new lesions appeared and existing lesions enlarged after steroid use. He reports a new sexual partner within the last four months.

Full blood count is within reference range with WBC 6.2 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein is 2 mg/L. Swab PCR of a purulent-looking lesion is negative for herpes simplex virus. Combined HIV antigen/antibody test returned negative. A punch biopsy was performed and sent for routine histology.

Dermoscopy of several lesions shows a central white-yellow amorphous core with surrounding fine linear 'crown' vessels and multiple tiny surface pores. Expression of one lesion produced a white curd-like core.

The patient later reports his partner has a 3-year-old who attends daycare and developed similar trunk papules last month. Histology of the biopsy shows markedly enlarged keratinocytes in the superficial epidermis containing large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

explanation: The diagnosis is Molluscum contagiosum virus. The numerous flesh-colored dome-shaped papules with central curd-like cores, spread after topical steroid use, dermoscopic central amorphous core with crown vessels, and histology showing enlarged keratinocytes with large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies confirm molluscum rather than herpes or bacterial folliculitis. Molluscum contagiosum is a cytoplasm-replicating poxvirus that produces characteristic Henderson-Patterson intracytoplasmic inclusions and spreads by direct contact, with lesions often proliferating when topical steroids are applied.

hints.text: A 39-year-old man presents with six weeks of profuse, watery, non-bloody diarrhoea and an 8 kg weight loss. He reports eight loose stools per day, progressive fatigue, and orthostatic symptoms. Examination shows dry mucous membranes and a cachectic appearance, temperature 37.8°C.

He has known HIV infection but has struggled with adherence to antiretroviral therapy for several months and has thrush. Recent laboratory testing documented a CD4 lymphocyte count of 0.03 × 10^9/L and a high plasma viral load. No recent travel, no antibiotic use, and no chronic inflammatory bowel disease history.

Routine stool bacterial culture and ova and parasite wet mount were negative. Modified trichrome stain performed by the hospital laboratory showed numerous small, ovoid 1.5–2 μm bodies in stool that were poorly visualised on standard microscopy.
CT enterography demonstrated mild concentric jejunal wall thickening and increased mesenteric fat stranding without focal obstruction or abscess.

Reference laboratory PCR targeting small-subunit rRNA from the stool was positive for an obligate intracellular spore-forming parasite. Electron microscopy of stool confirmed 1.5 μm ovoid spores containing a coiled polar filament.

explanation: Microsporidial enteritis causing protracted watery diarrhea in advanced HIV infection due to microsporidia spores. Severe chronic watery diarrhea in a patient with very low CD4 count, negative routine stool tests but numerous tiny 1.5–2 μm ovoid spores on modified trichrome, positive small-subunit rRNA PCR, and electron microscopy demonstrating a coiled polar filament are diagnostic of microsporidia rather than common bacterial or protozoan pathogens. Microsporidia are obligate intracellular spore-forming parasites related to fungi that invade enterocytes via a polar tubule and commonly cause protracted diarrhea in patients with CD4 counts below about 100 cells per microlitre.

hints.text: A 56-year-old woman, three months after renal transplantation, presents with three weeks of progressive proximal muscle weakness, low-grade fevers, and a 7 kg weight loss. On exam hip flexion strength is 3/5 bilaterally and there is diffuse tenderness of the thigh muscles. Temperature is 38.1°C.

Her immunosuppressive regimen includes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. She received anti-thymocyte globulin for induction and a recent steroid pulse for rejection four weeks ago. She has no known exposure to endemic parasites and has not travelled recently.
Creatine kinase is 820 U/L (reference 40–180 U/L), C-reactive protein 65 mg/L, and lymphocyte count 0.4 × 10^9/L. Blood cultures and serologies for common viral myositides are negative.
MRI of the thighs shows multifocal T2 hyperintense intramuscular lesions with enhancement after contrast, consistent with an inflammatory myositis and small microabscesses.

CT-guided muscle biopsy demonstrated intracellular ovoid 1–2 μm spores on modified trichrome stain. Electron microscopy revealed a coiled polar filament and PCR from tissue matched an obligate intracellular spore-forming parasite.

explanation: This presentation is most consistent with microsporidial myositis in a severely immunocompromised renal transplant recipient. The combination of profound T cell suppression, subacute proximal muscle weakness with elevated CK and multifocal enhancing intramuscular lesions, and tissue demonstration of 1–2 µm intracellular spores on modified trichrome with a coiled polar filament on electron microscopy is diagnostic of microsporidia rather than bacterial, viral, or typical parasitic myositides. Microsporidia are obligate intracellular, spore-forming pathogens whose tiny 1–2 µm spores require special stains or electron microscopy for detection and can cause focal organ infections such as myositis in profoundly immunosuppressed hosts.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents with a three-month history of intermittent, migratory swellings of the forearms and lower legs accompanied by itching and intermittent fatigue. She returned from a 10-month volunteer placement in rural central Africa two years ago. On examination there is a 4-cm, raised, mildly tender, non-pitting subcutaneous nodule on the left forearm. Temperature 36.8°C, other vital signs normal.

She was previously healthy, took malaria prophylaxis and routine typhoid vaccination while abroad, and reports no chronic medical conditions. During her placement she participated in community health programmes and received a single mass antiparasitic dose administered locally. She denies intravenous drug use or transfusions since returning home.

Full blood count shows WBC 12.0 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.8 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 130 g/L and platelets 260 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 4 mg/L. A peripheral blood smear taken at 23:00 shows no circulating parasites.

High-frequency ultrasound of the left forearm nodule demonstrates a thin tubular, anechoic structure about 2–3 mm in diameter that moves slowly along its long axis during real-time scanning. There is only minimal surrounding fluid and no abscess.

She recalls prolonged work near fast-flowing rivers and forested streams where daytime-biting tabanid flies were common. She also remembers one midday episode when she felt a crawling sensation in her left eye and a translucent, threadlike worm was observed crossing the conjunctiva and removed by a local clinician.

explanation: This is classic loiasis due to Loa loa, presenting with migratory subcutaneous swellings and an adult worm seen crossing the conjunctiva. The history of daytime exposure to tabanid flies in central Africa, repetitive transient subcutaneous swellings, a visibly moving tubular structure on ultrasound, prior conjunctival worm migration, and peripheral eosinophilia together point specifically to Loa loa rather than other filarial or nonfilarial causes, and a negative nocturnal blood smear fits the parasite's daytime periodicity. Adult Loa loa worms migrate in subcutaneous tissues and across the eye, while microfilariae show diurnal periodicity with peak peripheral blood levels during the daytime.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man, 11 months after orthotopic liver transplantation, presents with two weeks of fever, progressive jaundice, pruritus and right upper quadrant pain. On exam he is febrile to 38.3°C with scleral icterus and tenderness over the liver graft.

He is maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate and has had one episode of mild acute rejection treated with high-dose steroids three months earlier. He required an ERCP with biliary stent placement following a postoperative bile leak 3 months ago.
Ultrasound shows intrahepatic biliary dilatation. MRCP demonstrates irregular intrahepatic biliary stricturing, mucosal enhancement and no obvious stone or external obstructing mass.

Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and stent exchange did not resolve fever or cholestasis. Clinical improvement with falling bilirubin and resolution of fevers was only observed after a two-week course of oral albendazole.

Bile aspirate and liver biopsy stained with modified trichrome reveal numerous small ovoid intracellular organisms 1–2 µm in size. Electron microscopy of tissue demonstrates the characteristic coiled polar tubule.

explanation: This clinical picture represents microsporidial biliary infection causing cholangitis and intrahepatic biliary stricturing in a liver transplant recipient. Biliary strictures with mucosal enhancement after stent exchange that failed to clear fever or cholestasis, plus bile and liver biopsy showing abundant 1–2 µm intracellular spores on modified trichrome and a coiled polar tubule on electron microscopy, identify microsporidia as the cause rather than bacterial cholangitis or other opportunists, and the clinical response to albendazole supports a susceptible microsporidial infection. Microsporidia can invade biliary epithelium in immunocompromised patients and produce a sclerosing cholangitis-like picture that is diagnosed by special stains, electron microscopy, or PCR because routine cultures and imaging are not specific.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman, six weeks after allogeneic stem cell transplantation, presents with ten days of nonproductive cough, progressive dyspnoea and intermittent fevers. She is tachypnoeic and hypoxic requiring supplemental oxygen and has diffuse inspiratory crackles on lung auscultation.

Her post-transplant course was complicated by chronic graft-versus-host disease treated with prolonged systemic corticosteroids. She is lymphopenic with an absolute lymphocyte count of 0.3 × 10^9/L and prophylactic trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole was held for renal intolerance two weeks ago.

She received broad-spectrum antibacterial therapy, empirical voriconazole and a course of ganciclovir for low-level CMV viremia without clinical improvement. Fever and hypoxaemia persisted despite these measures.
High-resolution CT chest shows bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities with numerous small centrilobular nodules and a faint tree-in-bud pattern, greatest in the lower lobes.

Bronchoalveolar lavage cytology with modified trichrome stain demonstrates abundant small ovoid spores measuring about 1–2 µm. Transmission electron microscopy of BAL material confirms an intracellular organism with a coiled polar tubule.

explanation: The diagnosis is Microsporidia. The combination of prolonged corticosteroid use with lymphopenia, progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure with bilateral ground glass change and centrilobular nodules, failure to respond to broad antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral therapy, and abundant 1–2 µm spores with a polar tubule on BAL and electron microscopy distinguishes microsporidia from other opportunistic pneumonias like Pneumocystis or viral causes. Because microsporidial spores are very small and intracellular, diagnosis often requires modified trichrome or fluorescent stains, PCR, or electron microscopy, and different species have distinct tissue predilections that influence clinical manifestations.

hints.text: A previously well 6-year-old boy is brought to a community paediatric clinic with a 3-month history of increasing skin lesions on his trunk and arms. Parents report mild pruritus and nocturnal scratching. On examination there are approximately 25 discrete dome-shaped pearly papules, 2–5 mm in diameter, many with a central depression clustered on the torso and antecubital fossae. Vital signs are normal.

He has a long-standing history of atopic dermatitis managed with emollients and intermittent topical corticosteroids. He began twice-weekly public swimming lessons about 4 months ago. No other household contacts report similar lesions.
Dermoscopic examination in clinic shows a central cream-coloured core with surrounding crown vessels and absent scale. Lesions are superficial and limited to the epidermis on dermoscopy.

Clinic cryotherapy was applied to several lesions and produced immediate extrusion of a thick white curd-like core with rapid flattening of those papules. Lesions previously treated with mid-potency topical steroid appeared to increase in number at treated sites.

Punch biopsy of a persistent papule shows markedly enlarged keratinocytes containing abundant eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies that displace and compress the nucleus while sparing the dermal-epidermal junction.

explanation: The diagnosis is Molluscum contagiosum virus. The clinical picture of numerous dome-shaped papules with central depressions, dermoscopic cream-coloured cores, extrusion of a curd-like material after cryotherapy, and histology showing large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies that displace the nucleus are classic for a poxviral molluscum infection and distinguish it from HPV warts or common childhood papular eruptions. Molluscum bodies, also called Henderson-Patterson bodies, are large cytoplasmic inclusions of this cytoplasm-replicating poxvirus and are diagnostic on histology.

hints.text: A 60-year-old woman who received a renal transplant 2 years ago presents with a 9-month history of enlarging skin nodules on her left forearm. They began as small papules and progressed to several nodules 1–4 cm in diameter, some ulcerated and interfering with dressing changes. She is afebrile and the lesions are painful with occasional serous discharge.

Her current immunosuppressive regimen includes tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose prednisone. Kidney function is stable. She denies recent travel or new sexual contacts and reports no known sick contacts.

Ultrasound of the largest lesion demonstrates a superficially located dermal mass with mixed echogenicity and no deep fascial involvement. Contrast MRI shows lesion confined to skin and subcutaneous tissue without nodal enlargement.

Wide local excision of the largest nodule was performed but within weeks multiple smaller satellite papules appeared proximal to the incision. Topical antiviral application produced partial shrinkage of some nodules but new lesions continued to arise under ongoing immunosuppression.

Histopathology of the excised lesion shows acanthotic epidermis with numerous keratinocytes containing large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies that push nuclei to the periphery. PCR from the biopsy confirms DNA of a human cutaneous poxvirus.

explanation: The diagnosis is Molluscum contagiosum virus. The development of rapidly enlarging and recurrent nodules in the setting of potent immunosuppression, together with histology showing keratinocytes packed with eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies and PCR confirmation of a cutaneous poxvirus, identifies molluscum rather than bacterial infection or neoplasm. In patients with impaired cellular immunity molluscum can form large tumorous lesions that recur or satellite after local therapy because the virus replicates unchecked in epidermal keratinocytes.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to the transplant clinic with 10 weeks of profuse watery non-bloody diarrhoea, eight kilograms of unintentional weight loss, and daytime fatigue. He reports 8 to 10 watery stools daily, lightheadedness on standing, and has a thin, mildly dehydrated appearance with blood pressure 105/65 mmHg on arrival.

He received a deceased-donor renal transplant 14 months earlier and remains on tacrolimus and mycophenolate for immunosuppression. He denies recent foreign travel, has not taken antibiotics in the preceding three months, and has no known sick contacts.

Three separate stool specimens were negative by routine culture, C. difficile testing, and standard ova and parasite microscopy. Quantitative stool fat was elevated at 11 g/24 h, white cell count was 6.2 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L, and there was no peripheral eosinophilia.

CT enterography showed diffuse thickening of the proximal small-bowel mucosa with mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy and no focal mass or obstruction. Upper endoscopy demonstrated patchy villous blunting in the duodenum, and routine H&E review did not reveal helminths or obvious protozoal trophozoites.

Empiric oral ciprofloxacin and nitazoxanide produced no improvement. After starting oral albendazole 400 mg twice daily the patient reported marked clinical benefit within 10 days, stool frequency falling to 2 per day and appetite returning. A specialist stool stain and electron microscopy later identified small ovoid spores containing a polar filament on ultrastructural exam.

explanation: This is intestinal microsporidiosis causing chronic profuse watery diarrhea and malabsorption in an immunosuppressed transplant patient. The combination of chronic secretory diarrhea with weight loss, negative routine stool tests, proximal small-bowel villous blunting, elevated stool fat, clinical response to albendazole, and identification of small ovoid spores with a polar filament on electron microscopy distinguishes microsporidia from bacterial, viral, or common protozoal enteropathogens. Microsporidia are obligate intracellular, fungus-related parasites that produce tiny spores containing a polar filament which they use to inject infectious material into host cells and which are best detected by special stains or electron microscopy.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to a sexual health clinic with a 6-week history of clustered small bumps on her pubic area and inner thighs. She reports the lesions began as single papules and gradually increased in number; on examination there are multiple firm, flesh-coloured papules 3–6 mm in diameter, largely painless, without discharge or inguinal adenopathy.

She recently started a new sexual relationship three months ago and reports intermittent condom use. She has no history of genital herpes, wart treatments, or systemic immunosuppression and completed routine vaccinations in childhood.

Dermoscopy highlights several lesions with a central area of amorphous material and a peripheral rim of vascular dots in a subset of papules. No subcutaneous or deep tissue extension is seen on high-resolution ultrasound of a representative lesion.
Her recent partner reports a single small papule on his lower abdomen that appeared around the same time. She denies recent bathing in communal pools but notes shared towels during travel.

Excisional sampling of a lesion sent for histopathology shows marked hyperplasia of the epidermis and keratinocytes with conspicuous eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies. The pathology report interprets the findings as a viral epidermal infection producing intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

explanation: The diagnosis is Molluscum contagiosum virus. The history of recent sexual contact, clustered flesh-coloured umbilicated papules in the pubic region with dermoscopic central amorphous material and a partner with a similar lesion, together with histology showing eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies, supports molluscum rather than HPV, herpes, or folliculitis. Molluscum is commonly transmitted by direct or sexual skin-to-skin contact in adults and is histologically identified by large intracytoplasmic Henderson-Patterson inclusion bodies within infected keratinocytes.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 3 days of worsening productive cough, increased purulence of sputum and dyspnoea at rest. He is febrile 38.5 °C, tachypnoeic, O2 saturation 88% on room air and has diffuse expiratory wheeze with coarse crackles at the right base.

He has severe COPD on inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting bronchodilator therapy, is a current 40 pack-year smoker and completed a 7-day course of oral amoxicillin for presumed bronchitis 10 days before presentation. He lives independently and reports recent contact with a grandchild who had a 'cold' last week.

Peripheral blood shows leukocytosis 14.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 96 mg/L. Sputum microscopy reveals many neutrophils and a mixed bacterial flora; initial blood and sputum cultures are pending.
Chest radiograph demonstrates patchy consolidation in the right lower lobe with peribronchial thickening consistent with bronchopneumonia and chronic hyperinflation consistent with COPD.

After no clinical improvement on empirical IV ampicillin the team switched to IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and the patient improved within 48 hours. Sputum culture later grew small, non-haemolytic colonies on blood and chocolate agar, organisms that were gram-negative cocci in pairs, oxidase positive, tributyrin hydrolysis positive and produced beta-lactamase.

explanation: This presentation represents acute bronchopneumonia and a COPD exacerbation caused by Moraxella catarrhalis. The organism isolated from sputum matches the clinical picture of lower respiratory infection in a patient with severe COPD. The isolate was a gram negative diplococcus that was oxidase positive, hydrolysed tributyrin and produced beta lactamase, a biochemical pattern characteristic of Moraxella catarrhalis rather than Neisseria or Haemophilus. Clinical clues such as COPD, recent viral contact and failure to respond to amoxicillin are typical for M. catarrhalis pneumonia in older smokers. Moraxella catarrhalis commonly produces beta lactamases which often render amoxicillin ineffective, explaining frequent need for agents active against beta lactamase producing strains.

hints.text: A previously well 2-year-old girl is brought with 5 days of right ear pain, fever to 38.0 °C and persistent crying with poor sleep. Otoscopic exam shows a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with purulent middle ear effusion and markedly reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy.

She attends full-time daycare and had two prior episodes of acute otitis media in the past 6 months treated with oral amoxicillin. Her vaccinations are up to date for her local schedule and there is no history of immunodeficiency.
Tympanocentesis was performed and the aspirated fluid was purulent. C-reactive protein is 45 mg/L and middle ear fluid microscopy shows abundant neutrophils; culture was submitted.
A lateral skull radiograph was not suggestive of mastoid air cell opacification and there is no periosteal elevation on clinical exam to suggest mastoiditis.

After two courses of oral amoxicillin with incomplete clinical response the child improved rapidly when switched to oral amoxicillin–clavulanate. Middle ear aspirate culture later grew oxidase positive, gram-negative diplococci that were tributyrin hydrolysis positive and produced beta-lactamase.

explanation: This is acute otitis media due to Moraxella catarrhalis in a toddler. The middle ear aspirate culture identifies the organism responsible for the recurrent, amoxicillin refractory infections. The pathogen grew as oxidase positive gram negative diplococci that hydrolysed tributyrin and produced beta lactamase, a profile that distinguishes M. catarrhalis from other common otitis pathogens like Streptococcus pneumoniae. Daycare exposure, recurrent otitis and poor response to plain amoxicillin all fit M. catarrhalis which often produces beta lactamase. Moraxella catarrhalis commonly colonises young children and frequently produces beta lactamase, so beta lactamase inhibition or alternative agents are often required for eradication.

hints.text: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing bronchiectasis presents with 10 days of increasing purulent cough, new left-sided pleuritic chest pain and fevers. On exam she is febrile 38.9 °C, has reduced breath sounds and stony dullness at the left base with reduced air entry.

Her bronchiectasis follows childhood pneumonia; she uses intermittent low-dose oral prednisolone for symptom flares and produces sputum chronically. She reports no recent hospital admissions but had an upper respiratory infection two weeks ago.

White cell count is 18.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophilia and CRP 180 mg/L. Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded turbid pleural fluid with pH 7.05, fluid LDH 1,200 U/L and glucose 1.2 mmol/L, consistent with complicated parapneumonic effusion.
Contrast-enhanced CT thorax shows a loculated left pleural collection with adjacent airspace consolidation and bronchiectatic changes in both lower lobes.

After chest tube drainage and empirical piperacillin–tazobactam the patient remained febrile, so therapy was changed to IV ceftriaxone. Pleural fluid culture later grew small convex non-haemolytic colonies on blood agar; isolates were gram-negative cocci in pairs, oxidase positive, tributyrin hydrolysis positive and beta-lactamase producing, and the patient defervesced on ceftriaxone.

explanation: This is a complicated parapneumonic effusion from Moraxella catarrhalis complicating bronchiectatic lung disease. The pleural fluid and culture results identify the organism causing the empyema. Pleural fluid biochemistry showed an exudative, low pH, low glucose empyema and culture yielded oxidase positive gram negative diplococci with tributyrin esterase and beta lactamase production, which points to M. catarrhalis rather than more typical empyema pathogens. The patient’s chronic bronchiectasis and recent respiratory infection are predisposing factors for invasive Moraxella infection. Although often a mucosal coloniser, Moraxella catarrhalis can cause invasive lower respiratory infections including empyema in patients with underlying lung disease and it is commonly beta lactamase positive.

hints.text: A 46-year-old woman presents with 7 days of unilateral purulent nasal discharge, facial pressure and reduced sense of smell. She is febrile 38.2 °C and has marked tenderness over the left maxillary sinus with purulent rhinorrhoea on anterior rhinoscopy.

She had a dental extraction on the left upper molar two weeks earlier and uses fluticasone nasal spray chronically for allergic rhinitis. She cares for a toddler who has had recent episodes of otitis media.

Peripheral blood shows leukocytosis 12.4 × 10^9/L and CRP 72 mg/L. Endoscopically guided maxillary sinus aspiration produced purulent fluid and microscopy shows many neutrophils; culture was submitted.
CT paranasal sinuses demonstrates opacification of the left maxillary sinus without bony erosion or orbital extension.

Oral amoxicillin produced minimal improvement and the patient was switched to oral doxycycline with modest benefit. The sinus aspirate culture subsequently yielded oxidase positive, gram-negative diplococci that hydrolysed tributyrin and produced beta-lactamase; targeted therapy led to rapid symptom resolution.

explanation: This is acute maxillary sinusitis caused by Moraxella catarrhalis. The sinus aspirate culture identifies the organism responsible for the refractory sinus infection. The isolate was an oxidase positive gram negative diplococcus that hydrolysed tributyrin and produced beta lactamase, biochemically consistent with M. catarrhalis and distinguishing it from Neisseria and Haemophilus. The clinical setting of recent upper respiratory tract infection and poor response to amoxicillin is typical for beta lactamase producing M. catarrhalis sinusitis. Moraxella catarrhalis is a recognized cause of adult sinusitis and is distinguished in the lab by tributyrin esterase activity and frequent beta lactamase production which often underlies amoxicillin failure.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presents from his community clinic with three days of worsening productive cough and shortness of breath. He reports greenish sputum and has become unable to walk up one flight of stairs without stopping. On arrival his temperature is 38.1°C, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 90% on room air, and chest auscultation reveals diffuse expiratory wheeze with scattered coarse crackles.

He has moderate COPD managed with inhaled long-acting bronchodilators and a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, and a 40 pack-year smoking history. He has had three antibiotic-treated bronchitic exacerbations in the last two years and reports that two of his grandchildren had a recent upper respiratory infection, but he has not received pneumococcal vaccination in the past five years.

Blood tests show a white cell count 12.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 48 mg/L. A sputum Gram stain submitted on admission shows numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and predominantly small gram-negative diplococci in pairs.

Posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiographs demonstrate bronchial wall thickening and hyperinflation without a focal lobar consolidation or effusion. Findings were interpreted as acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis rather than dense lobar pneumonia.

Empirical oral amoxicillin was started but after 48 hours symptoms and sputum purulence persisted. Sputum culture later grew a predominant non-haemolytic colony that tested positive for beta-lactamase and was resistant to ampicillin but susceptible to amoxicillin-clavulanate; the patient improved markedly within 48 hours after the regimen was changed.

explanation: Acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis caused by Moraxella catarrhalis presenting as a COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum and hypoxia. The combination of a COPD patient with purulent sputum, sputum Gram stain showing small gram negative diplococci, growth of non‑hemolytic beta‑lactamase producing colonies resistant to ampicillin, and clinical nonresponse to amoxicillin with rapid improvement after adding a beta‑lactamase inhibitor is most consistent with Moraxella catarrhalis rather than typical pneumococcus or Haemophilus species. Moraxella catarrhalis commonly produces BRO type beta lactamases that confer resistance to ampicillin and explain its role in otitis media and COPD exacerbations in older adults.

hints.text: A 69-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with 48 hours of increased cough, purulent sputum and breathlessness. He was tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 90% on room air and had diffuse expiratory wheeze on auscultation.

He is a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history and uses inhaled tiotropium plus a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. He had a viral upper respiratory tract illness one week earlier and has had three treated exacerbations over the past two years.
White blood cell count was 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 48 mg/L. Sputum Gram stain showed many neutrophils and small gram-negative diplococci.
Chest radiograph demonstrated hyperinflation and increased peribronchial markings without focal lobar consolidation.
The patient did not improve on oral ampicillin but had marked clinical improvement within 48 hours after being switched to amoxicillin-clavulanate and a short course of doxycycline.

explanation: Bacterial exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease due to Moraxella catarrhalis presenting with increased purulent sputum and dyspnea. An older former smoker with COPD who developed purulent sputum and whose sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils and small gram negative diplococci, along with failure to improve on ampicillin and marked response after switching to amoxicillin‑clavulanate, points to beta‑lactamase producing Moraxella catarrhalis rather than other typical respiratory pathogens. Moraxella catarrhalis is a frequent cause of COPD exacerbations in older adults and often carries beta lactamases, so laboratory detection of small gram negative diplococci and beta‑lactamase activity is a key diagnostic clue.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to sexual health clinic with 10 days of fever up to 38.9°C, rigors, and a painful cluster of perianal papules that progressed to tense pustules. He reports painful defecation and swollen, tender inguinal nodes on examination, temperature 38.3°C and limited ambulation from rectal pain.

He is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and reports multiple recent male sexual partners, including one new partner two weeks before symptoms. He received childhood smallpox vaccination in infancy.
Pelvic MR performed for severe rectal pain shows mucosal thickening and oedema of the distal rectum and anal canal, consistent with proctitis, without abscess.

Lesion swab PCRs for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus are negative. Routine blood tests show white cell count 7.1 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 46 mg/L. Bacterial cultures from the lesion yield no growth.

Contact tracing identified the new partner, who was later confirmed by PCR and electron microscopy to harbour a large enveloped double-stranded DNA virus with brick-shaped virions; several other sexually linked cases had similar ulcerating anogenital lesions.

explanation: The diagnosis is Mpox virus. The painful perianal papules progressing to tense pustules with inguinal lymphadenopathy, negative HSV and VZV tests, epidemiologic linkage to a confirmed case, and detection by PCR and electron microscopy of a large enveloped double stranded DNA virus with brick shaped virions are diagnostic of mpox rather than herpes or bacterial proctitis. Mpox is an orthopoxvirus with characteristic large brick shaped virions and has caused recent outbreaks of anogenital lesions and proctitis transmitted by close sexual contact.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man five months after renal transplant is admitted with new fever, progressive diffuse maculopapular rash and worsening shortness of breath over 6 days. On exam he is febrile to 39.2°C, hypoxic on room air with oxygen saturation 90%, and has scattered pustular skin lesions on trunk and extremities.
He is on tacrolimus and mycophenolate for immunosuppression. He reports a houseguest who developed a similar febrile rash two weeks earlier but was not seen by a clinician.
Contrast chest CT demonstrates bilateral multifocal nodular air-space consolidation and small areas of cavitation, more pronounced in the lower lobes.
Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous acyclovir produced no clinical improvement after 72 hours. Supportive care continued while additional diagnostics were pursued.

Bronchoalveolar lavage and a skin lesion swab were sent for viral studies. PCR and electron microscopy of the skin specimen identified a large enveloped double-stranded DNA virus with brick-shaped virions, matching the agent also detected in the guest's lesions.

explanation: The diagnosis is Mpox virus. New fever, diffuse pustular rash, progressive hypoxemia with multifocal nodular consolidation and cavitation on chest CT, lack of response to broad spectrum antibiotics and acyclovir, and identification of a large enveloped double stranded DNA virus with brick shaped virions from skin lesions indicate disseminated orthopoxvirus infection consistent with mpox. Immunosuppressed patients can develop severe, disseminated mpox including viral pneumonitis and necrotic skin lesions, and diagnosis is confirmed by orthopoxvirus PCR and characteristic brick shaped virions on electron microscopy.

hints.text: A previously well 4-year-old child presents with 9 days of fever and a new generalized painful papulopustular rash. On exam there are multiple umbilicated pustules concentrated on the face and palms, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and the child refuses to use the right hand from pain.
The family recently acquired an exotic pet rodent from a local pet shop two weeks before illness onset. The child had close handling of the animal and the rodent died within days of arrival.
Routine bloods show white cell count 6.4 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. Swabs from multiple lesions are negative for bacterial pathogens and for varicella zoster virus by PCR.
Hand radiograph is normal without foreign body or osseous involvement. There is soft tissue swelling over the right palm without subcutaneous gas or collection.

The pet shop confirms the shipment included several imported rodents. A veterinary specimen from the dead rodent and a lesion swab from another child exposed at the shop were both shown by electron microscopy and PCR to contain a large enveloped double-stranded DNA virus with brick-shaped virions.

explanation: This presentation is most consistent with Mpox virus infection acquired from an infected rodent, causing a febrile illness with generalized umbilicated pustular rash and tender lymphadenopathy. The timing of rodent exposure with death of the animal, the characteristic painful umbilicated pustules concentrated on the face and palms, negative tests for varicella, and electron microscopy plus PCR identification of a large enveloped double stranded DNA brick-shaped virus point specifically to an orthopoxvirus rather than common bacterial or herpes causes. Mpox is an orthopoxvirus that classically produces firm, often synchronous umbilicated pustules and can be transmitted from infected rodents to humans, which helps distinguish it clinically from varicella where lesions are at different stages.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with a 6-day history of fever, myalgia and a progressive rash affecting the genital and perianal skin. He reports painful pustular lesions that began on the glans and now number about 10 discrete lesions ranging 2–6 mm across, with surrounding erythema and tender left inguinal lymphadenopathy of 2 cm. Temperature is 38.4 °C, he has difficulty sitting because of perianal pain, and he describes dysuria without frank discharge.

He is a man who has sex with men, HIV negative and taking oral pre-exposure prophylaxis. In the two weeks before symptom onset he had multiple condomless partners and attended a private house party in another city. He reports no recent childhood vaccination against the agent used historically in global smallpox campaigns.

Routine bloods show WBC 6.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 25 mg/L, ALT 58 U/L. Urethral and lesion NAATs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are negative. Lesion swab PCR for herpes simplex virus 1 and 2 is negative and non-treponemal serology is non-reactive; a lesion swab has been sent to the reference laboratory for further viral testing.

Pelvic MRI demonstrates superficial inflammation of the perianal skin and subcutaneous tissues without fistula or deep abscess. Ultrasound of the groin confirms a 2.1 cm reactive appearing inguinal lymph node without necrosis.

When contacted for enhanced exposure history the patient reports that one recent partner returned from travel to West Africa one week before his own illness and subsequently developed fever and a similar pustular rash. Local public health notes contemporaneous reports of cases among people who had close intimate contact in several cities.

explanation: This is Mpox virus infection presenting with localized genital and perianal pustular lesions and regional lymphadenopathy following intimate exposure during travel-associated transmission chains. Painful discrete genital lesions, tender inguinal nodes, negative testing for common sexually transmitted pathogens, a partner with a compatible febrile pustular illness after travel to West Africa, and epidemiologic links to contemporaneous outbreak clusters support Mpox rather than HSV, syphilis, or bacterial proctitis. In the 2022 to 2023 outbreak Mpox frequently presented with few localized genital or rectal lesions after close intimate contact, and prior smallpox vaccination can reduce but does not eliminate risk of symptomatic infection.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to a sexual health clinic with 6 days of severe rectal pain, tenesmus and fever. He had multiple small painful anorectal erosions on inspection and a tender left inguinal lymph node, temperature 38.2°C.

He reported receptive anal intercourse with a new male partner 10 days before symptom onset and transient systemic symptoms starting three days prior to the anorectal pain. He had a remote history of treated syphilis and takes no regular medication.

Blood tests showed CRP 84 mg/L and white cell count 9.0 × 10^9/L. Rectal swabs were negative by PCR for herpes simplex viruses and for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis; bacterial culture from superficial lesions yielded mixed skin flora.

Pelvic MRI performed for ongoing severe pain demonstrated circumferential rectal wall thickening consistent with proctitis and multiple enlarged perirectal and left inguinal lymph nodes, but no drainable abscess.

A lesion swab sent to the reference laboratory returned a strong positive signal for viral DNA of a large enveloped double-stranded DNA virus; electron microscopy of the swab material showed enveloped, brick-shaped virions approximately 200–250 nm, and whole-genome sequencing matched the human outbreak strain identified in 2022–2023.

explanation: This case represents Mpox virus proctitis following receptive anal intercourse, with severe anorectal pain and imaging evidence of rectal wall inflammation due to the virus. Severe rectal pain and proctitis with negative PCRs for herpes and common bacterial STIs, a compatible sexual exposure, and confirmation by lesion electron microscopy, PCR and whole genome sequencing matching the 2022 to 2023 human outbreak strain identify Mpox as the cause rather than bacterial or viral STIs alone. Mpox can cause isolated proctitis and severe anorectal pain in sexually exposed patients and may be mistaken for other STIs unless lesion PCR or sequencing is performed for confirmation.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of fever, malaise and a progressive skin eruption. Lesions began as scattered papules on the trunk and progressed to firm nodules with central crusting; oxygen saturation was 90% on room air.

He is 18 months post kidney transplant on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, with recent reduction in haemoglobin and new-onset lymphopenia noted at a routine clinic visit. He denied recent travel but recalled close-contact exposure at a crowded indoor event two weeks before the skin eruption began.

Laboratory tests showed lymphocyte count 0.6 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, AST 95 U/L and ALT 88 U/L. Blood cultures were negative and superficial skin swabs grew only mixed skin organisms; initial PCRs for herpesviruses were negative.

Chest CT demonstrated multiple bilateral nodular air-space consolidations and small dependent pleural effusions, changes felt to be atypical for bacterial lobar pneumonia and concerning for a viral or disseminated process.

Bronchoalveolar lavage and lesional swabs were positive by PCR for the DNA polymerase gene of a large enveloped double-stranded DNA virus; electron microscopy of lavage material showed brick-shaped virions ~200–250 nm and whole-genome sequencing matched the 2022–2023 human outbreak strain.

explanation: This is disseminated Mpox virus infection in an immunosuppressed kidney transplant recipient, causing progressive cutaneous lesions and viral pneumonitis. The combination of progressive umbilicated skin nodules, new lymphopenia due to immunosuppression, atypical bilateral nodular pulmonary infiltrates, and detection of a large enveloped double stranded DNA brick-shaped virus by PCR, electron microscopy and sequencing consistent with the 2022 to 2023 outbreak confirms disseminated Mpox rather than routine bacterial or herpes infections. Immunocompromised patients are at risk for severe and disseminated Mpox that can involve the lungs and other organs, and orthopoxviruses are large enough to be visualized as brick-shaped virions by electron microscopy.

hints.text: A 7-year-old girl was brought to paediatric clinic with 5 days of fever and a rapidly spreading vesiculopustular rash. The rash was most concentrated within areas of chronic eczema, producing multiple erosions and poor oral intake; temperature 38.5°C and child appeared lethargic.

Her mother returned from travel one week before onset and had a brief febrile illness with a small pustular lesion that resolved without medical attention. The child has a longstanding history of moderate atopic dermatitis treated with emollients and intermittent topical corticosteroid.

White cell count was 15.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 56 mg/L. Superficial bacterial culture from several lesions grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin, but the eruption continued to spread despite 48 hours of targeted antibiotics.
Soft-tissue ultrasound of a painful upper-arm lesion showed diffuse dermal and subcutaneous thickening without a focal abscess or deep collection to drain.

A viral swab obtained before antibiotic escalation returned positive PCR for a large enveloped double-stranded DNA virus; electron microscopy of lesion fluid showed brick-shaped virions ~200–250 nm and whole-genome sequencing matched the 2022–2023 human outbreak strain linked to human-to-human transmission.

explanation: The diagnosis is Mpox virus. The rapid vesiculopustular eruption concentrated in areas of chronic atopic dermatitis, a compatible household exposure with a resolving pustule, and PCR plus electron microscopy identifying large enveloped double-stranded DNA brick-shaped virions that matched the 2022–2023 outbreak strain confirm mpox as the cause; failure of improvement with targeted antibiotics despite Staphylococcus aureus growth reflects primary viral disease with secondary bacterial colonization rather than a simple bacterial cellulitis. Patients with atopic dermatitis are at increased risk for severe, disseminated orthopoxvirus infection because a disrupted skin barrier permits extensive viral replication, a pattern historically described with eczema vaccinatum.

hints.text: A 63-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with a 9-month history of productive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers, and 4 kg unintentional weight loss. She reports daily yellow sputum and increasing exertional dyspnoea; on examination her temperature is 37.8 °C and there are coarse crackles over the right midlung field.

She has known cylindrical bronchiectasis diagnosed 3 years earlier after recurrent chest infections and takes no chronic immunosuppressive medications. She has never smoked and has no history of treated tuberculosis or recent travel.
Routine bacterial sputum cultures on three occasions were negative. Blood count shows WBC 7.2 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 115 g/L, and CRP 28 mg/L.

High-resolution CT chest demonstrates multifocal cylindrical bronchiectasis with clusters of small nodules and tree-in-bud opacities concentrated in the right middle lobe and lingula, without large consolidations or mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

She is an avid indoor gardener and reports weekly use of a backyard hot tub. Three sputum specimens incubated for prolonged culture produced smooth, non-pigmented colonies after about two weeks; Ziehl-Neelsen staining of colonies revealed slender acid-fast bacilli.

explanation: Pulmonary Mycobacterium avium complex infection presenting as nodular bronchiectatic disease localized to the right middle lobe and lingula. Chronic productive cough in a patient with preexisting cylindrical bronchiectasis, focal tree-in-bud nodularity on CT, repeatedly negative routine sputum cultures, and slowly growing smooth nonpigmented acid-fast colonies after prolonged incubation point to MAC rather than typical bacterial pathogens or tuberculosis. MAC often causes an indolent nodular bronchiectatic syndrome that preferentially involves the middle lobe and lingula and commonly requires several weeks of culture to isolate.

hints.text: A 56-year-old woman receiving biological therapy for rheumatoid arthritis presents with a three-month history of persistent dry cough, low-grade fevers, and progressive weight loss. Her temperature is 37.7 °C and there are widespread fine inspiratory crackles on lung auscultation.
She has been treated with an anti-TNF agent for 20 months and had a negative interferon gamma release assay before starting therapy. She has no known TB contacts and no recent overseas travel.

Blood tests show WBC 8.5 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.8 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 118 g/L and CRP 60 mg/L. Sputum cultures for routine bacteria are repeatedly negative and sputum cytology shows mixed inflammatory cells.
Chest radiograph and CT chest demonstrate numerous small, diffuse nodules in a miliary pattern with several tiny cavitary nodules and mild bilateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures became positive only after prolonged incubation and acid-fast bacilli were seen on staining of the culture material. She reports gardening several times per week and working with compost and mulch without respiratory protection.

explanation: Disseminated pulmonary infection with Mycobacterium avium complex producing a miliary pattern in a patient receiving anti-TNF therapy. Immunosuppression from anti-TNF therapy and lymphopenia raises risk of mycobacterial disease, and the diffuse miliary nodules with tiny cavitary lesions combined with delayed culture growth and acid-fast bacilli on culture point to an environmental nontuberculous mycobacterium such as MAC rather than only reactivation tuberculosis. Anti-TNF agents increase susceptibility to both tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacteria, and MAC infections often require prolonged incubation to be detected and can present with diffuse or cavitary pulmonary disease.

hints.text: A previously well 3-year-old girl is brought with a 6-week history of progressive left submandibular swelling. The node is now 3 cm, firm with overlying erythema, she is afebrile and systemic examination is otherwise normal.

She has had normal growth and development, no BCG reaction concerns, and no household contact with active tuberculosis. Parents report the swelling did not respond to two courses of oral penicillin and amoxicillin.
Blood count is WBC 9.0 × 10^9/L and CRP 18 mg/L. A tuberculin skin test and interferon gamma release assay are both negative.
Neck ultrasound shows a heterogeneous, partly cystic left submandibular lymph node with internal septations and peripheral vascularity, suggesting necrotic lymphadenitis.

An excisional lymph node biopsy was sent for prolonged culture and, after about two weeks, colonies grew that stained positive with Ziehl-Neelsen for acid-fast bacilli. Parents describe frequent play in the backyard sandbox and putting soil-covered toys in her mouth.

explanation: Cervical lymphadenitis due to Mycobacterium avium complex presenting as a chronic unilateral submandibular node with necrotic features in a young child. A slowly progressive unilateral lymph node in a toddler that did not respond to beta-lactam antibiotics, accompanied by negative tuberculin and interferon gamma tests and growth of acid-fast bacilli after prolonged culture, is characteristic of environmental NTM infection such as MAC rather than typical childhood bacterial lymphadenitis or tuberculosis. In young children MAC is a leading cause of chronic cervicofacial lymphadenitis and diagnosis commonly relies on excisional biopsy and extended culture because routine tests are often unrevealing.

hints.text: A 63-year-old retired librarian presents with an 8-month history of daily productive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers and a 6-kg weight loss. Symptoms progressed slowly; on examination she has scattered inspiratory crackles over the right middle lung and reports reduced exercise tolerance but no haemoptysis or night sweats.

She is a lifelong non-smoker with a history of bronchiectasis diagnosed two years earlier after recurrent respiratory infections. She has no known immunosuppression, a negative HIV test six months ago, and has received multiple short courses of oral antibiotics for presumed bacterial exacerbations with only transient benefit.

Three separate expectorated sputum specimens were positive for acid-fast bacilli on fluorescent stain. A nucleic acid amplification test for pulmonary tuberculosis was repeatedly negative. Inflammatory markers were modestly raised, CRP 18 mg/L and white cell count 9.2 × 10^9/L.

High-resolution CT chest shows right middle lobe and lingula predominant cylindrical bronchiectasis with multifocal nodules and tree-in-bud opacities. There is no cavitation and no large consolidative lobar opacity.

She reports weekly use of a communal hot tub at her sports club. Culture of water from that hot tub grew a slow-growing, non-pigmented acid-fast organism on prolonged culture, and the environmental isolate matched the patient’s respiratory isolate by molecular typing.

explanation: Pulmonary infection with Mycobacterium avium complex presenting as nodular bronchiectatic disease in a patient with underlying bronchiectasis. The chronic subacute course with right middle lobe and lingula predominant bronchiectasis, multifocal nodules and tree-in-bud opacities together with repeatedly AFB positive sputum but negative tuberculosis NAAT point to a nontuberculous mycobacterial infection. Growth of a slow growing, nonpigmented acid-fast organism from both the patient and the communal hot tub with molecular matching confirms environmental acquisition of MAC. Mycobacterium avium complex is acquired from environmental water and soil sources such as hot tubs and household plumbing and classically causes a nodular bronchiectatic syndrome in older adults rather than person to person transmission.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents with 5 weeks of productive cough, low-grade fevers and 6 kg weight loss. He has reduced breath sounds and dullness at the right apex on examination and requires 2 L/min oxygen to maintain SpO2 94%.

He has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and has taken oral prednisone 20 mg daily for 3 months after a recent exacerbation. He is a retired gardener who never smoked heavily and has no known tuberculosis exposure.
White blood cell count 15.2 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 112 mg/L. Three sputum AFB smears were negative and routine bacterial cultures initially reported no rapid growth.
Contrast CT chest shows a 5 cm thick-walled cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe with surrounding nodular infiltrates and small loculated pleural effusion.

After bronchoscopy and prolonged incubation of aspirate, aerobic culture produced dry, chalky colonies after 5–7 days; microscopy showed branching filamentous gram-positive bacilli that were partially acid-fast. High-dose oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was started and clinical and radiographic improvement followed over weeks.

explanation: Pulmonary nocardiosis due to Nocardia asteroides causing a cavitary upper lobe infection in an immunosuppressed host. The subacute cavitary right upper lobe lesion in a patient on prolonged corticosteroids, together with dry chalky colonies that grew after several days and microscopy showing branching gram positive bacilli that are partially acid fast, distinguishes Nocardia from routine bacteria and from typical mycobacteria. The clinical and radiographic improvement after appropriate therapy further supports Nocardia as the pathogen. Nocardia species are weakly acid fast branching filamentous gram positive bacteria that grow slowly on aerobic media and preferentially cause cavitary pulmonary disease and disseminated infection in immunocompromised patients.

hints.text: A 60-year-old woman with chronic bronchiectasis presents with 7 weeks of cough, purulent sputum and progressive exertional dyspnoea. She reports night sweats and has lost 5 kg, but is afebrile on arrival and able to speak in full sentences.
Her bronchiectasis developed after childhood pneumonia; she uses inhaled corticosteroid therapy intermittently. She has no recent travel, no known tuberculosis contact and is HIV negative.

White blood cell count 13.3 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 68 mg/L. Three sputum samples were negative for acid-fast bacilli on standard mycobacterial smear and mycobacterial culture remained negative at two weeks.
High-resolution CT chest shows multifocal nodular infiltrates with cavitation, most prominent in the upper lobes, and a tree-in-bud pattern in the middle lobe.

After prolonged incubation of a sputum specimen on routine aerobic media, colonies with dry, chalky morphology grew at 5–7 days; modified acid-fast staining showed branching filamentous gram-positive organisms. The patient improved only after starting prolonged high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

explanation: Pulmonary nocardiosis caused by Nocardia asteroides presenting with multifocal cavitating nodular infiltrates in a patient with bronchiectasis. Initial negative mycobacterial smears and two week cultures do not exclude Nocardia because this organism often requires prolonged incubation on routine aerobic media; the later recovery of dry, chalky colonies and modified acid fast branching filamentous organisms together with response to high dose therapy identifies Nocardia rather than mycobacteria or common bacterial pathogens. Because Nocardia can be missed by standard mycobacterial workflows, a modified acid fast stain and prolonged culture on aerobic media help reveal its partial acid fast, branching filamentous morphology.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency clinic with three weeks of productive cough, low-grade fevers and 4 kg weight loss. Over the past five days he developed a dull frontal headache and increasing clumsiness of his right hand. On examination temperature 37.9°C, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, coarse crackles at the left upper lung field and a subtle right pronator drift were noted.

He has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and prednisone 15 mg daily for the last eight months. He is a former smoker, born and raised in a temperate rural region, with no known HIV infection and no prior tuberculosis treatment.

Blood tests show leukocytosis 13.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and CRP 112 mg/L. HIV antigen/antibody screen is negative. Initial blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours. Sputum bacterial culture was sent and remained pending.

Contrast CT chest demonstrates multiple bilateral nodules, the largest 3.2 cm in the left upper lobe with central cavitation and adjacent pleural thickening. MRI brain shows a single 2.2 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe with surrounding vasogenic oedema and mild mass effect.

He reports frequent gardening and recent handling of home compost without gloves, and a minor thorn scratch to the chest three weeks before symptom onset. Culture of aspirated material from the brain lesion and sputum grew dry, chalky colonies after 72 hours, and modified acid-fast staining of the colonies revealed weakly acid-fast, branching filamentous rods.

explanation: Disseminated nocardiosis due to Nocardia asteroides with pulmonary cavitary nodules and a ring enhancing cerebral abscess in an immunosuppressed patient. The combination of immunosuppression from methotrexate and prednisone, compatible pulmonary cavitating nodules, a single ring enhancing brain lesion and isolation of weakly acid fast branching filamentous organisms from both lung and brain specimens after prolonged aerobic culture confirms disseminated Nocardia rather than tuberculosis or fungal disease. The gardening exposure and thorn injury provide a plausible environmental inoculation or inhalational source. Nocardia commonly enters from soil by inhalation or direct inoculation and has a marked propensity to hematogenously seed the brain, so new neurological symptoms with compatible lung disease in an immunocompromised host should raise suspicion for Nocardia.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man with known HIV infection presents with a 3-week history of daily fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue and vague abdominal discomfort. On examination he is febrile to 38.5°C, pale, and has a spleen palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin with several small, non-tender inguinal nodes.

He reports intermittent adherence to antiretroviral therapy over the past year and stopped prophylaxis for opportunistic infections after a recent clinic lapse. His most recent CD4 count three months ago was 18 × 10^6/L and HIV viral load was high.

Haemoglobin 88 g/L, C-reactive protein 120 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L. Multiple sets of blood cultures including bottles placed on specialized media for acid-fast organisms yielded acid-fast bacilli after about 10 days of incubation.
Contrast CT abdomen demonstrates hepatosplenomegaly with numerous 3–8 mm low-density lesions in the liver and spleen consistent with microabscesses; no focal biliary obstruction is seen.

Empirical therapy with azithromycin and ethambutol was begun while awaiting final identification; fever subsided within 10 days and energy and appetite improved. Reference lab later reported slow-growing, non-pigmented acid-fast isolates from blood and tissue consistent with environmental slow-growing acid-fast bacilli that cause disseminated disease in advanced cellular immunodeficiency.

explanation: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex infection in advanced HIV presenting with systemic symptoms, hepatosplenomegaly and bone marrow involvement. Profound immunosuppression with a very low CD4 count, subacute fevers, splenomegaly with microabscesses, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and recovery of slow-growing nonchromogenic acid-fast bacilli from blood cultures after prolonged incubation point to MAC rather than tuberculosis or typical bloodstream pathogens. MAC is an environmental non-tuberculous mycobacterium that commonly causes disseminated disease in patients with CD4 counts below about 50 cells/µL and typically forms slow-growing smooth non-pigmented colonies on culture.

hints.text: A 56-year-old woman attends the respiratory clinic with nine months of productive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers and a 4 kg weight loss. She is a lifelong non-smoker, slender, with fine inspiratory crackles at the bases and reports reduced exercise tolerance; oxygen saturation 96% on room air.

She has a history of gastro-oesophageal reflux with chronic microaspiration and was diagnosed with mild bronchiectasis five years ago. She has no known immunodeficiency and no recent travel to TB-endemic regions.

Three expectorated sputum specimens were negative for routine bacterial pathogens and initially negative on acid-fast smear. Extended cultures kept on media for acid-fast organisms produced growth of acid-fast bacilli after approximately 14 days; bronchoalveolar lavage later yielded the same organism.
High-resolution CT chest shows multifocal cylindrical bronchiectasis with centrilobular nodules and tree-in-bud opacities predominantly affecting the right middle lobe and lingula.

She reports routine cleaning of an indoor ornamental fountain and regular visits to public spa pools with aerosolised water. Given the nodular bronchiectatic pattern, repeated positive cultures for slow-growing acid-fast bacilli, and domestic water aerosol exposure, clinicians commenced prolonged macrolide plus ethambutol-based therapy.

explanation: Nodular bronchiectatic pulmonary disease due to Mycobacterium avium complex causing chronic cough and focal bronchiectasis changes. The chronic productive cough in a slender non-smoker with preexisting bronchiectasis, the CT pattern of centrilobular nodules and tree-in-bud in the right middle lobe and lingula, and repeated isolation of slow-growing acid-fast bacilli from sputum and BAL favor an environmental NTM like MAC over tuberculosis or routine bacterial infection. MAC pulmonary disease often affects middle-aged to older non-smokers with bronchiectasis and requires repeated cultures because the organism may take two weeks or longer to grow from respiratory specimens.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis presents with two months of low-grade fevers, three weeks of multiple tender subcutaneous nodules on his forearms and progressive right wrist pain and swelling limiting hand use. Temperature 37.8°C, right wrist tender with reduced range of motion.

He has been treated with a tumour necrosis factor blocker and methotrexate for three years. He gardens frequently and recalls several splinters from rose bushes over the past six months but reports no recent systemic antibiotic courses.

CRP 65 mg/L, white cell count 8.6 × 10^9/L. Blood cultures are sterile. Aspirate of a skin nodule and synovial fluid from the wrist both showed numerous acid-fast organisms on Ziehl-Neelsen stain while routine bacterial cultures remained negative.

MRI of the wrist demonstrates distal radial osteomyelitis with cortical destruction and adjacent soft tissue abscesses. Whole-body PET-CT shows multiple FDG-avid cutaneous nodules and corresponding marrow uptake at the right distal radius.

Cultures on specialized media required 2–3 weeks to form smooth, non-pigmented colonies. Molecular testing identified slow-growing environmental acid-fast organisms that have been reported to cause soft tissue and bone infections after skin breach in patients receiving TNF-blocking therapy. He was started on clarithromycin plus ethambutol with gradual clinical improvement.

explanation: Cutaneous and osteoarticular Mycobacterium avium complex infection associated with immunosuppression from TNF-blocking therapy. The combination of indolent tender skin nodules, wrist osteomyelitis with cortical destruction, numerous acid-fast bacilli on tissue stains, and slow-growing non-pigmented colonies after weeks of incubation indicates an environmental slow-growing NTM such as MAC rather than common pyogenic bacteria or M. tuberculosis. TNF-blocker therapy increases risk for extrapulmonary non-tuberculous mycobacterial infections, and MAC can enter through skin breaches to cause localized soft tissue and bone disease with indolent culture growth.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents to clinic with three weeks of productive cough, low-grade fevers, night sweats and 4 kg weight loss. He reports progressive dyspnoea and new intermittent headaches for five days. On exam temperature is 37.9°C, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, and there are scattered crackles over the right lung base.

He has sarcoidosis treated with oral prednisone 15 mg daily for two years and type 2 diabetes with recent HbA1c 8.1%. He is a retired carpenter who spends weekends gardening and has no recent travel or tuberculosis contact.

Blood work shows WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Two sets of routine blood cultures and sputum cultures after 48 hours are reported as no growth and routine AFB smear is negative.

Chest CT demonstrates multiple nodular consolidations in the right upper and middle lobes with central cavitation. Contrast MRI of the brain shows a 1.8 cm ring-enhancing lesion in the left parietal lobe with surrounding vasogenic oedema.

Bronchoalveolar lavage cultured slowly growing dry, chalky colonies after six days. Modified acid-fast staining of the colonies showed branching filamentous gram-positive organisms that were weakly acid-fast and the patient began high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with clinical and radiographic improvement over the following weeks.

explanation: Pulmonary nocardiosis with hematogenous dissemination producing a brain abscess due to Nocardia asteroides. An immunosuppressed patient with cavitary pulmonary nodules and a ring enhancing cerebral lesion, together with slowly growing dry chalky colonies and weakly acid-fast branching filamentous gram-positive organisms on modified stain, distinguishes Nocardia from mycobacteria and routine bacteria. Nocardia are aerobic branching filamentous bacteria acquired from soil that are variably acid-fast and classically cause pulmonary disease that can spread to the brain in immunocompromised hosts, so modified acid-fast stains and prolonged culture incubation are helpful for diagnosis.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with two weeks of fever, productive cough and worsening right-sided weakness. He reports malaise and one episode of confusion at home. On exam temperature is 38.3°C and he has reduced power 3/5 in the right arm and leg.
He underwent a renal transplant three years ago and is maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose prednisone. He received a steroid bolus for rejection six weeks ago.

Chest CT shows multiple bilateral nodules, several with cavitation, predominantly in the upper lobes. Brain MRI demonstrates multiple rim-enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres with surrounding oedema, the largest measuring 2.4 cm.

Bronchoscopic sampling and stereotactic aspirate of a brain lesion were sent for culture. After extended aerobic incubation, colonies appeared that were dry and chalky and microscopy of colony scrapings revealed branching filamentous gram-positive organisms that were partially acid-fast on modified staining.
The patient was started on high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and showed gradual neurological improvement with shrinkage of the brain lesions on follow-up imaging over six weeks.

explanation: Disseminated nocardiosis due to Nocardia asteroides presenting with cavitary pulmonary nodules and multiple ring-enhancing brain abscesses. The combination of immunosuppression with a recent steroid bolus, upper lobe cavitating nodules and multiple cerebral ring-enhancing lesions, and isolation of dry chalky colonies of branching filamentous gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast after prolonged aerobic incubation is characteristic of Nocardia rather than routine bacteria or fungi. Nocardia are variably acid-fast because of mycolic acids and classically cause pulmonary disease with hematogenous spread to the brain, often requiring extended culture times for isolation.

hints.text: A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency clinic with 36 hours of rapidly progressive swelling, pain, and erythema of the right hand. He was febrile at 38.2°C, heart rate 102 beats/min, and had tense swelling over the dorsum and painful limitation of active finger extension; there was no obvious puncture wound on initial inspection.

He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and long-standing rheumatoid arthritis managed with methotrexate and prednisone 5 mg daily. He lives alone, performs routine gardening, and denied recent travel, intravenous drug use, or prior admissions. Symptoms evolved over less than two days from mild tenderness to marked swelling and systemic features.

Blood tests showed white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. A swab from the wound site and the first set of blood cultures flagged positive within 18 hours, yielding small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli on Gram stain.
Ultrasound of the hand demonstrated hypoechoic fluid tracking along the flexor tendon sheaths without obvious cortical bone erosion on plain radiographs. No foreign body or gas was identified.
On directed questioning after culture results, he recalled being scratched on the dorsal right hand by his indoor cat while trying to separate it from a neighbour's cat 48 hours before symptom onset.

explanation: Bacteremic Pasteurella multocida soft tissue infection causing rapidly progressive hand cellulitis and tenosynovitis after a cat scratch. Rapidly progressive cellulitis with systemic features, growth of small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli within 18 hours, and a history of a recent cat scratch strongly point to Pasteurella rather than typical skin flora such as staphylococci or streptococci. Pasteurella multocida commonly colonizes the mouths of cats and dogs and causes rapidly advancing wound infections that can become invasive in older or immunocompromised patients.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented to the emergency department with four days of fever, increasing productive cough and dyspnoea. He was febrile at 38.7°C, tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 24/min, required 3 L/min oxygen to maintain saturation 93%, and had coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds at the right base on auscultation.

He has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with inhaled bronchodilators and was given a 10-day course of oral corticosteroids for a recent flare. He is retired, lives alone, and has longstanding alcohol use but no recent hospital admissions.

White blood cell count was 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 150 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at 24 hours and showed small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli on Gram stain.
Chest radiograph demonstrated dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with a small right pleural effusion. CT chest confirmed lobar consolidation and small loculated effusion without cavitation.
On directed questioning the patient recalled being bitten on his right index finger by a neighbour's cat six days before symptom onset, and he had allowed the animal to lick the uncleaned wound.

explanation: Bacteremic Pasteurella multocida pneumonia occurring after a cat bite with wound contamination and bacteremic spread in a patient with chronic lung disease. Lobar consolidation with effusion, blood cultures yielding small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli within a day, and a recent cat bite with licking of the wound are classic for Pasteurella as the cause of respiratory infection rather than routine community bacteria. Pasteurella can produce invasive respiratory infections in patients with underlying lung disease or steroid exposure and typically appears as small pleomorphic coccobacilli on Gram stain.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 3-week history of intense generalized itching and progressively excoriated papules on the trunk and proximal limbs. He reports disturbed sleep because of the pruritus, has had low-grade fevers up to 38.2 °C, and on examination is tachycardic at 104 min^-1 with multiple crusted erythematous papules concentrated on the abdomen and along the waistline under clothing.

He is unhoused and has been alternating between crowded shelters for the past four months, wearing the same unwashed coat most days; he denies recent travel outside the region. He uses communal bedding at shelters, has poor access to laundry facilities, and has no prior diagnosis of dermatologic disease.

Full blood count shows hemoglobin 92 g/L with mean corpuscular volume 73 fL, WBC 11.2 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 28 mg/L. A bacterial swab of a secondary excoriated lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin.

A clinical photograph of the torso demonstrates densely grouped papules and excoriations in linear clusters aligned with the beltline and inner seams of the shirt, with relative sparing of the scalp and distal extremities.

Inspection of the patient's unwashed coat revealed numerous small wingless blood-stained arthropods and oval translucent eggs firmly attached to fabric fibers in the seams; laundering the coat at 65 °C and treating skin excoriations led to rapid reduction in pruritus and no further new lesions.

explanation: Infestation with body lice Pediculus humanus corporis causing intense pruritus, clustered excoriated papules along clothing lines, and secondary bacterial infection. The patient’s crowded shelter exposure and wearing an unwashed coat, lesions concentrated along the waistline and seams, and direct finding of wingless arthropods and eggs attached to fabric identify body lice rather than head lice, scabies, or simple dermatitis. Body lice live and lay eggs in clothing seams rather than on the scalp and can transmit serious pathogens such as epidemic typhus, trench fever and relapsing fever in settings of crowding and poor hygiene.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presented to the ophthalmology clinic with one year of gradual blurring in the right eye and increasing glare in bright light. She noted intermittent redness and foreign body sensation but no acute pain. Visual acuity was 0.3 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left. On slit lamp there were multiple small anterior corneal opacities and mild conjunctival injection.

She emigrated from a rural region of West Africa twenty years ago after living by river rapids until age 35. In childhood she had frequent intensely itchy rashes and a small painless cheek nodule that was surgically removed. She has no diabetes and uses no topical medications currently.

Full blood count revealed eosinophils 1.1 × 10^9/L, leucocytes 6.9 × 10^9/L. Serologic testing for syphilis and onchocerciasis-directed antibody testing performed at regional lab were pending. Skin snips were not initially performed.

Ophthalmic examination revealed punctate corneal stromal opacities and early pannus formation. Funduscopy showed patchy chorioretinal scarring in the periphery of the right eye and vitreous opacities on B-scan ultrasonography.

She confirmed repeated painful bites from very small flies at the river while fetching water as a child. Ophthalmology obtained a small skin snip from the forearm which released motile microfilariae on immediate microscopy, correlating with her eye findings and past subcutaneous nodule history.

explanation: This presentation is onchocerciasis due to Onchocerca volvulus causing chronic cutaneous disease with ocular involvement producing punctate corneal opacities and visual decline. The combination of lifelong riverine exposure to day‑biting blackflies, a history of intensely pruritic skin disease and a removed painless subcutaneous nodule, and demonstration of motile microfilariae from a skin snip point specifically to O. volvulus rather than bacterial or nonfilarial causes of keratitis. The parasite’s microfilariae migrate into the cornea and conjunctiva producing the punctate stromal opacities and conjunctival inflammation seen on exam. Onchocerca volvulus adults live in subcutaneous nodules and release microfilariae that migrate through skin and eyes; the vector is the Simulium blackfly and microfilariae, not the adult worms, are responsible for the inflammatory damage to the eye.

hints.text: A 58-year-old woman presented to the emergency clinic 36 hours after developing progressive pain and swelling of her left hand.
