Over two weeks his haemoglobin and symptoms began to improve after oral iron and a repeat anthelmintic course.

explanation: This presentation reflects chronic hookworm infection due to Necator americanus causing iron deficiency anemia from intestinal blood loss. The history of barefoot exposure in wet paddies, pruritic foot papules at penetration sites, eosinophilia, microcytic iron deficiency with positive fecal occult blood, a transient pulmonary infiltrate consistent with larval migration, and passage of slender 10–12 mm worms with crescentic cutting plates identify Necator americanus rather than other helminths. Necator americanus larvae penetrate the skin, migrate through the lungs and mature in the intestine where their blood‑feeding leads to chronic iron loss, and the buccal cutting plates distinguish them from Ancylostoma species which have teeth.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man on postoperative day 8 after emergency small-bowel resection developed new fevers and confusion on the surgical ward. He was febrile to 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, and noted to have a right internal jugular central venous catheter in place for nutrition and intravenous access.

He has type 2 diabetes with recent hyperglycaemia and has been receiving total parenteral nutrition through the central line for 6 days. He completed 7 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics for intra-abdominal sepsis and had no documented neutropenia prior to this febrile episode.

Two aerobic blood culture sets flagged positive after 48 hours. Gram stain of the positive bottles showed oval budding yeast; peripheral blood white cell count 13.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 156 mg/L.

Dilated fundus examination by ophthalmology demonstrated a 2 mm creamy, well-circumscribed intraretinal lesion in the right macula with surrounding vitreous haze. B-scan ultrasound confirmed particulate vitreous debris consistent with endogenous endophthalmitis.

The central line was removed and intravenous antifungal therapy was started, with defervescence and improved mentation within 48 hours. Microbiology later reported that the blood isolate produced germ tubes in serum and characteristic green colonies on chromogenic medium and was fluconazole-susceptible, findings concordant with the clinical response.

explanation: This is Candida albicans bloodstream infection complicated by endogenous endophthalmitis, most likely catheter associated. The combination of central venous catheter use, total parenteral nutrition, recent broad spectrum antibiotics and hyperglycemia with blood cultures showing budding yeast that produce germ tubes and green colonies on chromogenic medium, plus a characteristic retinal lesion, confirms Candida albicans as the source rather than other yeasts or bacterial causes of sepsis. Candida albicans commonly forms germ tubes and pseudohyphae and frequently causes catheter‑associated candidemia that can seed the eye, so ophthalmologic evaluation is important in bloodstream infection with Candida.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 4 days of high fever, severe myalgia, frontal headache and progressive nausea. He reported profound weakness and one episode of dark-coloured vomiting; temperature 39.1°C, pulse 108/min, and visible scleral icterus on examination.

He had returned five days earlier from a two-week humanitarian assignment in a West African country where he slept in village housing. He did not receive any pretravel immunization because of last-minute deployment and recalled numerous daytime and evening mosquito bites.

Initial bloods showed leukocytes 2.1 × 10^9/L and platelets 74 × 10^9/L. Liver enzymes were markedly elevated with aspartate aminotransferase 3 200 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 920 U/L, total bilirubin 86 μmol/L and INR 2.0.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a smooth, enlarged liver without biliary ductal dilatation or focal lesions. There was no sonographic evidence of portal vein thrombosis or obstructive biliary disease.

Local public health notified the hospital of an ongoing urban outbreak in the same region of a mosquito-borne febrile illness that presents with fever, jaundice and bleeding and is preventable by a single pretravel immunization. Several other travellers returning from that area have required admission with hepatic failure and haemorrhagic complications.

explanation: The diagnosis is Yellow fever virus. The short incubation after travel to West Africa with heavy mosquito exposure, high fever, severe myalgia, dark vomiting, scleral icterus, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, very high transaminases with coagulopathy, and reports of a local outbreak that is vaccine preventable are typical for yellow fever rather than alternative causes of acute hepatitis or febrile illness. Yellow fever is an Aedes‑transmitted flavivirus whose severe form produces marked hepatic necrosis with disproportionately high AST levels and bleeding, and it is largely preventable by a single dose live attenuated vaccine.

hints.text: A 78-year-old woman from a long-term care facility was brought to hospital with 48 hours of fever and progressive confusion. On arrival she was febrile at 39.2°C, hypotensive with blood pressure 85/52 mmHg and tachycardic at 112/min, and had an indwelling peripherally inserted central catheter in the right arm and a purulent sacral pressure ulcer.

Her medical history includes advanced dementia, insulin-treated diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease stage 4. Over the prior three weeks she had two separate courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected pneumonia and a urinary tract infection, and the central catheter had been placed seven days before this admission for intravenous fluids.

Blood cultures drawn on admission became positive at about 36 hours. Gram stain showed budding yeast forms, the routine automated biochemical system returned a low-confidence identification, and initial susceptibility testing reported a high minimal inhibitory concentration to fluconazole.

Contrast CT of the chest showed multiple small bilateral peripheral nodules, some with cavitation, interpreted as likely septic emboli. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no clear vegetations and the catheter tip imaging suggested a fibrin sleeve at the insertion site.

She was started on an echinocandin and the central catheter was removed, but repeat blood cultures remained positive after five days of therapy. A national reference laboratory using MALDI-TOF and sequencing returned identification of an emerging multidrug-resistant yeast notable for skin colonisation and transmission within healthcare facilities, prompting contact precautions and environmental screening at the sending care home.

explanation: Invasive candidemia due to Candida auris, a healthcare-associated multidrug-resistant yeast causing persistent bloodstream infection linked to catheter use and long-term care facility transmission. The patient has classic risk factors including an indwelling central catheter, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics and residence in a long-term care facility; blood cultures grew budding yeast that routine biochemical systems could not confidently identify, showed high fluconazole MIC and persistent positivity despite echinocandin therapy and catheter removal, with MALDI-TOF/sequencing confirming the emerging skin-colonizing organism. These findings distinguish C. auris from common Candida species that are more readily identified and usually fluconazole-susceptible. Candida auris is often misidentified by conventional biochemical systems, frequently shows fluconazole resistance, and readily colonizes skin and the hospital environment which drives healthcare-associated outbreaks and requires specialized laboratory methods for accurate detection.

hints.text: A 45-year-old male smallholder presented with 72 hours of fever, rigors and a rapidly painful swelling in his right axilla. He was febrile to 39.4°C, heart rate 112/min, and examination showed a 5 cm firm tender axillary lymph node with overlying erythema that limited shoulder abduction.

He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and smokes. He lives on a smallholding with chickens and a barn cat and reports frequent direct contact with animals and with soil while clearing brush, but had no recent hospital admissions or intravenous drug use.

Blood tests revealed WBC 16.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. Needle aspiration of the node was performed and the specimen grew small, non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar after 48 hours; isolates were oxidase-negative and initial blood cultures remained negative at 24 hours.

Ultrasound of the axilla showed a 5.5 cm complex hypoechoic collection with central necrosis and surrounding soft-tissue oedema, without clear fistula to skin. Chest radiograph was clear with no focal consolidation.

On targeted questioning the patient said that over the past month neighbours reported many sudden deaths of wild rodents around the village and his barn cat had recently returned with many insect bites after hunting. He also recalled handling a dead rat two weeks before symptom onset.

explanation: Bubonic plague caused by Yersinia pestis presenting as an acute, tender axillary bubo after likely flea-borne rodent exposure. The sudden painful regional lymphadenopathy with systemic fever following handling a dead rodent and reports of wild rodent die-off, together with growth of small non-lactose-fermenting oxidase-negative colonies, supports Y. pestis rather than routine bacterial lymphadenitis. The history of a barn cat with insect bites and characteristic epidemiology of rodent-flea transmission further points to plague. Yersinia pestis classically shows bipolar "safety-pin" staining and is transmitted to humans by flea bites from infected rodents, producing buboes that can progress to septicemic or pneumonic disease if not identified.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the antenatal clinic with 4 days of a diffuse pruritic rash, low-grade fever and aching joints. She is 10 weeks pregnant by dates, afebrile in clinic, heart rate 88/min, and has non-purulent conjunctival injection and a blanching maculopapular rash over the trunk and limbs.

Her past medical history is unremarkable and she is taking no regular medication. Her partner returned from a three-week business trip abroad 3 weeks ago; they conceived shortly thereafter and both recall multiple mosquito bites while he was away.

Blood tests show WBC 3.4 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L, platelets 190 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 4 mg/L. Serum IgM by ELISA was indeterminate with cross-reactive signal, while nucleic-acid testing detected viral RNA in urine but not in concurrent serum.

Targeted fetal ultrasound at 18 weeks gestation demonstrates focal intracranial calcifications and cranial measurements about 2 SD below the expected mean for gestational age. No other structural anomalies were identified on standard survey.

Local public health later confirmed increased reports of a day-biting mosquito transmitted febrile rash illness in the region where her partner travelled, and he had an uncomplicated brief febrile illness with rash on return.

explanation: Maternal Zika virus infection in early pregnancy with fetal findings consistent with congenital Zika syndrome, including intracranial calcifications and reduced cranial growth. Her prodrome of rash, conjunctivitis and arthralgia with recent exposure to a region reporting mosquito-transmitted rash illness, detection of Zika RNA in urine despite indeterminate serology, and targeted fetal ultrasound showing intracranial calcifications and small cranial measurements point to Zika as the cause of the fetal abnormalities rather than other congenital infections. Zika virus RNA is often detectable for longer in urine than in blood, and maternal infection during the first trimester carries the highest risk of fetal neurodevelopmental injury such as microcephaly and intracranial calcifications.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of worsening pain, swelling, and erythema of the left lower leg. He reports a shallow laceration over the shin three days earlier that he cleaned at home. On arrival temperature was 38.9°C, heart rate 110 min−1, and the left leg had tense oedema, scattered haemorrhagic bullae, and pain out of proportion to the area of erythema.

His past medical history includes alcohol-related cirrhosis with ascites and well established type 2 diabetes mellitus. He takes oral diuretics and metformin. He has not taken recent antibiotics and reports progressive deterioration in mobility of the leg since the injury.

Blood tests showed white cell count 18.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 16.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 220 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures and a wound swab grew a pure culture of Gram-negative bacilli on aerobic media. The isolate was oxidase positive and produced beta-haemolytic colonies on blood agar.

Contrast CT of the lower leg demonstrated subcutaneous fat stranding with gas tracking along the superficial and deep fascial planes and a 3 cm fluid collection adjacent to the tibial periosteum. The appearance raised concern for a rapidly progressive necrotizing soft tissue infection requiring urgent surgical review.

On further questioning he recalled slipping and briefly submerging the injured leg in a shallow freshwater canal while clearing vegetation two days before presentation. Microbiology confirmed the same oxidase positive, motile Gram-negative rod from wound and blood cultures, resistant to ampicillin and first generation cephalosporins but susceptible to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone.

explanation: Necrotizing soft tissue infection with bacteremia due to Aeromonas hydrophila following freshwater exposure. A rapidly progressive painful leg infection with haemorrhagic bullae, gas tracking along fascial planes and matching oxidase-positive, motile Gram-negative bacilli from wound and blood cultures after submersion in freshwater is characteristic of Aeromonas rather than typical skin flora. The organism's beta-hemolysis and intrinsic resistance to ampicillin with susceptibility to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone further support Aeromonas hydrophila as the pathogen. Aeromonas species are freshwater-associated oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods that can cause fulminant necrotizing infections in patients with liver disease or diabetes and are often resistant to penicillins and first-generation cephalosporins while remaining susceptible to fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents with 6 months of progressive left lower-limb swelling and 2 months of scrotal fullness. Symptoms are worse at the end of the day and limit his walking. Exam shows non-pitting oedema of the left leg with thickened skin and a 3 cm left-sided hydrocele, T 37.8°C.

He was raised in a rural, coastal community in a tropical country and moved to the city five years ago. Since adolescence he has had intermittent febrile episodes with painful groin swelling treated sporadically with antibiotics. No prior surgeries or known immunodeficiency.
Full blood count: WBC 10.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.6 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 4 mg/L. HIV rapid test negative. Routine urine and renal function within reference range.
Scrotal ultrasound shows a 4 cm simple hydrocele and multiple thin, linear echogenic tubular structures within the scrotal sac that show continuous, twitching motion on real-time imaging.

A late-night peripheral blood film taken at 23:00 shows sheathed, motile larval forms. The nuclear column does not extend to the tip of the tail, and parasites are more numerous on night films; he reports frequent night-time mosquito exposure in childhood.

explanation: This presentation is classic lymphatic filariasis due to Wuchereria bancrofti causing chronic unilateral lower limb lymphedema and a hydrocele. The disease explains the progressive non-pitting swelling, recurrent febrile groin episodes, and scrotal involvement. Night-time blood films showing sheathed microfilariae with a nuclear column that does not extend to the tail tip, greater parasite density on nocturnal films, a marked 'filarial dance' of motile tubular structures on scrotal ultrasound, and eosinophilia point specifically to Wuchereria bancrofti rather than other causes of leg swelling. The rural tropical upbringing with heavy night-time mosquito exposure and recurrent adenolymphangitis episodes further supports vector-borne filarial infection of the lymphatics. Wuchereria bancrofti is transmitted by nocturnal mosquitoes and adult worms live in lymphatic vessels, producing hydroceles and episodic inflammatory attacks that drive chronic lymphedema.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man on day 12 of mechanical ventilation in the surgical intensive care unit developed a new fever to 38.9°C and a sudden increase in purulent tracheal secretions. Over 24 hours his oxygenation worsened, FiO2 requirement rose from 0.4 to 0.7, and nursing staff noted thick, greenish secretions at the endotracheal tube with coarse crackles over the right hemithorax.

He was admitted three weeks earlier after a motor vehicle collision and required exploratory laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure. His course has included a central venous catheter, urinary catheter, and two 7-day courses of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, most recently piperacillin-tazobactam, stopped four days ago for presumed intra-abdominal source control.

White blood cell count is 16.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. An endotracheal aspirate Gram stain showed small Gram-negative coccobacillary organisms; culture on MacConkey agar produced pale non-lactose-fermenting colonies and the isolate was oxidase negative.

Chest radiograph compared with the study 48 hours earlier shows a new dense consolidation in the right lower zone with air bronchograms and a small right pleural effusion. There is no focal abdominal collection on recent CT to suggest recurrent intra-abdominal sepsis.

Surveillance cultures from the ventilator circuit suction canister and the sink drain at the bedside grew the same oxidase-negative non-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus with an identical antibiogram. The organism was resistant to third-generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, and carbapenems and remained susceptible only to polymyxin-class agents and tigecycline; several nearby ICU beds showed colonization with the same strain.

explanation: This is ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by Acinetobacter baumannii, with evidence of a multidrug-resistant ICU outbreak. The organism is causing new consolidation and purulent tracheal secretions in a patient with prolonged mechanical ventilation and prior broad-spectrum antibiotics. The finding of small oxidase-negative Gram-negative coccobacilli that produce pale non-lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar, identical isolates from the sink and suction canister, and resistance to cephalosporins, aminoglycosides and carbapenems are characteristic of Acinetobacter baumannii and point away from other non-fermenters. The ventilated trauma patient and environmental reservoir in the bedside plumbing are classic for A. baumannii nosocomial transmission and outbreak seeding. Acinetobacter baumannii survives well on dry surfaces and hospital plumbing and frequently causes difficult to treat outbreaks because it readily acquires carbapenem and broad-spectrum resistance.

hints.text: A 26-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with 7 days of progressively severe bifrontal headache, nausea and photophobia. She is febrile to 38.3°C, has marked neck stiffness on examination and reports intermittent paresthesia of the lips and fingertips, but no focal limb weakness.

Symptoms began a week after she returned from a three-week visit to relatives in rural Southeast Asia. She has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications, and recalls frequent street-food meals and several swims in a slow-moving inland river while overseas.

Blood count shows leukocytes 9.1 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.8 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture opening pressure 26 cm H2O. CSF analysis: leukocytes 280 × 10^6/L with 40% eosinophils, protein 1.0 g/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L. Gram stain and routine bacterial culture are negative. PCR testing for common viral meningitides is negative.

Contrast MRI of the brain shows diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement greatest in the basal cisterns and mild enhancement of multiple cranial nerve roots including the trigeminal and facial nerves. There is no focal parenchymal abscess or space occupying lesion.

On further questioning the patient recalls eating a dish at a market that included small raw freshwater snails and raw freshwater shrimp about two weeks before symptom onset. A fresh wet mount of CSF performed in the laboratory demonstrated motile microscopic larvae consistent with a migrating nematode larva.

explanation: This is eosinophilic meningitis due to Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm, acquired during travel to Southeast Asia. The clinical syndrome explains severe meningitic headache, cranial nerve irritation, and marked CSF eosinophilia. The combination of recent travel with ingestion of raw freshwater snails and shrimp, CSF with a high leukocyte count and 40% eosinophils, negative bacterial and viral studies, basal leptomeningeal enhancement and cranial nerve root enhancement on MRI, and motile nematode larvae observed in the CSF point specifically to A. cantonensis rather than other parasitic or bacterial causes of meningitis. The exposure history and direct visualization of larvae in CSF are particularly discriminating. Angiostrongylus cantonensis is most commonly acquired by ingesting infected gastropods or contaminated produce and its larvae migrate through the human central nervous system but do not develop into adult worms in people.

hints.text: A previously well 7-year-old boy presents with a 3-week history of progressive patchy hair loss and increasing tenderness at the back of his scalp. Parents report worsening pruritus and nightly rubbing; on examination there are two 3–5 cm scaly alopecic plaques with numerous broken hairs and a separate 4 cm erythematous, boggy, tender plaque over the occiput; temperature is 37.9 °C and posterior cervical nodes are palpable.

No chronic illnesses or recent systemic antibiotic use. The family first treated the areas with an over-the-counter topical corticosteroid for presumed eczema with transient reduction in erythema but progressive hair loss continued. He attends primary school and plays regularly with neighbourhood children.

Full blood count shows WBC 8.3 × 10^9/L and CRP 18 mg/L. KOH preparation of scalp scale and plucked hairs reveals branching septate fungal hyphae; routine bacterial cultures from the boggy plaque are sterile. A fungal culture has been submitted and is pending.

Scalp ultrasound of the occipital lesion demonstrates a 3.5 cm superficial heterogeneous fluid collection within the subcutaneous tissue with increased peripheral vascularity and no calvarial involvement. The pattern is consistent with an intense inflammatory scalp process rather than a simple pustule.

Parents report that a stray kitten was brought into the house 5 weeks before symptoms began and several neighbours subsequently developed scaly patches on their forearms. After 7–10 days of incubation the fungal culture produced a rapidly expanding white, woolly colony; microscopy of the colony preparation showed abundant thick-walled, spindle-shaped multicellular macroconidia and hair mounts demonstrated fungal elements on the external hair surface.

explanation: This is inflammatory tinea capitis presenting as a kerion caused by the zoophilic dermatophyte Microsporum canis. The illness accounts for patchy alopecia, broken hairs, a tender boggy scalp plaque, and regional lymphadenopathy in a child. The child’s history of recent household kitten exposure with secondary community cases, KOH showing septate branching hyphae, a rapidly expanding white woolly colony on culture, abundant thick-walled spindle macroconidia on microscopy, and fungal elements visible on the external hair surface all fit Microsporum canis and an ectothrix pattern that provokes an intense inflammatory reaction. The boggy tender lesion is typical of a kerion caused by a zoophilic species and helps distinguish it from noninflammatory tinea or bacterial abscess. Microsporum canis is a common animal-associated dermatophyte that produces ectothrix hair invasion with abundant macroconidia and often causes inflammatory kerions after contact with infected pets.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presented to an urban emergency department with a six-week history of low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. He reports a 6 kg weight loss and now becomes breathless after climbing a single flight of stairs. On examination he is afebrile, pulse 98 min−1, blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, has a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla and a palpable spleen 3 cm below the costal margin.

The patient has a long history of alcohol use disorder and intermittent rough sleeping over the past two years, with four months in a crowded municipal shelter before presentation. He denies injecting drug use. Dental hygiene is poor and he reports multiple prior episodes of skin excoriation from itching, but he has not sought regular primary care.

Initial blood tests showed haemoglobin 92 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 86 fL, white cell count 7.4 × 10^9/L and platelets 210 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein was 72 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 58 mm/h. Three separate sets of blood cultures incubated for seven days remained sterile; serology and PCR testing for common culture-negative endocarditis agents were negative.

Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 12 mm highly mobile vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet with moderate to severe mitral regurgitation. Contrast CT of the chest showed multiple small peripheral wedge-shaped infarcts consistent with embolic phenomena.

Shelter staff brought in discarded clothing and bedding that the patient had used, and public health inspection identified heavy infestation with body lice on the clothing. The patient described intense pruritus and repeated informal attempts to delouse while staying in the shelter.

explanation: This is culture negative subacute infective endocarditis due to Bartonella quintana causing a large mitral valve vegetation with systemic emboli and splenomegaly. The combination of weeks of low grade fever, new mitral regurgitation with a mobile vegetation, sterile prolonged blood cultures and marked social risk factors including heavy body lice infestation and homelessness points to Bartonella quintana rather than more common culture positive causes. Bartonella quintana is a fastidious Gram negative bacillus transmitted by body lice that commonly causes chronic bacteremia and culture negative endocarditis in people with homelessness and poor hygiene.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presents to the emergency department with three weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats, progressive malaise and a painful lump in his left thigh. He reports a new productive cough and has lost 5 kg over three weeks. On arrival he is febrile 38.6°C, pulse 102/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Examination shows a 5 cm tender, indurated subcutaneous mass with central softness on the left anterolateral thigh and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base.

Medical history notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus for 12 years, with recent HbA1c 9.2%. He drinks alcohol but denies tobacco or injected drugs. He says the thigh lump followed a small skin abrasion on the same leg several weeks earlier; he had no prior surgeries or known chronic lung disease.

Blood tests show white cell count 16.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at 48 hours for a Gram-negative bacillus that was oxidase positive on preliminary testing. Preliminary susceptibility from the laboratory reported resistance to gentamicin.

Contrast CT of chest and abdomen shows consolidation with small cavitary nodules in the right lower lobe and multiple discrete low-attenuation lesions in the liver and spleen, the largest measuring 2.5 cm in the spleen, consistent with multiple abscesses. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the thigh mass returned purulent fluid.

On further questioning the patient reports return six weeks ago from a three-month work contract in rural northeastern Thailand where he spent long days planting rice in flooded paddies and sustained the shallow leg abrasion while working in wet soil.

explanation: This presentation is disseminated melioidosis caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei with pulmonary involvement, multifocal visceral abscesses and a soft tissue collection. A diabetic patient with recent work in flooded rice paddies who developed a painful inoculation-site abscess, cavitary lung nodules and multiple liver and splenic abscesses combined with an oxidase positive, gentamicin resistant Gram negative bacillus is most consistent with B. pseudomallei. Burkholderia pseudomallei is a soil and water organism endemic to Southeast Asia and northern Australia that shows bipolar staining, intrinsic resistance to many aminoglycosides, and can cause acute or chronic disseminated infection.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented to a district hospital after four days of high fever, severe myalgia and frontal headache with progressive lethargy. During the prior 24 hours he developed gum bleeding and several new bruises, was febrile to 39.0°C, pulse 116/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, and had scattered petechiae on his trunk.

He is previously well and works as a shepherd in a nearby upland community, living in a household that cares for several goats and sheep. Family members report that a number of small ruminants had brief fevers earlier in the month, and he had no recent travel outside the district or known chronic medical conditions.

Initial blood tests showed WBC 1.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.2 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 124 g/L, and platelets 24 × 10^9/L. Transaminases were markedly elevated with AST 1,820 U/L and ALT 520 U/L, creatinine 180 µmol/L, INR 2.0, and aPTT prolonged. Malaria smear and routine blood cultures were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated moderate hepatosplenomegaly and small-volume ascites. Chest radiograph showed small bilateral pleural effusions without focal airspace consolidation.

On targeted reinterview he said that two weeks before illness he assisted neighbours with slaughtering goats for a celebration, handled fresh carcass blood with bare forearms, and removed several embedded hard ticks from his lower legs by hand. Two people who helped with the slaughter became febrile within a week and a nurse who treated him at the local clinic has since developed febrile illness and mild bleeding.

explanation: The diagnosis is Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. Rapid onset fever with severe myalgia, bleeding, extreme thrombocytopenia and markedly elevated AST after removal of hard ticks and handling of raw carcass blood, together with secondary cases among contacts and a healthcare worker, is characteristic of Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus rather than common bacterial sepsis or malaria. Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever is a Nairovirus transmitted by Hyalomma ticks and direct contact with infected animal or human blood and it can cause nosocomial outbreaks, so high risk exposures require strict infection control.

hints.text: A 42-year-old woman presented with six weeks of dull right upper quadrant pain and intermittent low-grade fevers. She reported increasing fatigue and a 5 kg weight loss over that period. On examination temperature was 38.0 °C, there was mild tender hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin, and no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.

She had no prior liver disease, did not drink alcohol to excess, and was not taking hepatotoxic medications. Three months earlier she spent eight weeks volunteering in rural highland villages, helping at a school and assisting on small livestock holdings. She denied blood transfusion, intravenous drug use, or immunosuppressive therapy.

Full blood count showed leukocytosis 15.2 × 10^9/L with marked eosinophilia 4.2 × 10^9/L. Liver tests had a cholestatic pattern with alkaline phosphatase 560 U/L, gamma glutamyl transferase 290 U/L, alanine transaminase 68 U/L, and total bilirubin 28 µmol/L. Viral hepatitis serology was negative and blood cultures showed no growth.

Abdominal ultrasound showed heterogeneous, subcapsular hypoechoic tracts in the right hepatic lobe and moderate intrahepatic biliary dilatation. MR cholangiopancreatography demonstrated serpiginous, nonenhancing filling defects within the right hepatic ducts that appeared mobile on real-time sequences.

On repeat history she recalled eating raw watercress and other aquatic plants at village meals along mountain streams during the volunteer stay. Stool microscopy subsequently revealed operculated ovoid eggs measuring approximately 140 × 80 µm, consistent with a large hepatic trematode.

explanation: This is hepatic fascioliasis due to Fasciola hepatica causing eosinophilic hepatitis, biliary obstruction and mobile intraductal flukes. The history of eating raw aquatic plants, marked peripheral eosinophilia, cholestatic liver test pattern, subcapsular serpiginous hepatic tracts on imaging and large operculated eggs on stool microscopy together point to Fasciola hepatica rather than other helminths or biliary disease. Fasciola hepatica is a large liver fluke acquired from freshwater plants that migrates through liver parenchyma producing eosinophilic inflammation and later lives in the biliary tree where it releases large operculated eggs detectable in stool.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with three weeks of progressive right calf pain and difficulty walking. She reports the lesion began as an itchy papule that formed a blister which ruptured ten days ago; exam shows a 5 cm tender indurated area over the distal calf with a shallow serous-draining ulcer and a palpable firm linear cord beneath the skin, temperature 37.9 °C and able to bear only partial weight on the affected leg.

She returned two months ago from a six-month stay in a riverside village where she helped collect water and worked barefoot in shallow standing pools during the dry season. She has no chronic medical conditions, is not taking immunosuppressive drugs, had no recent injections or puncture wounds to the leg, and reports no obvious insect bite prior to onset.

Blood tests show WBC 12.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 110 g/L and CRP 42 mg/L. Blood cultures remain negative and routine bacterial culture of the wound yields no pathogenic growth after 48 hours.

Soft-tissue ultrasound of the calf demonstrates a long tubular anechoic structure in the subcutaneous plane measuring at least 30 cm in visible length, with surrounding oedema and a tract extending towards the skin ulcer. Venous duplex study shows no deep venous thrombosis.

During a bedside procedure gentle traction on material emerging from the ulcer delivered an intact, slender, white cylindrical organism approximately 60 cm long that was photographed and sent to parasitology; the wound was irrigated and the patient reported progressive pain relief over the following week with resolution of serous drainage and restored ability to weight-bear.

explanation: This presentation is classic dracunculiasis due to Dracunculus medinensis, with an adult female worm emerging through a cutaneous ulcer on the lower leg. The clinical syndrome is a migrating subcutaneous helminth producing a blister that ruptures and discharges a long cylindrical worm. The patient’s history of prolonged exposure to riverside standing water, an initial itchy papule progressing to a ruptured blister and serous-draining ulcer, a palpable linear subcutaneous cord, ultrasound showing a long tubular structure, and extraction of a 60 cm white worm are diagnostic for Guinea worm rather than a bacterial soft tissue infection or other helminths. Negative wound cultures and eosinophilia support a parasitic etiology and the characteristic appearance and emergence behavior of the adult female confirm Dracunculus. Dracunculus medinensis is transmitted by drinking water containing infected copepods, after which the adult female migrates to subcutaneous tissue and creates a skin blister to release larvae when the wound contacts water.

hints.text: A 19-year-old university student presents to the emergency department with five days of worsening sore throat, progressive left-sided neck pain and swelling, and two days of pleuritic chest pain with blood-tinged sputum. He is febrile to 39.2°C, heart rate 116/min, respiratory rate 24/min and SpO2 91% on room air. On exam he has tender, firm swelling along the left lateral neck beneath the angle of the mandible and reduced neck extension.

He was previously well. The illness began as a sore throat and malaise nine days ago; he briefly took a three-day course of oral amoxicillin prescribed in primary care for presumed bacterial pharyngitis with initial improvement followed by recrudescence of fever and new chest symptoms. He denies recent dental procedures, intravenous drug use, foreign travel, or immunosuppression.

Admission bloods show white blood cell count 22.3 × 10^9/L with 88% neutrophils and C-reactive protein 246 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive in the anaerobic bottles at 48 hours; Gram stain from the anaerobic bottle demonstrated pleomorphic gram-negative rods.

Contrast CT of neck and chest demonstrates a non-opacified segment of the left internal jugular vein consistent with thrombosis and multiple bilateral peripheral nodular cavitary lesions in both lungs, findings felt most consistent with septic emboli.

The patient remained febrile on empiric ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Metronidazole was added to cover anaerobes and within 48 hours fevers settled and oxygenation improved. Final anaerobic culture at the reference laboratory identified an obligate anaerobic, non-spore-forming gram-negative bacillus originating from oropharyngeal flora that was metronidazole-susceptible.

explanation: This is Lemierre syndrome from Fusobacterium necrophorum, manifesting as septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic septic pulmonary emboli. The clinical course began as pharyngitis and progressed to neck sepsis and cavitating lung lesions. A young previously healthy patient had antecedent sore throat followed by unilateral neck pain with IJV thrombosis on CT and multiple cavitary lung nodules consistent with septic emboli, while anaerobic blood cultures grew pleomorphic gram-negative rods that responded to metronidazole, all pointing to F. necrophorum rather than typical streptococcal pharyngitis or community pneumonia. The timing after a brief antibiotic course and growth in anaerobic bottles further supports an obligate anaerobic oral pathogen causing Lemierre syndrome. Fusobacterium necrophorum is an oropharyngeal anaerobe that can invade after pharyngitis to cause septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and metastatic emboli, often presenting with high fevers and cavitating pulmonary lesions.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to a regional hospital with 10 days of fever, diffuse myalgia, and a progressively painful sore throat that impaired swallowing. He complained of lightheadedness when standing and increasing fatigue. On arrival he was febrile to 38.8 °C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 94/62 mmHg, and appeared dehydrated. The oropharynx was erythematous with scattered petechial spots on the soft palate.

He was previously well and had taken a short course of oral amoxicillin prescribed at a primary clinic without improvement. He works in hospital environmental services and reported that two coworkers had recent febrile illnesses, one requiring brief admission. He had no known chronic illnesses and was not on regular medications.

Initial blood tests showed leucopenia with a white cell count 2.4 × 10^9/L and thrombocytopenia with platelets 65 × 10^9/L. Alanine aminotransferase 240 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 680 U/L. Creatinine 150 μmol/L. Urinalysis showed proteinuria and microscopic haematuria. Malaria rapid test and two sets of aerobic blood cultures were negative.

Chest radiograph showed mild bilateral interstitial markings and a small bilateral pleural effusion. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatomegaly without focal lesions and a spleen at the upper limit of normal size. Non-contrast CT brain was normal.

Further history revealed he had returned three weeks earlier from a six-week stay in rural eastern Sierra Leone helping on a relative's farm. He had slept in a mud-walled dwelling where household rodents were frequently seen and food stores were noted to be contaminated with droppings. Local public health identified a small household cluster of febrile illnesses during his visit, including a pregnant family member who died.

explanation: The picture is most consistent with Lassa fever, a viral hemorrhagic illness acquired in West Africa with multisystem involvement including mucosal bleeding, hepatic and renal dysfunction, and hypotension. The syndrome fits a rodent-associated arenavirus infection with potential household spread. Travel to rural eastern Sierra Leone with rodent exposure and a local household cluster including a fatal case, combined with fever, painful pharyngitis with palatal petechiae, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, high transaminases, and negative bacterial cultures, point to Lassa virus rather than bacterial sepsis or endemic malaria. The pattern of mucosal bleeding, renal involvement and epidemiologic clustering is characteristic of Lassa. Lassa virus is transmitted primarily via exposure to Mastomys rodent excreta and can cause gradual onset fever, pharyngitis, bleeding and multisystem disease, with person to person spread possible in households and healthcare settings.

hints.text: A 38-year-old previously well male research assistant presented to the emergency department on day 6 of illness with high fever, severe myalgia, diffuse abdominal pain and profuse watery diarrhoea. He was hypotensive at 86/52 mmHg, tachycardic 118/min, febrile to 39.7°C and noted to have injected conjunctivae and scattered petechiae on his palate. Urine output was markedly reduced since the previous day and he was lethargic but arousable.

He had returned 10 days before symptom onset from a 12-day field study in rural southern Uganda where the team sampled water and surveyed abandoned mine workings. He reported spending several nights inside an old limestone shaft while carrying equipment and walking through accumulations of bat guano. He took intermittent antimalarial prophylaxis and had no chronic medical conditions or immunosuppression.

Initial labs showed white blood cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L, platelet count 28 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 135 g/L, creatinine 220 μmol/L. Liver enzymes were markedly elevated with AST 1 250 U/L and ALT 680 U/L. Coagulation studies revealed INR 2.6, activated partial thromboplastin time prolonged, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L and lactate 6.8 mmol/L. Blood cultures and malaria thick films were negative.

Contrast CT abdomen performed because of worsening pain showed diffuse small-bowel and colonic wall thickening with mucosal hyperenhancement, moderate ascites and no localized intra-abdominal collection. Chest radiograph showed developing bilateral patchy air-space opacities.

A high-containment reference laboratory examined the patient’s serum. Electron microscopy demonstrated long filamentous viral particles, and a specialised molecular assay detected a high load of a single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus that matched sequences previously recovered from haemorrhagic fever outbreaks linked to caves and mines in that region.

explanation: This presentation represents Marburg virus disease, a filoviral hemorrhagic fever acquired from exposure to bats in caves or mines, causing severe systemic illness with coagulopathy and multiorgan failure. The clinical course shows high viral pathogenicity with gastrointestinal symptoms, shock and bleeding diathesis. The recent cave and bat guano exposure in Uganda, rapid onset of high fever with severe diarrhea, conjunctival injection and petechiae, profound thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy, markedly elevated transaminases and lactate, and electron microscopy showing long filamentous particles with a matching negative-sense RNA sequence all localize the diagnosis to a filovirus such as Marburg rather than bacterial sepsis or another viral hepatitis. The combination of epidemiology, clinical hemorrhagic features and molecular confirmation is diagnostic. Marburg virus is a filovirus related to Ebola that is associated with bat reservoirs in caves and mines and causes severe hemorrhagic fever with high mortality and risk of human to human transmission via bodily fluids.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to a regional hospital with an eight-week history of a productive cough and three episodes of frank haemoptysis. He reported gradually worsening left-sided pleuritic chest pain and exertional breathlessness, and had lost 4 kg over two months. On examination temperature was 37.9°C, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 95% on air, and chest auscultation revealed reduced breath sounds and coarse crackles at the left base.

He was previously well, HIV negative, and a non-smoker. Two months before cough onset he had travelled for two weeks to rural river valleys in Southeast Asia where he attended several communal meals; he received a week of oral amoxicillin from a local clinic without improvement. He denied known tuberculosis contact and had no recent hospital admissions or intravenous procedures.

Full blood count showed WBC 11.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.8 × 10^9/L (24%). C-reactive protein was 48 mg/L. Three sputum specimens were negative for acid fast bacilli by smear and mycobacterial culture remained sterile at two weeks. Thoracentesis yielded a serous exudative effusion with pleural fluid WBC 1.2 × 10^9/L composed of 67% eosinophils, protein 42 g/L, LDH 360 U/L, and pH 7.36.

Chest CT demonstrated a 3.5 cm thick-walled cavitary lesion in the posterior segment of the left lower lobe with adjacent patchy consolidation and several small subpleural nodules. A moderate left pleural effusion was present with subtle linear bandlike opacities extending from the cavity toward the pleura. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy was seen.

On further questioning he recalled eating a local dish containing undercooked freshwater crab during the river festival. Direct microscopy of a fresh sputum wet mount and of centrifuged pleural fluid identified ovoid, operculated eggs measuring about 80–100 μm by 45–70 μm, consistent with a trematode that infects the lung.

explanation: This presentation is pulmonary paragonimiasis caused by Paragonimus westermani, producing a chronic cavitary lung infection with pleural involvement. The combination of chronic productive cough with haemoptysis, marked peripheral and pleural eosinophilia, travel to Southeast Asian river valleys with ingestion of undercooked freshwater crab, CT showing a subpleurally oriented cavitary lesion and linear tracks, and identification of large operculated trematode eggs in sputum and pleural fluid point directly to Paragonimus rather than bacterial pneumonia or tuberculosis. Paragonimus metacercariae in undercooked freshwater crustaceans migrate from intestine to the lungs producing chronic cough and haemoptysis, and the diagnosis is supported by finding characteristic operculated eggs or by serology.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of progressive frontal headache, malaise and new confusion. On examination he was febrile at 38.4 °C, had photophobia and nuchal rigidity, and was somnolent but intermittently oriented to person and place.

He received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 18 days before presentation and is maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. The operation and early recovery were uncomplicated, the donor had an unexpected intracranial bleed, and two other organ recipients from the same donor have developed febrile illnesses in the same interval.

Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 260 mmH2O, CSF white cell count 160 × 10^6/L with 90% lymphocytes, protein 1.2 g/L and glucose 3.3 mmol/L (serum glucose 6.6 mmol/L). Blood tests revealed leukopenia 1.8 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 85 × 10^9/L and transaminitis with AST 220 U/L and ALT 140 U/L. CSF Gram stain and bacterial cultures were negative and PCRs for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus and enterovirus were negative.

Brain MRI showed diffuse leptomeningeal contrast enhancement and patchy T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter. Susceptibility-weighted sequences disclosed a few tiny foci of microhaemorrhage not accounted for by infarct.

Public health investigation found the donor worked in a rodent breeding facility and kept pet hamsters at home. PCR testing of archived donor organ tissue and specimens from the donor's mouse colony yielded an identical sequence to the virus detected in this patient's CSF.

explanation: The diagnosis is Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus. The timeline of neurologic illness soon after transplant, lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis with high protein, systemic leukopenia thrombocytopenia and transaminitis, MRI leptomeningeal and temporal lobe involvement with microhaemorrhages, concurrent illness in other organ recipients, and identification of identical viral sequence in donor tissue and the donor's rodent colony all indicate LCMV transmission from an infected rodent-exposed donor rather than common herpesviruses or enterovirus. LCMV is an arenavirus carried by rodents and can be transmitted via organ transplantation to cause severe meningoencephalitis and systemic cytopenias in immunosuppressed recipients, with diagnosis by PCR or sequencing.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presented to the regional hospital with a 2-week history of diarrhoea that progressed from watery to bloody stools. He reported 8–12 bowel movements per day, crampy lower abdominal pain, fatigue with a 4 kg weight loss, and on arrival had temperature 38.5°C and marked right lower quadrant tenderness on palpation.

He lives in a rural village and performs general outdoor work; he has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and no known immunosuppressive therapy. Two weeks before symptom onset he drank untreated well water intermittently while helping with heavy chores for neighbours; he denied recent international travel or antibiotic use.

Laboratory tests showed white blood cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, haemoglobin 98 g/L and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. Stool testing returned positive for fecal leukocytes and occult blood, bacterial culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin were negative; routine stool ova and parasite screening had been requested and was pending.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen demonstrated segmental wall thickening of the cecum and ascending colon with pericolonic fat stranding, without discrete abscess. Colonoscopy showed multiple deep, discrete ulcers in the cecum and proximal colon with friable surrounding mucosa; endoscopic biopsies revealed acute mucosal necrosis and heavy neutrophilic inflammation but no organisms identified on initial H&E.

On further questioning he admitted daily assistance with his neighbour's small-scale pig herd and frequent handling of fresh manure. A stool wet mount performed because of the exposure showed large, actively motile trophozoites about 50–150 μm in size with uniform surface ciliation and a single large, kidney-shaped macronucleus; thick-walled cyst forms were also seen.

explanation: This is invasive colitis due to Balantidium coli presenting with bloody diarrhea and discrete cecal and colonic ulcers. The rural exposure to pigs and fresh manure, the CT and colonoscopic finding of deep discrete ulcers with heavy neutrophilic necrosis, and demonstration on stool wet mount of very large, actively motile ciliated trophozoites with a distinct macronucleus and cysts identify Balantidium as the cause rather than bacterial colitis or Entamoeba histolytica. Balantidium coli is the largest pathogenic intestinal protozoan and is a zoonosis from pigs that can produce flask-like ulcers and is diagnosed by seeing large ciliated trophozoites with a prominent macronucleus on stool microscopy.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a 5-month history of productive cough, night sweats, progressive weight loss of 10 kg and a painful ulcer on the hard palate. On examination he is afebrile at 37.4°C, has a 2.5 cm indurated ulcer with a friable granular base on the right posterior hard palate and several firm, nonfluctuant cervical lymph nodes measuring 2–3 cm.

He is a current smoker with a 20 pack-year history and drinks alcohol socially. He emigrated from a rural region of South America 12 years ago and has had multiple outpatient courses of amoxicillin and doxycycline without improvement; he is not known to be immunosuppressed and is HIV antibody negative.

Haemoglobin 105 g/L, white blood cell count 11.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L, CRP 46 mg/L and ESR 62 mm/h. Sputum acid fast smear and nucleic acid amplification for Mycobacterium tuberculosis are negative.
Chest CT shows bilateral, predominantly upper-lobe reticulonodular opacities with several thin-walled cavities and mild mediastinal lymphadenopathy, without focal lobar consolidation.

He reports childhood and young-adult work as a farm labourer disturbing soil and plant material. Biopsy of the palatal ulcer sent for mycology grew a dimorphic fungus: at 25°C it produced mould colonies and at 37°C yeast colonies; microscopy from the yeast phase showed large mother cells with multiple narrow-based buds radiating from a single cell.

explanation: This clinical picture represents chronic paracoccidioidomycosis due to Paracoccidioides brasiliensis with pulmonary involvement and mucosal ulceration. The long indolent course with upper lobe reticulonodular disease and cavities, a painful friable palatal ulcer, South American rural soil exposure, and recovery of a dimorphic fungus that forms mould at 25°C and yeast at 37°C with characteristic large mother cells bearing multiple narrow-based buds identify Paracoccidioides rather than tuberculosis or other endemic mycoses. Paracoccidioides is a thermally dimorphic fungus endemic to rural South America whose yeast phase classically shows multiple peripheral narrow-based buds in a pilot wheel appearance and which commonly causes pulmonary disease with mucocutaneous lesions.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man in the surgical intensive care unit on day 12 after emergency sigmoid resection developed new fever and worsening oxygenation. Over 48 hours he became febrile to 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, his ventilator FiO2 requirement rose from 40% to 70%, and staff noted copious purulent tracheal secretions with new right-sided crackles on auscultation.

His background includes type 2 diabetes and COPD. He required endotracheal intubation on admission with tracheostomy on day 5, has a right internal jugular central line, and received 10 days of broad-spectrum therapy including meropenem and vancomycin for intra-abdominal sepsis; he underwent bronchoscopy with saline lavage on day 10.

Blood tests show WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 220 mg/L. A tracheal aspirate Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods and preliminary culture yielded a non-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus with an antibiogram resistant to meropenem and gentamicin and susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and levofloxacin.

Chest radiograph and subsequent CT show a new dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with surrounding patchy air-space opacities and small bilateral peribronchial infiltrates, no cavitation, and no large pleural effusion.

Environmental cultures from the ICU found the same non-fermenting Gram-negative organism with an identical antibiogram in a sink aerator and on the reusable bronchoscope washing tray; the isolates matched the patient’s tracheal aspirate by laboratory typing.

explanation: This is ventilator-associated pneumonia due to Stenotrophomonas maltophilia acquired in the ICU, with environmental contamination of water and bronchoscope equipment. The infection fits a hospital-acquired non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus causing progressive respiratory failure in a patient exposed to broad-spectrum antibiotics. A non-fermenting gram-negative rod from a tracheal aspirate that is meropenem resistant but susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and levofloxacin, combined with matching isolates from a sink aerator and bronchoscope tray, points to S. maltophilia rather than other non-fermenters like Pseudomonas or Acinetobacter. The patient’s prolonged ICU stay, prior carbapenem exposure, tracheostomy and bronchoscopy are classic predisposing factors for this water-associated organism. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia commonly lives in wet hospital reservoirs and is intrinsically resistant to many beta-lactams including carbapenems, which helps distinguish it from other non-fermenting gram-negative bacilli.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presented to the regional hospital with four weeks of fever, night sweats, nonproductive cough and 8 kg weight loss. He was febrile to 38.6°C, respiratory rate 22/min, had multiple non-tender cervical and inguinal lymph nodes and new hepatosplenomegaly on palpation.

He was diagnosed with HIV three months earlier and had not yet started antiretroviral therapy or opportunistic infection prophylaxis. Recent laboratory testing showed a CD4 count of 45 × 10^6/L and an HIV viral load of 1.2 × 10^6 copies/mL.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 85 g/L, leucocyte count 2.2 × 10^9/L with neutropenia, platelets 90 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 72 mg/L. Bone marrow aspirate with Giemsa stain demonstrated numerous small oval yeastlike organisms inside macrophages, and peripheral blood cultures later became positive for yeast forms.

Contrast chest CT demonstrated bilateral diffuse reticulonodular and peribronchial nodules with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed splenomegaly to 15 cm without discrete focal hepatic lesions.

He emigrated from northern Thailand nine months earlier after years working on river valley rice farms. After seven days incubation a blood culture isolate grew a mould at 25°C that produced a diffusible red pigment and the same isolate converted to a yeast phase when incubated at 37°C.

explanation: This presentation represents disseminated talaromycosis due to Talaromyces marneffei in advanced HIV infection. The clinical syndrome includes prolonged fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and bone marrow involvement with systemic fungemia. A severely immunocompromised patient from Southeast Asia with intracellular oval yeast forms in macrophages, blood culture positive for yeast, and a dimorphic isolate that produces a red diffusible pigment at 25°C and converts to a yeast at 37°C is diagnostic for Talaromyces marneffei rather than other opportunistic fungi. The geographic exposure and very low CD4 count make this organism far more likely than Candida or Histoplasma in this context. Talaromyces marneffei is a dimorphic fungus endemic to Southeast Asia that characteristically yields a red pigment in culture at 25°C and shows intracellular yeast forms in macrophages during disseminated infection in patients with low CD4 counts.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the respiratory clinic with 10 days of worsening productive cough, pleuritic left-sided chest pain and low-grade fevers. He had tachypnoea of 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 91% on room air and purulent sputum, and was limited to walking 50 metres before dyspnoea worsened.

He has known non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis diagnosed eight years ago after recurrent pneumonias, and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Five days before presentation he finished a 10-day outpatient course of oral levofloxacin for a presumed exacerbation with only modest symptomatic improvement.

Blood tests showed WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 96 mg/L. Sputum culture incubated on routine media produced a non-lactose fermenting gram-negative rod after 48 hours; the isolate had an unusual antibiogram with resistance to gentamicin and colistin but retained susceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ceftazidime. Blood cultures were negative.

High-resolution CT thorax demonstrated cylindrical bronchiectasis most pronounced in the right middle lobe and lingula, a new left lower lobe consolidation with small central cavitation, and small adjacent pleural fluid.

Environmental cultures from the patient’s home jet nebulizer and a multi-dose saline bottle used at his outpatient respiratory clinic grew the same non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus with an identical antibiogram and matching molecular fingerprint; the organism also grew in solutions containing benzalkonium chloride.

explanation: This is a respiratory infection caused by Burkholderia cepacia complex linked to contaminated respiratory equipment in a patient with bronchiectasis. The organism has caused a new lobar consolidation and symptomatic deterioration despite recent fluoroquinolone therapy. A non-lactose fermenting gram-negative rod from sputum with resistance to gentamicin and colistin but retained susceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ceftazidime, plus identical isolates from the patient’s nebulizer and clinic saline with matching fingerprints and growth in benzalkonium chloride, is typical for B. cepacia rather than other gram-negative rods. The background of bronchiectasis and prior antibiotic exposure predisposes to colonization and infection by this environmental and disinfectant-tolerant organism. Burkholderia cepacia complex survives in moist medical solutions and can resist common disinfectants, which contributes to healthcare-associated transmission and makes eradication from respiratory equipment challenging.

hints.text: A 34-year-old previously well man presented to a district hospital with five days of high fevers, rigors, severe headache and progressive lethargy. On arrival he was febrile to 39.8°C, pulse 116/min, blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, noted to be jaundiced with dark urine and complained of reduced urine output over 24 hours.

He had returned eight days earlier from a two-week field survey in northern Borneo where he slept in makeshift forest camps and worked at dawn and dusk. He did not take any chemoprophylaxis, recalled numerous mosquito bites, had no chronic illnesses and no previous history of blood-borne infections.

Initial blood tests showed haemoglobin 88 g/L, platelet count 48 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 65 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 780 U/L, creatinine 120 µmol/L and C-reactive protein 38 mg/L. Thick and thin blood films demonstrated parasitaemia estimated at 2.4% of erythrocytes with mixed parasite stages; two rapid antigen tests for common human erythrocytic parasites were non-diagnostic and a pan-target PCR was sent to reference laboratory.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a spleen length of 16.5 cm without focal lesions. On hospital day 3 the patient developed worsening oxygenation and chest radiograph demonstrated new bilateral interstitial opacities consistent with evolving lung injury.

While working in the camps he repeatedly observed long-tailed macaques close to sleeping shelters and a number of co-workers reported brief febrile illnesses after the trip. Real-time PCR from the reference laboratory returned positive for an erythrocytic parasite that completes its asexual erythrocytic cycle every 24 hours and is known to circulate in macaque reservoirs in forested areas of Southeast Asia, confirming a simian-origin infection.

explanation: This is severe Plasmodium knowlesi malaria acquired in forested Borneo, presenting with high fevers, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and evolving organ dysfunction. The infection reflects zoonotic transmission from macaque reservoirs and a rapidly progressive erythrocytic infection. Travel to northern Borneo with macaque exposure, daily-fever pattern consistent with a 24-hour asexual erythrocytic cycle, mixed parasite stages on smear, negative routine rapid tests, and PCR confirmation together identify P. knowlesi rather than P. falciparum or vivax. The laboratory picture of hemolysis, jaundice, thrombocytopenia and rising creatinine is typical of severe knowlesi malaria which can progress quickly. Plasmodium knowlesi is a zoonotic malaria species from Southeast Asian macaques that often requires molecular testing for definitive diagnosis because its blood-stage forms can resemble other human malaria species on microscopy.

hints.text: A 68-year-old retired schoolteacher presented in late August with 3 days of fever, progressive confusion, and a new unsteady gait. On arrival temperature 38.6°C, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 142/78 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 13 for disorientation; exam notable for mild bilateral pronator drift and a coarse intention tremor on finger-to-nose testing.

She lives in a midwestern river-valley city and had no recent travel or hospital admissions. Past medical history includes hypertension and well controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin; she had a 48-hour prodrome of headache and myalgias before cognitive decline and takes no immunosuppressive drugs.

Lumbar puncture on hospital day 2: opening pressure 18 cm H2O, CSF WBC 140 × 10^6/L with 80% lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, glucose 3.5 mmol/L with serum glucose 6.8 mmol/L. CSF bacterial culture and PCR for herpes simplex and enteroviruses were negative. Peripheral white cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 6 mg/L.

MRI brain on day 2 showed bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the thalami and caudate nuclei with mild surrounding oedema and no diffusion restriction. Routine EEG demonstrated diffuse background slowing without epileptiform discharges.

Local public-health alerts reported increased mosquito activity and multiple dead corvids in her neighbourhood that week. Paired serum and CSF testing returned positive IgM directed at a mosquito-borne arbovirus; plaque reduction neutralization testing produced a fourfold higher neutralizing titre to the urban midwestern North American arbovirus than to other regional mosquito-borne viruses.

explanation: This is neuroinvasive infection with St. Louis encephalitis virus causing an acute arboviral encephalitis in an older adult. The presentation is consistent with seasonal mosquito-borne flavivirus infection with focal subcortical involvement and CSF inflammation. Late summer onset in a midwestern river valley with local mosquito activity and dead corvids, lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis and elevated protein, MRI thalamic and basal ganglia T2/FLAIR signal, and CSF and serum IgM with a fourfold higher neutralizing titre point to St. Louis encephalitis virus rather than nonarboviral or bacterial causes and distinguish it from other regional arboviruses. The paired IgM in CSF plus plaque reduction neutralization testing provides specific serologic confirmation of this flavivirus as the cause. St. Louis encephalitis virus is a mosquito transmitted flavivirus of Culex mosquitoes that causes seasonal outbreaks in North America and often produces thalamic and basal ganglia involvement with older adults at higher risk for severe neuroinvasive disease.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with 3 weeks of intense nocturnal groin itching and disturbed sleep. He reports multiple excoriations and erythematous papules across the pubic region and proximal inner thighs, temperature 36.9°C, and no urethral discharge.

He reports a new sexual partner six weeks ago and inconsistent condom use. He denies recent travel but says both he and his partner have been sharing towels and slept in the same bed the week before symptoms began.

Sexually transmitted infection screening was negative. Full blood count shows white cell count 7.4 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 0.30 × 10^9/L. Bacterial swab from an excoriated papule grew normal skin flora.

Dermatoscopy of the pubic hair-bearing skin reveals numerous small, oval, translucent eggs firmly cemented to the shafts of coarse hairs and occasional tiny, wingless insects clasping individual hairs with stout forelegs.

On return visit the patient brings a video from his partner showing several minute, broad-bodied insects clinging to pubic hair and a few similar organisms visible on the partner's eyelashes. Both partners report itching and visible 'specks' on hair.

explanation: This presentation is pubic lice infestation due to Phthirus pubis causing intense nocturnal pruritus and excoriation of pubic and perigenital skin. Transmission was likely sexual contact and possibly shared fomites between partners. The dermatoscopic and videographic findings of small broad wingless insects clinging to coarse hairs, and numerous oval translucent eggs firmly cemented to hair shafts, are diagnostic for Phthirus pubis and distinguish it from head lice and scabies which have different morphology and distributions. Involvement of eyelashes in the partner and the pattern of lesions supports close contact transmission rather than a primary dermatologic or bacterial cause. Phthirus pubis is a crab louse with stout grasping legs that preferentially infests coarse body hair and attaches nits firmly to hair shafts, and it is most commonly spread by intimate contact though fomites can also transmit it.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to outpatient clinic with a 3-month history of intermittent crampy abdominal pain, postprandial bloating, and a 5 kg unintentional weight loss. He also noted episodic perianal pruritus and occasional loose stools. On examination he was afebrile, pulse 78/min, blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, and had mild conjunctival pallor without abdominal tenderness or organomegaly.

He was born and raised in a river-valley rural district and moved to the regional city 9 months ago for work. He has no chronic illnesses and takes no immunosuppressive medications. He reports regularly attending family gatherings where home slaughter of livestock occurred and often ate meat prepared at those events, but he denies foreign travel outside the region.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 110 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 76 fL, neutrophils 4.0 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L. Routine stool bacterial culture and assays for common protozoa were negative. Faecal occult blood was intermittently positive and concentrated stool parasitology was requested.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a slender, curvilinear echogenic structure about 2–3 mm in width within the lumen of the proximal colon that changed position with patient manoeuvres. CT enterography showed no mural thickening or obstruction and no extraintestinal lesions.

Two days later the patient brought a pale segmented ribbon expelled in stool. Macroscopic length measured about 3.6 m and width approximately 3 mm. Microscopy of gravid proglottids showed more than 20 lateral uterine branches per side and the scolex lacked hooklets. He confirmed frequent consumption of lightly cooked strips of local meat at family events.

explanation: This is intestinal taeniasis due to Taenia saginata, the beef tapeworm, presenting with intermittent abdominal discomfort, weight loss and passage of long gravid proglottids. The disease reflects ingestion of undercooked beef containing cysticerci with establishment of an adult intestinal tapeworm. The epidemiology of frequent consumption of lightly cooked local meat and the expelled 3.6 meter segmented ribbon together with microscopic proglottids showing more than 20 lateral uterine branches per side and a scolex lacking hooklets identify Taenia saginata and distinguish it from Taenia solium which has fewer uterine branches and hooklets on the scolex. The imaging and intermittent fecal occult blood are compatible with a long intraluminal worm rather than invasive intestinal disease. Taenia saginata is acquired from ingesting cysticerci in undercooked beef, produces long adult worms that lack scolex hooklets, and is distinguished from T. solium by the higher number of lateral uterine branches in gravid proglottids.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with three weeks of intense itching localized to the groin and suprapubic region, worst at night. On examination he has multiple excoriated papules on the scrotum and over the pubic hair, temperature 36.8°C, and sleep disturbed by the pruritus.

He reports a new sexual partner one month ago and intermittent condom use. He denies recent travel, systemic symptoms, or previous dermatologic disease. He bathes daily and uses shared towels at the gym occasionally.

Complete blood count shows leukocytes 6.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.2 × 10^9/L. Nucleic acid amplification tests for common urethral sexually transmitted pathogens are negative. Bacterial swab of an excoriation grows mixed skin flora only.
Dermatoscopic inspection of pubic hair at 10× magnification shows small dark specks adherent at hair bases and tiny translucent ovoid structures attached along individual hair shafts.

On targeted microscopy of removed material a 1.5 to 2 mm wingless arthropod was seen clasping a pubic hair with stout grasping legs and several elongate eggs cemented to hair shafts. The patient reports his partner had similar symptoms.

explanation: This case represents pubic lice infestation with Phthirus pubis causing nocturnal groin pruritus and excoriated papules. Close sexual contact with the partner is the most likely route of transmission. The combination of intense night‑time itching in the pubic region, dermatoscopic dark specks and translucent ovoid nits attached to hair bases, and direct microscopy showing a 1.5 to 2 mm wingless arthropod with stout grasping legs is diagnostic for Phthirus pubis and excludes mites and other lice that do not cement eggs to coarse hair in the same pattern. Negative STI testing and the partner having similar symptoms support localized ectoparasitic spread rather than a systemic infection. Adult Phthirus pubis are small crab‑like lice that cling to coarse hair and deposit nits firmly cemented to shafts, and while sexual contact is the main mode of spread, contaminated bedding or towels can also transmit infestation.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the university health clinic with a 3-week history of intense pruritus localized to the groin and both axillae. She reports worse itching at night with sleep disruption, and examination shows multiple excoriated erythematous papules in the inguinal folds and scattered follicular papules in the axillae, temperature 36.8°C and otherwise well.

She is sexually active and began a relationship with a new partner about 6 weeks ago. She tried over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream and oral antihistamines without relief, denies recent travel, has no chronic immunosuppressive conditions, and the partner noted onset of similar itching around the same time.

Complete blood count shows WBC 7.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.2 × 10^9/L. Bacterial culture from excoriated lesions grew mixed skin flora. Skin scraping for mites was negative and potassium hydroxide preparation showed no fungal elements.

Dermoscopy of inguinal hair demonstrates multiple small, oval translucent adherent structures firmly attached along hair shafts, each approximately 0.5 mm, and a few dark brown particulate fragments at hair bases.

She produces a photograph from her partner taken at home showing tiny slow-moving insects clinging to groin hair, with prominent grasping forelegs visible and small whitish eggs glued to hair shafts after recent intimate skin-to-skin contact and occasional shared bedding.

explanation: This presentation is pediculosis pubis from Phthirus pubis causing intense pruritus of the groin with secondary involvement of axillary hair. The clinical picture reflects an intimate contact transmitted ectoparasitic infestation with partner concordance. Nocturnal itching localized to coarse body hair, visible slow-moving insects with prominent grasping forelegs on groin hair, firmly adherent oval nits on hair shafts on dermoscopy, and a partner with similar symptoms point to pubic lice rather than scabies or fungal folliculitis; negative skin scraping for mites and the hair-attached eggs are characteristic for Phthirus pubis. Phthirus pubis is a small crab louse that clamps to coarse hairs with specialized forelegs and spreads mainly by sexual or close personal contact, with nits glued to hair shafts that are resistant to simple washing.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male with a lower-leg blast injury presents three weeks after field debridement with increasing malodorous wound drainage, low-grade fever to 38.1 °C and progressive pain that limits weight bearing. On examination the wound margin is erythematous with purulent drainage and exposed cortical bone at the distal tibia.

He underwent multiple debridements and external fixation at a forward field surgical unit, received short courses of ceftriaxone and metronidazole there, and was evacuated to a tertiary hospital two weeks ago for repeat washouts. He is otherwise healthy and not immunosuppressed.
Leukocyte count 12.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 154 mg/L. Blood cultures remain negative. Serial wound swabs were sent and poor clinical response followed initial empiric therapy with vancomycin and cefepime.

Plain radiographs show cortical irregularity and a developing sequestrum of the distal tibia. MRI demonstrates a contiguous sinus tract to a 2 cm intramedullary abscess with marrow edema consistent with chronic osteomyelitis.

Repeated wound cultures grew a monomicrobial oxidase-negative, non-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus that grew on MacConkey agar. The isolate was resistant to ceftazidime, cefepime, gentamicin and levofloxacin and remained susceptible to ampicillin-sulbactam and colistin. Environmental swabs from the field operating tent and a contaminated saline bag yielded genetically indistinguishable isolates.

explanation: This is chronic osteomyelitis due to Acinetobacter baumannii acquired from a contaminated field surgical environment. The infection reflects a nosocomial or environment-associated wound pathogen causing persistent post-traumatic bone infection. A monomicrobial oxidase-negative, nonfermenting gram-negative coccobacillus growing on MacConkey agar in the setting of prior field care and matching environmental isolates strongly implicates Acinetobacter baumannii; the organism's characteristic resistance pattern and link to contaminated saline and the operating tent distinguish it from Pseudomonas and Enterobacteriaceae.
