He reported daily heroin use and had recently purchased a new batch of black tar heroin. He was hepatitis C positive and had taken oral flucloxacillin for presumed cellulitis without clinical improvement.

White cell count was 30.1 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 220 mg/L. Blood cultures were drawn and bedside wound swab cultures were non-diagnostic after 24 hours while he became progressively more systemically unwell.

MRI of the thigh demonstrated extensive subcutaneous and fascial plane oedema with preserved muscle enhancement and only minimal fluid signal to suggest a discrete abscess. The pattern suggested severe soft-tissue oedema rather than classical purulent necrotising infection.

He admitted injecting heroin that he believed had been cut with an unknown powder. Deep tissue and blood cultures grew large, nonmotile Gram-positive boxy rods forming non-haemolytic colonies, with a polypeptide capsule visible on special stain and typical colony morphology on blood agar.

explanation: This is injectional anthrax presenting as rapidly progressive, massive non-pitting soft tissue oedema with systemic sepsis after injection of contaminated heroin. The pattern is distinct from typical purulent cellulitis or classical necrotizing infection. The rapid onset of severe painful swelling with only a small entry wound, minimal purulence, extensive fascial and subcutaneous oedema on imaging, and cultures growing large nonmotile Gram positive boxy rods with a polypeptide capsule and nonhaemolytic colonies are diagnostic for Bacillus anthracis and separate it from staphylococcal or streptococcal cellulitis and clostridial infections which usually show different clinical features and organism characteristics. The minimal pus and disproportionate oedema are a hallmark of anthrax soft tissue infection. Injectional anthrax, linked to contaminated heroin in outbreaks, often causes massive oedema and systemic toxicity with little purulence, reflecting toxin-mediated vascular leak rather than the suppuration seen in typical bacterial soft tissue infections.

hints.text: A 52-year-old warehouse worker presents with 4 days of fever, dry cough, progressive shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. He is increasingly dyspnoeic at rest, temperature 39.2°C, blood pressure 92/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min and oxygen saturation 88% on room air.
He has well controlled hypertension and is an ex-smoker. He works in a storage facility and performs heavy lifting and occasional handling of incoming sacks but reports no known immunodeficiency.

White blood cell count 21.4 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 220 mg/L, serum lactate 3.5 mmol/L. Blood cultures flagged positive at 18 hours and Gram stain shows large, non-branching Gram-positive rods; preliminary laboratory note records the isolate as non-motile and gamma-haemolytic.
Chest radiograph and contrast CT show marked mediastinal widening with bilateral pleural effusions. There is no focal lobar consolidation to account for the effusions.

Warehouse records confirm he unloaded a shipment of raw animal hair and hides from an overseas source three weeks before symptom onset. Several other workers reported respiratory illness after the same shipment.

explanation: This presentation is inhalational anthrax due to Bacillus anthracis, causing fulminant mediastinitis with sepsis and respiratory compromise after inhalation of contaminated animal products. Marked mediastinal widening with pleural effusions and severe systemic toxicity without focal lobar consolidation, together with large non-motile, non-haemolytic Gram-positive rods and a history of exposure to raw animal hair and hides, is classic for inhalational B. anthracis rather than other Bacillus species which are usually motile and haemolytic. Bacillus anthracis has a unique poly-D-glutamic acid capsule and produces lethal and edema toxins, and spores from animal products can cause inhalational disease after a prolonged incubation.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man returns from a rural visit and presents with 6 days of severe sore throat, odynophagia and progressive neck swelling. He has high fever 39.5°C, muffled voice and difficulty swallowing saliva, and large tender lateral cervical lymph nodes on exam.
He travelled to a village where he assisted at a communal slaughter and ate meat that may have been undercooked. He has no chronic medical conditions and is HIV negative.

White blood cell count 18.0 × 10^9/L and CRP 160 mg/L. Throat swab and blood cultures after 48 hours grew large encapsulated Gram-positive bacilli; laboratory reported non-haemolytic colonies and lack of motility.

Contrast CT of the neck shows marked pharyngeal wall thickening, extensive soft tissue oedema and multiple enlarged cervical nodes with central low attenuation consistent with necrosis. Airway patency is preserved but narrowing is present at the oropharynx.

Local health authorities report that several people who shared the same communal meal developed severe gastrointestinal illness and one died. The slaughtered animal had been reported ill in the days before slaughter.

explanation: This is oropharyngeal/gastrointestinal anthrax from Bacillus anthracis presenting as severe pharyngitis with necrotic cervical lymphadenitis after ingestion or handling of infected meat. The combination of severe sore throat with pharyngeal wall thickening, necrotic cervical nodes, culture of large encapsulated non-motile, non-haemolytic Gram-positive bacilli, and a communal meal from a diseased animal points to B. anthracis rather than routine streptococcal or staphylococcal pharyngitis or other Bacillus species. Gastrointestinal and oropharyngeal anthrax result from ingestion of spores from infected animals and often produce necrotic ulceration and hemorrhagic lymphadenitis due to the bacterium's capsule and toxin-mediated tissue damage.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man who injects drugs presents with a 4-day history of rapidly progressive swelling and pain of his right thigh after an injection. He is febrile 38.6°C, hypotensive 85/55 mmHg and has tense oedema of the entire upper thigh with marked regional tender lymphadenopathy.
He injects heroin daily and reports using a recently obtained batch from a large social event. He is hepatitis C positive and not on antiviral therapy. He has no diagnosed immunodeficiency otherwise.

White blood cell count 26.0 × 10^9/L and rising creatinine 132 μmol/L. Gram stain of blood and aspirate from the site shows large Gram-positive bacilli in chains; preliminary microbiology notes describe non-motile, non-haemolytic colonies.
CT of the right thigh shows extensive deep soft tissue oedema with fluid tracking along fascial planes and no gas formation. There is no discrete encapsulated abscess amenable to simple drainage.

Local harm-reduction services reported a cluster of severe soft tissue infections linked to the same heroin supply. Several users required surgery and intensive care, and the batch was suspected to be contaminated with animal-derived cutting material.

explanation: This case represents injectional anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis presenting with rapidly progressive soft tissue edema, systemic toxicity, and deep fascial involvement after contaminated heroin use. Extensive tense swelling without gas formation, severe sepsis, large non-motile, non-haemolytic Gram-positive bacilli recovered from blood and tissue, and a cluster linked to contaminated heroin distinguish injectional B. anthracis from typical cellulitis pathogens and from gas-forming clostridial infections. Injectional anthrax produces pronounced edema from edema toxin and can present with diffuse soft tissue involvement and systemic toxicity even without a discrete abscess or gas formation.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously healthy woman presents to the emergency department with profuse vomiting and lightheadedness that began about 3 hours after a late-night meal. She reports 12 episodes of non-bloody emesis over 6 hours and crampy lower abdominal discomfort. On arrival blood pressure is 95/58 mmHg, heart rate 110 bpm, and mucous membranes are dry.

Earlier that evening she attended a small house party and ate fried rice that had been left at room temperature and reheated at home. No other attendees have sought care. She takes no regular medications and has no chronic medical problems.

Serum sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 120 μmol/L. White cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L. A sample of vomitus was sent for microbiology and a portion of the leftover rice was submitted for culture.
Abdominal radiograph shows non-specific bowel gas without obstruction or free air. Point-of-care ultrasound shows a collapsible inferior vena cava consistent with intravascular volume depletion.

Culture of the leftover rice and the vomitus grew a rapidly growing, aerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod. Mass spectrometry detected a heat-stable emetic toxin in the rice extract that matched the organism recovered from the vomitus.

explanation: This is the emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning causing rapid-onset profuse vomiting and dehydration after reheated rice ingestion. The short incubation of about three hours after reheated rice, recovery of a rapidly growing spore-forming Gram-positive rod from the food and vomitus, and detection of a heat-stable emetic toxin identify B. cereus emetic syndrome rather than diarrheal Bacillus cereus disease or other bacterial foodborne causes. The emetic syndrome is mediated by cereulide, a heat-stable cyclic peptide that resists cooking and refrigeration and triggers acute vomiting by acting on the central nervous system and mitochondria.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presents 18 hours after sustaining a penetrating eye injury while mowing the lawn. He complains of severe right eye pain and sudden loss of vision in that eye. On exam visual acuity in the right eye is hand movements only, there is conjunctival injection, a visible hypopyon, and intraocular pressure 30 mmHg.

The injury occurred when a metal fragment struck his eye and soil was visible on the wound. He rinsed briefly with tap water and delayed definitive care until the following day. He has no systemic illnesses and is not on immunosuppressive therapy.
Vitreous aspiration Gram stain shows large Gram-positive rods. Full blood count is 8.6 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 58 mg/L. Vitreous fluid and a swab of the wound are sent for culture.
B-scan ocular ultrasound demonstrates dense vitreous opacities and membrane formation consistent with endophthalmitis without retinal detachment.

Despite prompt intravitreal and systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics the eye deteriorated rapidly and required enucleation. Culture from vitreous and the contaminated soil grew a fast-growing, aerobic, motile, spore-forming beta-haemolytic Gram-positive rod that matched the wound isolate.

explanation: This presentation is fulminant post-traumatic Bacillus cereus endophthalmitis causing rapid intraocular destruction and loss of vision in the affected eye. A penetrating soil-contaminated injury with very rapid severe eye pain, hypopyon and a vitreous Gram stain showing large Gram positive rods that cultured as fast-growing, motile, spore-forming beta-hemolytic bacilli pinpoints Bacillus cereus rather than less virulent post-traumatic organisms. The environmental source and matching wound and vitreous isolates explain the aggressive course despite early broad-spectrum therapy. Bacillus cereus is an environmental spore former that can produce proteolytic toxins and enzymes that rapidly destroy intraocular tissues when soil or plant material is inoculated into the eye, producing fulminant endophthalmitis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency clinic 18 hours after sustaining a penetrating injury to his right eye while gardening. He reports worsening eye pain, marked decrease in vision, and purulent discharge; temperature 38.4°C, there is a dense hypopyon and poor pupillary reaction on examination.

He described a metal spike that had been coated in soil and plant debris, and he delayed presentation because he rinsed the eye at home. He has no prior ocular surgery, is otherwise healthy, and is not taking any immunosuppressants.
Vitreous aspiration showed 1.2 × 10^9/L white cells and Gram stain demonstrated large Gram-positive bacilli. Peripheral white cell count was 14.2 × 10^9/L and blood cultures were pending.
B-scan ultrasonography of the globe revealed dense vitreous opacities with early membrane formation and localized retinal thickening, without obvious intraocular foreign body.

Vitreous cultures grew rapidly within 18 hours on blood agar as large, flat colonies with beta-haemolysis; isolates are motile, spore-forming Gram-positive rods and show high-level resistance to penicillin but are susceptible in vitro to vancomycin and gentamicin.

explanation: This is classic Bacillus cereus post-traumatic endophthalmitis following soil-contaminated ocular penetration with a rapidly progressive inflammatory reaction. The history of gardening with a soil-coated metal spike, rapid onset severe intraocular inflammation with hypopyon, vitreous Gram stain showing large Gram positive bacilli and cultures of motile, spore-forming, beta-hemolytic colonies that are penicillin resistant strongly indicate B. cereus rather than other Gram positive rods. The organism's growth characteristics and resistance profile help distinguish it from nonmotile or nonhemolytic Bacillus species and from less aggressive flora. Bacillus cereus is typically motile, beta-hemolytic and carries beta-lactamases so it is often resistant to penicillins, which helps distinguish it from nonmotile Bacillus species such as B. anthracis.

hints.text: A 35-year-old office worker developed abrupt onset of profuse vomiting and diffuse cramping nausea two and a half hours after a shared lunch. He is afebrile, mildly tachycardic at 102/min, and reports that several colleagues who ate the same meal had similar symptoms.

He ate a warm rice and chicken salad that had been prepared the previous evening and reheated in the office kitchen, then left on a hot steam table for several hours prior to serving. He has no chronic illness and takes no regular medication.

Basic metabolic panel shows potassium 3.1 mmol/L and bicarbonate 20 mmol/L consistent with ongoing losses. Stool studies returned negative for common enteric bacterial pathogens and rotavirus antigen at 24 hours.
Abdominal radiograph and point-of-care ultrasound showed no bowel obstruction or ileus and no free intraperitoneal air.

Culture of leftover rice grew high counts of a spore-forming, motile Gram-positive rod that produced large, beta-haemolytic colonies and yielded a bioassay-positive, heat-stable emetic activity in the food extract.

explanation: This is Bacillus cereus foodborne emetic syndrome caused by ingestion of a preformed heat-stable toxin in reheated rice. The very short incubation of about two hours after reheated rice, a cluster of affected colleagues, and recovery of a spore-forming, motile gram-positive rod from the rice with a bioassay-positive heat-stable emetic activity identify B. cereus rather than enteric bacteria or viral gastroenteritis. The combination of epidemiology and toxin testing is diagnostic for the emetic form. The emetic syndrome is mediated by cereulide, a heat-stable cyclic peptide toxin produced in food that resists reheating and causes vomiting within a few hours of ingestion.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously well man presents to the emergency department with 3 hours of severe nausea and uncontrollable vomiting. He has had eight episodes of non-bloody emesis and cannot tolerate oral fluids. He is tachycardic at 110 beats per minute, blood pressure 100/68 mmHg, and has dry mucous membranes; abdominal exam is soft and non-tender.

He attended a catered party last evening and ate a portion of reheated fried rice. A colleague who ate the same dish vomited within 2 hours. He reports no diarrhoea, no recent antibiotics, and no chronic medical conditions.

WBC 9.0 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 142 g/L, creatinine 130 μmol/L consistent with mild prerenal azotaemia, potassium 3.1 mmol/L. Stool PCR for common enteropathogens was negative. Leftover rice was submitted for microbiological analysis.
Focused abdominal ultrasound shows normal bowel peristalsis and no free fluid. Plain abdominal radiograph demonstrates no obstruction or ileus.

Culture of the leftover rice yielded heavy growth of large, motile, spore-forming Gram-positive rods producing beta-haemolytic colonies. A bioassay detected a preformed heat-stable emetic toxin in the rice.

explanation: This is Bacillus cereus emetic food poisoning from reheated fried rice resulting in rapid onset severe vomiting and transient dehydration. The brief 1 to 4 hour incubation after reheated rice, multiple similarly affected diners, and heavy growth of motile, spore-forming, beta-hemolytic Gram positive rods with detection of a preformed heat-stable emetic toxin in the rice distinguish B. cereus from other causes of acute vomiting. The clinical timing and food testing are the key discriminators for the emetic form. Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and can germinate during warm storage, producing the heat-stable emetic toxin in rice and other starchy foods if they are improperly cooled or reheated.

hints.text: A 36-year-old woman presents with sudden crampy abdominal pain and profuse watery diarrhoea that began about 10 hours after a family buffet. She reports eight watery stools in 6 hours and lightheadedness on standing. Temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 100 beats per minute, and the abdomen is diffusely tender without peritoneal signs.

She ate a beef and vegetable stew that had been prepared in the morning and kept on a steam table. Several other guests developed diarrhoea 8 to 12 hours after the meal. She has no recent travel and has not taken antibiotics recently.
WBC 12.5 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance. Stool examination shows fecal leukocytes. Stool culture and analysis of the leftover stew demonstrated enterotoxin activity in culture supernatant.
Abdominal CT enterography shows mild segmental small-bowel wall thickening and mesenteric stranding consistent with enteritis. There is no abscess or obstruction.

Microbiology of the leftover stew grew heavy growth of large, motile, spore-forming Gram-positive rods that produced beta-haemolytic colonies. The culture supernatant showed heat-labile enterotoxin activity on epithelial cell assay.

explanation: Acute Bacillus cereus foodborne diarrheal illness causing enteritis with profuse watery diarrhea beginning about 10 hours after eating contaminated meat stew. The delayed 8 to 12 hour onset after a beef and vegetable stew kept warm on a steam table, fecal leukocytes and enterotoxin activity in the leftover stew, and growth of motile, spore-forming beta-hemolytic Gram-positive rods point to the B. cereus diarrheal syndrome rather than other common enteric pathogens. B. cereus has two distinct toxin syndromes: a heat-labile enterotoxin produced in the intestine that causes watery diarrhea 8 to 16 hours after ingestion and a separate heat-stable emetic toxin associated with reheated rice.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male farm worker presents 12 hours after sustaining a penetrating eye injury with a wooden splinter. He reports severe eye pain and rapidly decreasing vision. Visual acuity in the injured eye is light perception only, there is marked conjunctival injection, a visible corneal laceration, and a 2 mm hypopyon on slit lamp exam.

The injury occurred while trimming a tree and the splinter was visibly contaminated with soil. He delayed presentation for 8 hours because of distance from the clinic. He is otherwise healthy with no immunosuppression.
Vitreous aspirate Gram stain shows large Gram-positive rods. Cultures grew heavy growth within 24 hours of motile, spore-forming Gram-positive rods forming beta-haemolytic colonies on blood agar.
B-scan ocular ultrasound demonstrates dense vitreous opacities and early retinal thickening consistent with fulminant endophthalmitis. There is concern for impending retinal detachment.

The eye deteriorated rapidly despite intravitreal and systemic antimicrobial therapy and emergent vitrectomy was required. Material recovered at surgery and the removed splinter yielded identical motile, spore-forming Gram-positive rods.

explanation: Fulminant post-traumatic Bacillus cereus endophthalmitis causing rapid intraocular infection and severe vision loss after a soil-contaminated penetrating eye injury. The history of a wooden splinter contaminated with soil, very rapid deterioration despite therapy, Gram stain showing large Gram-positive rods, and identical motile spore-forming beta-hemolytic isolates from the vitreous and splinter are characteristic for B. cereus rather than other ocular pathogens. B. cereus survives in soil and on organic foreign bodies and produces potent tissue-damaging toxins that can cause rapidly progressive, necrotizing endophthalmitis after penetrating trauma.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with abrupt nausea and repetitive vomiting that began 2.5 hours after a work lunch. She reports nine episodes of non-bloody emesis, lightheadedness on standing, dry mucous membranes, and a heart rate of 112 beats per minute with blood pressure 100/60 mmHg.
She takes no regular medications, is not pregnant, has no chronic illnesses and no recent antibiotic use. She reports no fever, no abdominal pain beyond cramping, and no respiratory symptoms.
Serum sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, creatinine 118 µmol/L. White blood cell count 8.7 × 10^9/L. Blood cultures obtained on admission show no growth at 24 hours.

Plain abdominal radiograph shows normal bowel gas pattern without dilatation or free air. Focused abdominal ultrasound demonstrates normal bowel wall thickness and no evidence of obstruction or fluid collection.

Fourteen of 20 coworkers who ate the same catered rice-based dish developed profuse vomiting 2 to 4 hours after the meal. Culture of a leftover, reheated rice sample grew heavy growth of a spore-forming, aerobic Gram-positive rod producing beta-hemolytic colonies that survived the reheating process.

explanation: Bacillus cereus emetic food poisoning from reheated rice causing abrupt profuse vomiting and volume depletion within a few hours of ingestion. The classic rapid onset of vomiting 2 to 4 hours after a rice-based meal, many coworkers affected, and recovery of heat-resistant spore-forming Gram-positive rods from reheated rice indicate the preformed emetic toxin of B. cereus rather than a typical diarrheal enterotoxin-mediated infection. The emetic syndrome is caused by a heat-stable cyclic peptide toxin called cereulide that resists cooking and provokes rapid vomiting often without fever.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with a 4-day history of a skin lesion on his right forearm. He reports an initially itchy papule that became a tense vesicle and then developed into a painless black ulcer, with marked non-pitting oedema from the wrist to the proximal forearm and limited elbow flexion; temperature 37.8°C and he appears well otherwise.

He is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, and has no diabetes or known immunosuppression. He cleaned the lesion at home with an over-the-counter antiseptic and the swelling progressed despite local care; he denies systemic symptoms apart from mild malaise.
Full blood count shows WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 11.0 × 10^9/L. Gram stain of exudate from the lesion reveals large Gram-positive rods in chains; blood cultures were drawn and are pending.

Soft-tissue ultrasound of the forearm demonstrates marked subcutaneous oedema extending around the lesion without a discrete fluid collection or abscess and no evidence of deep fascial involvement. A screening chest radiograph is normal.

On further questioning he reports employment at a small tannery; five days before lesion onset he handled a recently imported bale of raw goat hides and sustained a minor puncture to the forearm. Two co-workers have had similar small skin lesions in the same interval.

explanation: Cutaneous anthrax due to Bacillus anthracis presenting as a painless black eschar with extensive surrounding non-pitting edema after contact with raw animal hides. The painless necrotic ulcer with marked non-pitting edema following handling of raw goat hides in a tannery, multiple similar cases among coworkers, and large Gram-positive rods on Gram stain are classic for B. anthracis and help distinguish it from ordinary bacterial cellulitis or abscesses. Bacillus anthracis is a nonmotile, nonhemolytic encapsulated bacillus that produces edema toxin and lethal toxin and typically causes a painless eschar with disproportionate edema at the cutaneous infection site.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to clinic with a 3-week history of productive cough, intermittent fevers and an enlarging skin lesion on his left forearm. He reports fevers to 38.5 °C, a 2 kg weight loss, and on examination has a 2.5 cm crusted, verrucous plaque over the forearm with decreased breath sounds and crackles at the right lung base.

He is previously well, takes no regular medications and has no known immunosuppression. He completed a 7-day course of oral amoxicillin prescribed for presumed bacterial bronchitis with no clinical change and has had progressive symptoms since onset.

Blood tests show WBC 12.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 9.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 78 mg/L. Sputum bacterial cultures and PCR for common respiratory viruses are negative; fungal cultures have been requested from bronchoalveolar lavage and skin biopsy.
Contrast chest CT demonstrates a 4.5 cm mass-like consolidation in the right lower lobe with air bronchograms and adjacent pleural thickening, without a simple pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy.

Histology and wet mount of the forearm biopsy show large yeast forms with thick walls and broad-based budding. Cultures from both the skin and BAL grew a slow-growing dimorphic fungus; the patient recalled clearing vegetation and disturbing riverbank soil during a community volunteer day four weeks before presentation.

explanation: This is pulmonary blastomycosis with cutaneous dissemination caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis. The combination of a mass-like right lower lobe consolidation, a verrucous crusted skin plaque, riverbank soil exposure, and tissue showing large thick-walled yeast with broad-based budding and dimorphic culture from both sites is diagnostic for Blastomyces rather than Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Cryptococcus or bacterial causes. Blastomyces is a thermally dimorphic fungus found in moist soils and riverbanks and classically produces large broad-based budding yeasts on tissue stain, often disseminating to skin and bone even in immunocompetent hosts.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department 4 hours after a late dinner with abrupt profuse vomiting and diffuse crampy abdominal pain. He is a line cook, appeared dehydrated with dry mucous membranes, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg and was afebrile.
He reported sudden onset of symptoms while at work. No chronic medical problems, not on regular medications, no recent travel, and two coworkers had milder nausea earlier in the evening.

Bloods: WBC 12.4 × 10^9/L, Na 135 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, creatinine 120 µmol/L. Microscopy of vomitus and stool showed numerous large Gram-positive rods; PCR for common viral gastroenteritis pathogens was negative.
Plain abdominal radiograph and contrast-free CT showed non-obstructive bowel gas pattern, no free air, and no focal bowel wall thickening or intra-abdominal collection.

He had reheated fried rice that had been held at room temperature overnight. Leftover rice culture grew an aerobic, motile, spore-forming, beta-haemolytic Gram-positive rod and several coworkers who ate the same dish developed profuse vomiting within 2–4 hours.

explanation: This presentation fits the emetic food poisoning syndrome caused by Bacillus cereus from reheated rice. The rapid onset of profuse vomiting within 2 to 4 hours after eating rice held at room temperature, a small outbreak among coworkers, and isolation of a motile, spore-forming, beta-hemolytic Gram-positive rod from the food all point to preformed cereulide toxin from Bacillus cereus rather than viral gastroenteritis or enterotoxin-producing gram negative bacteria. The emetic syndrome of B. cereus is mediated by a heat-stable preformed toxin called cereulide and typically presents within 1 to 6 hours after ingestion, classically linked to reheated or improperly stored rice.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a three-month history of progressive right knee swelling and nocturnal pain that has limited his ability to climb stairs. On examination the knee is tense with a 1.5 cm draining sinus medially and range of motion reduced to 20 degrees, temperature 37.8 °C.

He is a manual labourer who received a single intra-articular corticosteroid injection six weeks before the worsening of symptoms and completed a short course of oral doxycycline without benefit. He has no diabetes, no known immunodeficiency, and no prior tuberculosis.

Plain radiograph of the knee shows a lytic metaphyseal lesion with cortical irregularity and periosteal new bone formation. MRI demonstrates marrow oedema of the proximal tibia with cortical breach and a sinus tract extending to the subcutaneous tissue.

Three months earlier he spent several long weekends dredging riverbank mud and stacking rotting logs while building a private dock, and recalls heavy dust exposure during that work. A few co-workers had brief coughs that resolved without treatment.

Debridement tissue histology shows thick-walled yeasts 8–15 µm in diameter with single broad-based budding on GMS and PAS stains. Culture from the specimen incubated at 25 °C produced a mould phase after 10 days that converted to the yeast form on thermic subculture.

explanation: This is osteoarticular blastomycosis causing chronic tibial metaphyseal osteomyelitis and a draining sinus from Blastomyces dermatitidis. Chronic knee swelling with a lytic bone lesion and sinus tract after riverbank mud exposure combined with histology showing thick-walled 8–15 µm yeasts with single broad-based budding and culture demonstrating mould-to-yeast conversion confirms Blastomyces rather than bacterial osteomyelitis or other fungal pathogens. Blastomyces often causes extrapulmonary disease in bone and joints, and definitive laboratory identification relies on seeing broad-based budding yeasts in tissue and demonstrating thermal dimorphism in culture.

hints.text: A 46-year-old woman presents with an eight-week nonproductive cough, 5 kg weight loss, night sweats and a 2 cm crusted papule on her left cheek. She is afebrile in clinic and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.

She is a landscaper who smokes five cigarettes per day and reports no significant past medical history. Multiple courses of oral antibiotics have not improved symptoms and there is no history of immunosuppression or recent travel outside the region.

Chest CT shows a 3.5 cm cavitating mass in the right upper lobe with several smaller satellite nodules and mild mediastinal adenopathy. PET-CT demonstrates moderate fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the dominant lesion, raising concern for malignancy.

Two months before symptom onset she spent several days clearing brush and turning composted riverbank soil for a community riverside garden. She recalls heavy dust exposure and frequent breaks without masks.

Bronchoscopic transbronchial biopsy of the lung lesion and punch biopsy of the cheek papule both show thick-walled yeasts with single broad-based budding on silver stain. Fungal culture from both sites grew a dimorphic fungus that converted to yeast-phase on incubation at 37 °C.

explanation: This is pulmonary blastomycosis presenting as a cavitary FDG-avid lung mass with simultaneous cutaneous involvement from Blastomyces dermatitidis. The combination of a cavitating upper lobe mass with PET avidity, an associated crusted skin papule, occupational exposure to disturbed riverbank soil, and identical histology from lung and skin showing thick-walled yeasts with broad-based budding and dimorphic culture conversion distinguishes Blastomyces from malignancy and other endemic fungi. Blastomycosis can mimic lung cancer on imaging including PET scans, so tissue diagnosis demonstrating broad-based budding yeasts and culture dimorphism is key to distinguishing it from neoplasm.

hints.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks gestation presents with ten days of worsening dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain and fever to 39.0 °C. She has multiple verrucous papulonodular lesions on both forearms and is tachypnoeic with SpO2 89% on room air.
She is otherwise healthy and works as an outdoor educator who leads canoe trips for school children. She received oral amoxicillin for presumed community-acquired pneumonia without response.

Chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy alveolar consolidation, more pronounced in the right mid-lung. Obstetric ultrasound shows a viable foetus with normal heart rate and growth appropriate for gestation.

Approximately four weeks before presentation she led a canoe trip where the group repeatedly disembarked onto muddy riverbanks and handled damp logs. Several children on the trip reported brief coughs in the following week.

Bronchoalveolar lavage cytology and punch biopsy of a forearm lesion show large thick-walled yeasts with single broad-based budding on fungal stains. Culture of respiratory and skin specimens produced a mould at 25 °C that converted to yeast-phase at 37 °C.

explanation: Disseminated blastomycosis from Blastomyces dermatitidis presenting with primary pulmonary infection and cutaneous dissemination. The combination of environmental exposure to damp riverbanks and decaying wood, pulmonary consolidation with respiratory failure, verrucous papulonodular skin lesions, large thick‑walled yeasts with single broad‑based budding on histology, and thermal dimorphism with mould growth at 25 °C converting to yeast at 37 °C is diagnostic of Blastomyces rather than other fungi or bacterial pneumonias. Broad‑based budding thick‑walled yeasts on tissue stains are the classic morphologic hallmark that distinguish Blastomyces dermatitidis from other dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma and Coccidioides.

hints.text: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-month history of progressive right submandibular swelling and intermittent low-grade fevers. On examination there was a 3.5 cm firm, poorly mobile node with a small draining sinus and mild trismus on mouth opening.

She is otherwise well, takes only levothyroxine, and reports no known immunodeficiency. Two courses of oral amoxicillin failed to improve the mass; four months earlier she had an uncomplicated lower molar extraction.

Bloods: leukocytes 7.1 × 10^9/L, CRP 14 mg/L. Routine bacterial cultures of pus were sterile. Excisional lymph node histology showed granulomatous inflammation with central necrosis and scant acid-fast organisms on Ziehl-Neelsen stain.
Neck ultrasound and contrast CT demonstrated a multiloculated 3.8 cm rim-enhancing necrotic lymph node without adjacent bone involvement. Chest CT showed no pulmonary nodules or cavitation.

After three weeks on solid medium small smooth colonies produced yellow pigment on light exposure. Environmental sampling of her household well yielded an identical slow-growing acid-fast isolate, and 16S rRNA sequencing matched the species historically linked to cervicofacial lymphadenitis.

explanation: Cervicofacial nontuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis due to Mycobacterium scrofulaceum. A chronic draining submandibular lymph node with granulomatous necrosis, scant acid‑fast bacilli, sterile routine cultures, slow growth on solid medium with yellow pigment after light exposure, and matching environmental and 16S sequencing results point to a slow‑growing photochromogenic nontuberculous mycobacterium rather than Mycobacterium tuberculosis or common pyogenic organisms. M. scrofulaceum is a slow‑growing photochromogen from environmental sources that classically causes cervicofacial lymphadenitis and produces yellow colonies when exposed to light.

hints.text: A 9-year-old girl is brought to clinic with 48 hours of sore throat, odynophagia and fever to 39.0 °C; on examination she has diffuse pharyngeal erythema with blanching, finely papular sandpaper rash over the trunk sparing the area around the mouth, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy and a ‘strawberry’ appearance of the tongue.

Illness began 2 days after return from school; no recent antibiotics, no chronic medical problems, immunisations up to date. Mother reports two classmates had similar sore throats last week; no household members with chronic skin disease.

Blood count: leucocytes 13.5 ×10^9/L with neutrophil predominance; CRP 62 mg/L. Throat swab Gram stain shows gram‑positive cocci in chains; culture on blood agar produced small, completely haemolytic colonies; catalase negative.
Lateral neck radiograph performed to exclude a deep neck collection shows normal prevertebral soft tissues and no evidence of retropharyngeal or parapharyngeal abscess.

Empiric oral phenoxymethylpenicillin started; she became afebrile within 24 hours and throat pain improved rapidly. Isolate from throat culture was bacitracin‑sensitive and PYR‑positive on laboratory testing.

explanation: Acute streptococcal pharyngitis with scarlet fever features caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus). The acute onset of fever, sore throat, tender anterior cervical nodes, sandpaper rash with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, gram‑positive cocci in chains on throat culture, complete beta hemolysis, bacitracin sensitivity and PYR positivity identify S. pyogenes rather than viral causes or other streptococci. Scarlet fever results from erythrogenic exotoxins produced by toxigenic S. pyogenes strains, which are encoded on lysogenic phage and cause the characteristic diffuse sandpaper rash.

hints.text: A 23-year-old woman presents to a community clinic with 48 hours of dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She reports recent onset of visible haematuria and a new sexual partner 3 days ago. She is afebrile; examination shows suprapubic tenderness without costovertebral angle tenderness.

No prior urinary tract infections. Uses combined oral contraceptive pills and occasionally spermicidal lubricant. Not pregnant, no diabetes, no recent antibiotic exposure and no urinary instrumentation.
Point-of-care bladder scan demonstrates a post-void residual of 30 mL. Renal and pelvic ultrasound obtained to exclude calculi or obstruction are unremarkable.

Primary-care clinician prescribed a 5‑day course of oral nitrofurantoin empirically. After 72 hours she reports only partial improvement and returns because the laboratory has called with culture results.

Midstream urine: leucocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative. Microscopy—numerous leukocytes, no Gram-negative bacilli. Culture: >10^5 CFU/mL of small, pale yellow colonies; Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, urease-positive; isolate resistant to novobiocin.

explanation: Acute uncomplicated cystitis caused by Staphylococcus saprophyticus in a young sexually active woman. The clinical picture of dysuria and recent sexual activity together with a urine culture showing >10^5 CFU/mL of Gram‑positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative, urease positive and novobiocin resistant identifies S. saprophyticus and distinguishes it from coagulase‑negative staphylococci like S. epidermidis and from typical nitrite‑positive Enterobacterales. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of acute cystitis in young women and is classically differentiated in the lab by novobiocin resistance among coagulase‑negative staphylococci.

hints.text: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 24 hours of fever to 38.2 °C, rigors, acute dysuria and cloudy urine. Symptoms began shortly after removal of a short-term indwelling urinary catheter.

History of benign prostatic hyperplasia managed with an α‑blocker; recently required catheterisation for acute urinary retention while traveling. Type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin, glycaemic control reported as good. No recent antibiotic therapy prior to hospital admission.
Ultrasound bladder scan demonstrates a large post-void residual of 220 mL. Renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and no renal calculi.

The only notable exposure was an in-hospital urethral catheter in place for 36 hours; insertion was described as straightforward with a single staff operator and standard aseptic technique documented.

Urinalysis: leucocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative. Urine culture: >10^5 CFU/mL of small, white colonies. Gram stain: Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Isolate is catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, urease-positive and resistant to novobiocin.

explanation: This presentation represents an acute catheter-associated urinary tract infection due to Staphylococcus saprophyticus. The combination of frank dysuria after recent urethral catheterisation, a urine culture with >10^5 CFU/mL of small white colonies, Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase-positive and coagulase-negative, urease-positive and resistant to novobiocin specifically identifies S. saprophyticus rather than other coagulase-negative staphylococci. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a urease-positive, coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is distinguished from S. epidermidis by novobiocin resistance and is a recognized cause of urinary tract infection due to its ability to adhere to uroepithelium.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman employed at a neighborhood daycare presents with 10 days of progressive fatigue and anorexia, 4 days of dark urine and pale stools, and two days of visible jaundice. She reports mild right upper quadrant discomfort but no vomiting or abdominal distension. On exam she is afebrile at 37.8°C, icteric, and has a 2 cm tender hepatomegaly, no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.

She has no known chronic medical conditions, drinks alcohol only socially, and has never used injection drugs. Four weeks earlier several toddlers in her room had an episode of vomiting and diarrhoea while she continued routine diapering and food handling. She does not recall prior immunization against the enteric viral causes of acute hepatitis.

Blood tests show ALT 1 950 U/L, AST 920 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L, total bilirubin 150 μmol/L, INR 1.1. Full blood count is within reference range with WBC 7.8 × 10^9/L and platelets 230 × 10^9/L. Screening tests for chronic viral hepatitis markers and for autoimmune hepatitis were negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates mild hepatomegaly and homogeneous increased echogenicity. The gallbladder is normal and the common bile duct is not dilated. There are no calculi and no focal hepatic lesions.

She was managed with outpatient supportive care and hydration. Over two weeks her jaundice and transaminases began to fall and clinical recovery followed. Convalescent testing showed detectable IgM directed against the acute enterically transmitted hepatotropic virus and stool PCR detected the corresponding viral RNA, confirming an acute, self-limited infection caused by a non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus.

explanation: This is acute hepatitis A virus infection causing a self-limited icteric hepatitis. The history of recent exposure to young children with gastrointestinal illness, the abrupt onset of jaundice with very high transaminases and normal synthetic function, and confirmatory acute-phase IgM serology with stool PCR for a non-enveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus establish HAV as the cause rather than a chronic or autoimmune hepatitis. Hepatitis A virus is a non-enveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus transmitted by the fecal-oral route that usually causes an acute, self-limited hepatitis with IgM anti-HAV indicating recent infection and no chronic carrier state.

hints.text: A 72-year-old woman, 18 hours after repair of a displaced femoral neck fracture, develops sudden profuse non-bloody vomiting with lightheadedness and one episode of watery diarrhea. On arrival to the ward she is tachycardic at 112 beats/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, afebrile, with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor.

Past medical history notable for hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She ate the ward meal the evening before symptom onset and sat in the communal day room. Nursing staff report that two other postoperative patients on the same ward and one healthcare worker reported vomiting within the same 24 hour period.

Laboratory testing shows white cell count 6.4 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L, sodium 129 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L and creatinine 200 μmol/L, from a baseline of 85 μmol/L. Stool microscopy shows no fecal leukocytes. Routine stool culture and toxin testing for Clostridioides difficile are negative. A stool sample has been submitted for molecular testing.

Non-contrast abdominal CT performed to exclude postsurgical complications shows diffusely fluid-filled stomach and proximal small bowel without transition point, no free air, and no focal bowel wall enhancement to suggest ischemia.

In an outbreak investigation public health staff link 38 of 118 attendees at a hospital fundraiser to a single catered buffet item handled by a food worker who became symptomatic the morning after the event. RT-PCR performed at the public health laboratory detected a small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus in stools from the index food worker and from this patient.

explanation: This is an outbreak of acute norovirus gastroenteritis leading to profuse vomiting, dehydration and acute kidney injury from volume loss. The abrupt onset of predominant vomiting, short incubation, multiple linked cases from a shared food exposure, absence of fecal leukocytes and detection of a small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus in stool by RT-PCR together point to norovirus rather than bacterial enteritis or C. difficile. Norovirus is a highly contagious non-enveloped positive-sense RNA calicivirus that commonly causes explosive vomiting outbreaks in closed settings and is readily transmitted via contaminated food, surfaces and person-to-person contact.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents to clinic with nine months of progressive exertional dyspnea and several episodes of near-syncope. He also reports intermittent palpitations and reduced exercise tolerance; on examination blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, irregular pulse 56/min, elevated jugular venous pressure to 6 cm, displaced apical impulse and bilateral ankle pitting oedema.

He was born and raised on a small farm in rural Bolivia and emigrated to the city 28 years ago. He has no history of hypertension, diabetes, heavy alcohol use, or coronary artery disease, and no family history of cardiomyopathy.

NT-proBNP is 2 100 ng/L, high-sensitivity troponin T is within reference range, haemoglobin 128 g/L, white cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 4 mg/L. Serologic testing for common viral causes of myocarditis and HIV are negative.

Transthoracic echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with global hypokinesis, LVEF 28% and a discrete thin-walled apical aneurysm with regional akinesis. Coronary angiography demonstrates unobstructed epicardial coronary arteries.

On directed questioning he recalls childhood residence in a mud-walled home where nocturnal blood-feeding reduviid insects nested in the walls and household members reported insect bites to the face. A distant cousin who lived in the same village died in middle age of progressive heart failure.

explanation: This clinical picture is chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy due to prior Trypanosoma cruzi infection presenting with dilated cardiomyopathy, conduction disease and an apical ventricular aneurysm. The patient’s childhood residence with nocturnal reduviid insect exposure in Bolivia, the decades-long latency followed by progressive systolic heart failure with a thin-walled apical aneurysm and unobstructed coronary arteries are classic for T. cruzi cardiac disease rather than ischemic or other inflammatory cardiomyopathies. Trypanosoma cruzi infection is transmitted by triatomine insect feces and often causes chronic myocarditis that manifests years later as dilated cardiomyopathy, conduction abnormalities and characteristic left ventricular apical aneurysms.

hints.text: A 78-year-old woman resident of a long-term care facility presents with an 8-week history of progressive, severe pruritus. The itch is markedly worse at night and has caused poor sleep and repeated scratching. On examination she has widespread excoriated papules and erosions on the trunk and proximal limbs and thick, yellowish crusted plaques with fissuring on both palms. Temperature 37.2°C. She has lost 3 kg and requires help with dressing.

Medical history is notable for giant cell arteritis treated with oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for the past 3 months. Facility nursing notes record an initial treatment with a potent topical corticosteroid that gave little benefit. There is no recent travel, no new systemic antibiotics, and no known insect bites.

Full blood count shows WBC 14.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 2.9 × 10^9/L and haemoglobin 118 g/L. C-reactive protein is 18 mg/L. A superficial swab from an eroded area grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin.

Clinical photographs show confluent hyperkeratotic crusted plaques on the palmar surfaces and dorsal hands, with deep fissuring and embedded scale. Bedside dermatoscopy reveals numerous short linear whitish tracks within the thick crusts but no single focal ulcer or necrotic lesion.

Over the next two weeks several other residents and two nursing staff reported new-onset nocturnal pruritus. Direct skin scrapings of the crusted plaques examined by light microscopy demonstrated numerous oval arthropod bodies and clusters of eggs within the superficial keratin layer. Facility contacts were screened and symptomatic contacts began topical therapy.

explanation: This presentation represents crusted (Norwegian) scabies due to Sarcoptes scabiei, with a heavy mite burden causing widespread hyperkeratotic crusted plaques and pruritus in an immunosuppressed nursing home resident. The combination of long nocturnal pruritus, steroid immunosuppression, thick confluent crusted plaques with fissuring on the hands, rapid spread to multiple contacts, and light microscopy demonstrating numerous oval arthropod bodies and eggs is diagnostic of Sarcoptes scabiei rather than eczematous dermatitis or simple bacterial infection. Crusted scabies occurs in immunosuppressed or debilitated patients and contains thousands of mites within hyperkeratotic crusts, making it much more contagious and epidemiologically important than ordinary scabies.

hints.text: A 68-year-old woman resident of a long-term care facility presented with 18 hours of sudden-onset profuse non-bloody vomiting and watery diarrhoea. She reported lightheadedness and had produced very little urine over the past 12 hours. On arrival temperature 37.1°C, heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, dry mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill; abdominal examination was diffusely tender without guarding.

Medical history includes hypertension and osteoarthritis. She had a total hip arthroplasty two weeks earlier and takes a proton pump inhibitor; she denied recent antibiotics. Nursing staff noted that several other residents on the same ward developed brief vomiting overnight, but most recovered at the facility and were not febrile.

Blood tests showed white cell count 8.7 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 6 mg/L, sodium 152 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L (baseline 70 µmol/L). Stool microscopy showed no fecal leukocytes and no visible blood. Preliminary stool bacterial culture and testing for a toxin-producing enteric bacterium were negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen performed to exclude complication showed diffuse small-bowel wall thickening and fluid-filled loops consistent with enteritis, without focal collection, bowel obstruction, or ischemic change.

Infection control reported that 27 of 36 residents who attended a communal brunch developed vomiting and diarrhoea within 24–48 hours. Stool RT-PCR returned positive for a small, non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus that was included on the facility's viral gastroenteritis panel.

explanation: This is an outbreak of norovirus gastroenteritis causing acute onset vomiting and watery diarrhoea with dehydration and prerenal acute kidney injury in an elderly care facility. The very rapid onset after a communal meal, numerous simultaneous cases with predominant vomiting, absence of fecal leukocytes or blood and low inflammatory markers, plus stool RT-PCR identifying a small non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus, distinguish norovirus from bacterial enteritis. Norovirus is a highly contagious non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus that produces short incubation outbreaks in closed settings and is readily transmitted by vomitus and fecal contamination.
